1114-the-merchant-of-venice:
Antonio, a Venetian merchant, borrows from Shylock the moneylender to help his friend Bassanio woo Portia, pledging a pound of his own flesh if he fails. When his ships are lost, Shylock demands his bond, and Portia, disguised as a lawyer, saves Antonio with a quibble. William Shakespeare's comedy mixes romance and courtroom drama.

Shylock's famous plea for common humanity complicates a play long staged as simple comedy, and modern audiences weigh its mercy against its prejudice. The trial scene and the casket test still grip the stage. The play endures as both a crowd-pleaser and a hard moral problem.
1167-a-strange-disappearance:
Anna Katharine Green, America's first great woman detective writer, tells of a young woman who vanishes from a New York house, leaving only a ring and a mystery. A detective and his aide trace her through boarding houses, false names, and a villain's plot, with the law and love both in play.

Green, who wrote The Leavenworth Case, builds the puzzle with care and keeps the solution hidden to the last chapter. The novel mixes sensation with courtroom sense. It suits readers who like classic detection and the New York of the gaslight age.
1185-history-of-the-conflict-between-rel:
John William Draper was an American scientist of the nineteenth century. He argues that science and the Roman Church fought a long war. The fight ran from the fate of Greek learning to Galileo, Darwin, and the Vatican Council. He tells the tale as a clash between inquiry and dogma, with libraries burned and thinkers silenced.

Draper writes as a partisan of science, and his history is one-sided by modern lights, but it shaped a whole generation's view of faith and reason. The book's famous "conflict thesis" still frames popular debate. It serves as both history and a document of Victorian science at war.
1266-lavender-and-old-lace:
Myrtle Reed tells of two old maids, Jane and Mary, who keep a prim house full of lavender and old lace. Young lovers whose romance stirs their own buried pasts come to stay. A niece's visit, a lost letter, and a garden's secrets bring old loves back to light.

Reed writes with sentiment and a light, old-style charm, and the tale ends in weddings and reconciliations. The book was a bestseller in its day, and it suits readers who like gentle romance, pretty detail, and a story that believes in second chances.
1331-abc-s-of-science:
Charles Oliver offers an ABC of science for young or beginning readers, taking topics in alphabetical order and explaining each in short, clear terms. The book aims to make science friendly, not fearsome. Oliver's ABC form lets a child dip in anywhere, learning a new fact on each page.

Simple entries cover common facts and ideas, with examples a child can grasp. As an early popular science primer, it shows how Victorians and Edwardians tried to open the world of science to everyone. The book's simple language suits early readers, who can sound out science words with help.
1353-off-on-a-comet-a-journey-through-pl:
Jules Verne's adventure begins on the coast of Algeria, where Captain Hector Servadac and his orderly wake to find the land itself changed overnight. A comet has grazed the earth and carried away a whole region, with its people, animals, and sea, on a wild ride through planetary space.

Aboard their flying fragment, Servadac and his companions map new shores, meet other castaways, and reckon the comet's course among the planets. Verne mixes astronomy lessons with jokes, quarrels, and peril. It is a bold, cheerful voyage tale about science, courage, and life on a world adrift.
1411-domestic-peace:
Balzac sets this brief sketch on a November night in 1809, when Napoleon's empire stands at its height and Paris is full of balls and uniforms. At one such ball, a married couple's peace is tested by flirtation, gossip, and the sharp eyes of a crowded room, all within the space of a single evening.

The tale turns on glances, dances, and words that mean more than they say, and on how quickly a small slight can grow into a quarrel. Told with brisk economy, it shows Balzac's gift for reading a marriage in one social scene. It is a miniature of pride, jealousy, and forgiveness.
1447-the-illustrious-prince:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's thriller follows Hamilton Fynes, an Englishman drawn into a web of state secrets, and Penelope Morse, an American girl caught between East and West. A fatal despatch, an interrupted theatre party, and a duel of wits with a foreign agent drive the plot through London and beyond.

Oppenheim's hero moves among diplomats, inspectors, and spies, where a word out of place can cost a life or a treaty. The pace is swift and the setting is polished. It is a classic Edwardian tale of espionage, romance, and the hidden wars fought in drawing rooms.
1505-the-rape-of-lucrece:
Shakespeare's narrative poem, dedicated to the Earl of Southampton, tells of Tarquin's assault on Lucrece, the chaste wife of Collatine, and of her grief, her accusation, and her death. In long, ornate stanzas the poem dwells on Lucrece's lament, her plea to night and opportunity, and her final appeal to her husband and father.

Her death sparks the revolt that ends the Tarquins' rule in Rome, turning a private crime into a public revolution. The poem's rhetoric is rich and its feeling is intense. It is a major early Shakespeare work, prized for its verse and its tragic power.
1515-the-merchant-of-venice:
Shakespeare's Venice comedy follows Antonio, a merchant who borrows from Shylock the moneylender to help his friend Bassanio woo Portia of Belmont. Shylock's bond demands a pound of flesh if the loan fails, and when Antonio's ships are lost, the bond is called in a Venetian court.

Portia, disguised as a young lawyer, saves Antonio by the letter of the law, and the play's comedy darkens around Shylock's forced conversion. Modern readers debate its treatment of Jews with good reason. The Merchant remains a brilliant, troubling play about money, mercy, and law.
1553-the-hidden-masterpiece:
Balzac's Hidden Masterpiece opens on a cold December morning in 1612, when a poor young painter stands before a house in the Rue des Grands-Augustins in Paris. Inside, the aged master Frenhofer guards a portrait he has laboured over for ten years, a work no eye has seen and which may be genius or madness.

Two younger painters, Porbus and Poussin, bargain for a glimpse, offering a beautiful model in exchange, and the unveiling shocks them all. Balzac's tale asks what art is for, and what perfection costs. It is a profound, brief masterpiece about creation, obsession, and the limits of sight.
1614-the-golden-fleece-a-romance:
Julian Hawthorne's Golden Fleece opens with a professor on a hot veranda, thermometer at eighty-seven degrees, punching pipe ash with his finger while nature woos the soul to languor. From this languid start the romance follows the professor and his companions, including a general, through talk, travel, and romantic entanglement.

Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel, writes in a romantic manner of his own, full of colour and adventure, and the tale's energy never quite abates. The Golden Fleece is a period romance, less famous than its author's name, but full of old-fashioned charm.
170-the-haunted-hotel-a-mystery-of-moder:
A London doctor dies under strange circumstances, and his widow remarries in Venice. Wilkie Collins's Haunted Hotel, a mystery of modern Venice, follows Countess Narona to a hotel built on a palace with a dark past. Guests sense a presence, and a headless horror walks the rooms.

Collins divides the tale into four parts, moving from London salons to Venetian canals. A postscript ties the ghost to murder, opium, and a hidden crime. The novel mixes sensation fiction with a modern setting. It remains a chilling lesser-known Collins mystery.
178-confidence:
Bernard Longueville lingers in Siena, sketching and watching two women who will shape his life. Henry James's Confidence follows Bernard, his friend Gordon, and Angela Vivian through Italy and beyond. Gordon asks Bernard to judge Angela's character, a trust that tangles all three.

James studies confidence itself: who deserves it, who betrays it, and how lovers test it. Italian springs, Paris rooms, and American returns set the comedy of manners. The novel's talk and observation matter more than plot twists. It shows James refining the international theme. James's talk of trust and betrayal anticipates the subtler novels of his middle years.
1909-darwin-and-modern-science:
A. C. Seward edits Darwin and Modern Science, essays written to mark the centenary of Charles Darwin's birth and the fiftieth anniversary of the Origin of Species. Seward opens with Darwin's own account of his success, and the essays that follow take up evolution across the sciences.

A chapter citing the author's Anthropogenie and its fundamental law of organic evolution shows the volume's range: from embryology to botany, each science measuring what Darwin changed. The book is a snapshot of science in 1909, confident in Darwin and still arguing over details. It remains a useful record of how the theory looked fifty years on.
19693-fighting-for-peace:
Samuel Kinkade Cowan titled his book Fighting for Peace, a phrase that carries its own argument. The pairing was much debated after the First World War. Many writers then asked how war could serve peace. The copy preserved here wanders into a gazetteer entry on Potsdam, the Prussian court city near Berlin. That entry notes Potsdam lost its second-capital status in 1918.

Scraps like that show how war books were assembled from mixed stock. Memoir, argument, and reference matter often shared one binding. The title alone marks the book's era. After 1918, every peace plan had to answer the trenches. Cowan's title states the paradox those plans had to solve.
19709-danger-in-deep-space:
Danger in Deep Space is a young readers' space adventure in the Solar Guard setting. It opens with an order to cut thrust on the main drive rockets. A tall officer in Solar Guard uniform watches the telescanner screen. Earth grows larger across the Western Hemisphere view. The cadets of the Solar Guard face trouble far from home.

Space cadet stories taught science through cliff-hangers. Rockets, scanners, and ranks gave young readers a future navy in space. Each chapter ended on danger, as serial fiction must. This volume belongs to the Tom Corbett style of space patrol tales. It shows how the 1950s sold the space age to boys. The optimism is as period-true as the rockets.
19872-three-french-moralists-and-the-gal:
Three French Moralists and the Gallantry of France studies French character through its classic moralists. Edmund Gosse wrote it during the Great War. He takes a wartime utterance almost at random as a test. It distinguishes the Frenchman's attitude in violent action, he says. Other races are equally brave and effective, he grants. The French manner, though, has its own gallantry. Montaigne's heirs stand behind that manner.

France's moralists, La Rochefoucauld chief among them, anatomized motive and honor. Gosse, a man of letters, links their tradition to soldiers of 1914. The book is criticism serving an alliance. It tells British readers why France fights as she does. Elegant and slight, it is a wartime essay with real learning.
20066-ethics-in-service:
William Howard Taft published Ethics in Service in 1915, a set of talks on public duty. Taft had served as president and knew public life from the top. He warns against the claim that we can learn nothing from the past. Some act as if new plans could make men wholly new at once.

Taft argues that human motives stay much the same across time. Good service, then, rests on old virtues used with care. The book speaks to officials, lawyers, and citizens alike. Readers get a calm, firm case for duty, law, and steady character in public work.
20072-with-the-colors-songs-of-the-ameri:
Everard Jack Appleton published With the Colors in 1917, songs of the American service. The poems speak of the flag in plain, strong words. It is not just for show, one verse insists at the start. To those who follow it, the flag means their country, right or wrong.

Appleton wrote for troops entering the First World War. His verses aim to lift hearts and stiffen resolve in camp and field. The book holds march songs, tributes, and tales in rhyme. Readers get a sense of how Americans in 1917 sang about duty, home, and the flag they served.
20084-the-beach-of-dreams-a-romance:
H. De Vere Stacpoole wrote The Beach of Dreams, a romance of the sea. Raft, a big red-haired sailor, has used the sea since age twelve. At thirty-two, he has twenty years of ships and storms behind him. His past blurs into fo'c'sles, bar-rooms, and blazing suns.

Stacpoole knew ships and far ports, and his tales breathe salt air. On some beach of dreams, such men seek rest, love, or gold. The sea gives and takes in equal measure in his work. Readers get romance shaped by real sailor life, rough edges and all.
20156-strife-and-peace:
Strife and Peace is a novel set amid the grand mountains of Norway. A huge chain runs out toward Romsdahlshorn, whose foot meets the Atlantic. Southward it takes names like Langfjeld, Sognefjeld, Filefjeld, and Hardangerfjeld. For a hundred and fifty miles, nature shows all her grandeur there.

Such a stage suits a tale of hearts in conflict and calm. Strife and peace, as the title promises, rule lives as well as lands. Fjords, farms, and fierce weather shape the people on the page. Readers get Scandinavian romance with the land itself as a lead presence.
20192-orrain-a-romance:
S. Levett-Yeats published Orrain, a romance, in 1904, set in old France. The narrator's great-uncle, the Bishop of Seez, shapes his early fate. At that bishop's urging, his mother sends him to become a churchman. At seventeen, he is packed off to the College of Cambrai in Paris.

A church career chosen by others sets up a life of conflict. Levett-Yeats wrote tales of India and Europe with a soldier's eye. Old France gives this romance duels, courts, and faith under strain. Readers get historical romance told by a hero caught between callings.
20194-the-petticoat-commando-boer-women-:
Johanna Brandt wrote The Petticoat Commando, on Boer women in secret service. On October 11, 1899, martial law was declared across two Boer republics. The Transvaal and Orange Free State braced as British subjects fled. In Pretoria, Boers and their friends stayed to face the coming war.

For eight months, they enjoyed Boer freedom under Boer martial law. Brandt tells how women passed news, hid men, and aided the cause. Her account comes from inside that tense, watched capital city. Readers get a rare woman's view of the Boer War's hidden front.
2025-my-lady-caprice:
Jeffery Farnol tells a light romance. A young man, sent fishing by a domineering aunt, finds himself drawn into the orbit of Lisbeth, an orphan with little family but much spirit. The aunt, Lady Warburton, watches every move through her lorgnette. Farnol, a popular romancer of the early twentieth century, set many tales in a gallant, half-imagined past.

Chapters named for treasure, outlaws, moon magic, and a blasted oak carry the pair through pranks, misunderstandings, and tender scenes. Farnol writes in a warm, old-fashioned voice, and the book charms more by tone than by surprise. Lisbeth's spirit carries the romance, and Farnol lets her tease and test her lover before she trusts him.
20257-a-political-romance:
Laurence Sterne wrote A Political Romance, a sharp satire of church politics in York. Master Trim has set his heart on an old watch-coat in church. It has hung there for many years, unused and forgotten by most. Trim wants it made into a warm petticoat and a jerkin.

He begs his reverence, in a plaintive tone, to consent to the plan. Behind that small plea sit feuds over posts, pride, and petty power. Sterne, author of Tristram Shandy, turns a coat into a comic weapon. Readers get brief, biting satire from one of English prose's great wits.
20296-the-stranger-in-france:
The Stranger in France holds sketches taken on the spot during a trip there. The writer penned them at first for private reading by close friends. At their urging, he now offers them to the public eye. He names William Hayley among the friends he is proud to list.

Such travel sketches prize fresh scenes over deep research or plans. Markets, roads, inns, and manners fill the pages in quick strokes. Trips to France after war years drew keen English interest then. Readers get an early, lively set of French impressions from an English guest.
2034-waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since:
Walter Scott's first novel, published in 1814, follows Edward Waverley, a young Englishman whose wavering loyalties carry him into the Jacobite rising of 1745. Drawn to Scotland, its clans, and its cause, he must choose between romance and duty. Scott published Waverley anonymously in 1814, and its success made him the age's most famous novelist.

Scott mixes real history with invented lovers, soldiers, and lairds, and his 1829 introduction explains the sources behind the tale. Waverley founded the historical novel in English, and its influence runs through a century of fiction. The Jacobite rising of 1745 was still within living memory, which gave the novel its sharp historical edge.
2041-the-house-of-the-wolf-a-romance:
Stanley Weyman sets a romance in France at the time of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in August 1572, told as the memoir of Anne, Vicomte de Caylus. A warning cry of wolf sends the young noble on the road to Paris, where danger waits. Weyman presents the tale as a modern version of a French memoir said to date from about 1620.

Entrapped, threatened by a vidame, and caught in the Paris matins, Caylus must protect a woman and his own life through a night of slaughter. Weyman writes a swift historical adventure, full of swordplay, disguise, and Huguenot peril. The massacre of 1572 gives the romance its terror, since friends became foes in a single night in Paris.
20445-the-coast-of-chance:
The Coast of Chance is a novel of fashionable life, where wealth and glitter set the stage. Its heroine pauses before a mirror and studies her own reflection. For a moment she sees herself only as a figure in the foreground of a picture.

Through that open door, the room beyond shines with a bright, hard glitter. The image sets the book's tone: beautiful surfaces, sharp light, and feelings kept under polish. The story follows its heroine along the risky coast where chance, love, and social standing meet, in a world that watches every move.
20523-religion-and-art-in-ancient-greece:
Ernest A. Gardner's Religion and Art in Ancient Greece studies how Greek faith shaped Greek art. Gardner taught archaeology and knew the temples and statues at first hand. The book asks what worshippers believed their gods' images really were.

The better educated, Gardner writes, would regard the images as symbolic aids. They helped focus the force of religious ideas and hopes. But among common people, the images tended to be taken for much more. That gap between symbol and idol, he shows, runs through the whole story of Greek art and worship.
20566-rogers-isms-the-cowboy-philosopher:
Will Rogers published Rogers-Isms in 1919, billed as the cowboy philosopher on the peace conference. Rogers had gone to Paris where the Great War's peace was being made. He reported back in the Oklahoma drawl and rope-trick humor that made him America's favorite wit.

His jokes land on high and low alike. They say the most perfect English in this country is spoken in Sing Sing, he writes, and at the federal prison in Atlanta. They claim a knife never touched a lip there. You can see, he adds, where that junk leads you. The book mixes manners, politics, and nonsense.
20659-ministry-of-disturbance:
Ministry of Disturbance is a science fiction story of a far-future emperor and his robot court. The ruler sits in a palace where machines wait on every wish. He notices that the robot is still beside his chair, waiting for dismissal, though the audience has ended.

He orders it to summon the cleaning robots and sends it away. He could as easily have summoned them himself, or let the guards who would be in checking the rooms. The story uses that idle, absolute power to ask what an emperor is for, in a tale of revolt inside a perfect palace.
20662-the-measurement-of-intelligence:
Lewis M. Terman's The Measurement of Intelligence explains the Binet-Simon intelligence scale and its American revision, the Stanford-Binet. Terman, a Stanford psychologist, turned the French tests into standard American practice. The book lays out the scale's nature, its making, and its special character.

Its method rests on age standards. Children are tested against what most children of their age can do, across the kinds of mental functions the scale calls into play. Binet, Terman notes, would test general intelligence itself. The book founded an industry of testing, with effects on schools that are argued about still.
20764-the-death-of-saul-and-other-eisted:
Prize poems from Welsh contests fill The Death of Saul and its companion pieces. One verse urges the bard not to fear sharp critics. Grass grows strong where mowers wound it, the poem says, and so does the poet.

The eisteddfod, Wales's famed contest of song and verse, shaped this book. Bible tales, hymns, and Welsh pride meet in its pages. Saul's fall gives the lead poem a grave, grand theme. English verse here carries a Welsh heart, with music and moral weight in each piece. Readers meet a culture that crowned its poets in public contest.
2079-from-the-memoirs-of-a-minister-of-f:
Stanley Weyman presents episodes from the memoirs of a French minister. They run from the clockmaker of Poissy and a pair of tennis balls to two mayors, a lost cipher, and the governor of Gueret. Each chapter is a self-contained adventure in power. Weyman set many romances in France under Henry IV, a king he clearly admired.

The minister, writing to answer critics who say he hid his failures, tells of farming taxes, court life at Fontainebleau, and a cat and a king. Weyman writes brisk historical romance, with intrigue kept light and the past in bright colour. The minister's episodes read like short stories, so a reader can dip in at any chapter.
20796-the-colors-of-space:
Earth stuns young Bart in The Colors of Space, a 1963 tale of star travel. He first saw Earth at age twelve, thrilled to reach mankind's old home world. The first sight that met him off the starship was the Lhari spaceport.

Marion Zimmer Bradley wrote this tale of a human youth among alien Lhari. Bart must pass in a world where men are few and suspect. Mistrust, hidden plans, and first contact strains drive the plot. The book shows early Bradley at work on themes she later made famed: outsiders, identity, and the cost of belonging among strangers.
20803-the-war-of-independence:
Old textbooks, says John Fiske, never asked why men stood where they stood at Yorktown. They missed the living questions behind the War of Independence. Big histories, he adds, bury key facts in a sea of small ones.

Fiske wrote American history that plain readers could grasp and enjoy. His War of Independence sorts the cardinal facts from the minor ones with care. Causes, campaigns, and the birth of a nation take clear shape. The book reflects his gift: deep study told in brisk, lucid prose that made history a popular subject in his day.
20869-the-skylark-of-space:
Praise calls The Skylark of Space one of the great space flight tales for years to come. Love and romance weave through its science, the notices stress. E. E. Smith wrote it with Lee Hawkins Garby in the pulp dawn.

A chance lab find gives Richard Seaton a drive that leaps the stars. Foes chase his Skylark for the secret of its vast power. Smith's first novel launched the space opera age in earnest. Readers still come to it for sheer scale: worlds, fleets, and wonders piled high at breakneck speed, with heart beneath the roar.
20988-islands-of-space:
John W. Campbell took the helm of Astounding Stories in 1937 and raised science fiction's bar. Islands of Space, his own tale from 1956 in book form, shows the hand that did it. Moreau, Fuller, and a faster-than-light drive star in its pages.

Arcot's crew leaps between island universes in a ship of wild power. Black suns, alien worlds, and space battles crowd their vast tour. Campbell wrote bold, idea-rich tales before he turned famed editor. This one keeps his early fire: big physics, brave crews, and the thrill of a cosmos far larger than men had dared dream.
20995-fighting-in-france:
Earl and Leon Platt, two American boys in French khaki, rest behind the lines in Champagne. Ross Kay opens Fighting in France, from 1916, in a province already scarred by heavy war. The Big War, as all then called it, frames their service.

Kay's Fighting series followed American lads through the Great War's fronts. Trenches, raids, gas, and guns fill this French volume's brisk chapters. The Platt boys serve before America joins the war in full. Such tales let home readers track the conflict through young eyes, keen, scared, and proud by turns on foreign soil.
21086-the-penang-pirate-and-the-lost-pin:
John Conroy Hutcheson pairs two shorter sea tales in one volume. In the first, the captain of the Hankow Lin suspects pirates will attack his ship on the return voyage from Canton to Australia. He lays plans to spoil their fun, and the pirate schooner is beaten when it strikes.

The second tale follows a pinnace from HMS London, left behind off the East African coast during a hunt for slave dhows. A storm drives the boat toward Madagascar, and some of the crew are lost. The bosun, who tells the story years later in England, brings the rest ashore.
21547-the-gap-in-the-fence:
Frederica J. Turle sets The Gap in the Fence at Haver Grange, in a 1914 Sunday School Union tale. The empty Grange, long marked to let furnished, draws the local children in. They treat its mossy walks and weedy beds as their own special ground.

A queer visitor, then a little foreign girl, breaks the quiet of the place. Chapters move through fairies, gypsies on the common, and Una's pet and questions. Watson Charlton's twelve pictures show the cast, from Ruth to Tom. Sad days and a father's secret close a gentle tale of village children and their finds.
21557-newton-forster-or-the-merchant-ser:
Newton Forster serves in merchant ships, not the Royal Navy, in Captain Marryat's novel of 1832. It was Marryat's third book and his first with a merchant hero. A preface growls at kind friends whose unsought remarks cut deeper than any critic's.

Marryat knew both services, and he shows the merchantman's risks as keenly as the warship's. Trade voyages, press gangs, wrecks, and love ashore shape Newton's rise. The tale argues that courage and skill are not the navy's alone. Its two volumes move fast, in the full early Marryat manner, with storms, chases, and hard bargains throughout.
2159-a-little-tour-in-france:
Henry James tours France in this travel book, visiting towns, chateaux, and cathedrals with the eye of a novelist. James notes architecture, light, and manners, and he judges each place by what it gives the imagination. James toured France in 1882, visiting chateaux along the Loire and beyond.

The tour, an early Gutenberg file later improved in an illustrated edition, reads as James at his most observant and leisurely. Lovers of France and of James's prose will enjoy its slow, rich descriptions. His little tour, leisurely and observant, reads like a novelist's notebook, not a guidebook.
21698-rivers-of-ice:
R. M. Ballantyne brings a bluff sailor home in Rivers of Ice, opening near London Bridge at mid-century. The man looks under forty though past fifty, with a saltwater face and shaggy black hair. A huge beard and broad hat hint at the diggings and the backwoods.

A street boy nearby strikes a pose, lips pursed like a rosebud in a dirty bush. Ballantyne's eye for such figures fills the tale with London colour. The rover's return draws old shipmates and new dangers together. Glaciers give the book its title, but its heart lies in the sailor's search for home and kin.
21709-the-walrus-hunters-a-romance-of-th:
Written in 1893, near the end of R. M. Ballantyne's life, this northern tale brings two peoples together in the ice country. A Dogrib band and an Eskimo band start as wary foes, as was common between their peoples. In the course of the story, members of the two groups become close friends and work toward a shared goal.

The editor of this edition calls it one of Ballantyne's very best books, full of action from start to finish. Hunting, travel, and hard weather in the far north fill the pages. Readers also come away knowing more about how both peoples lived, hunted, and saw the world around them.
21711-the-world-of-ice:
Old sailor John Buzzby stands at the heart of this Arctic whaling tale by R. M. Ballantyne. Buzzby is a true-blue tar of the old school, first awake each morning and last asleep each night. The opening chapters look back over his long life at sea, his fights, and the strange sights he has seen.

Then a whaling cruise begins, carrying the crew into the frozen seas of the far north. Ballantyne builds the story around ice, cold, and the daily work of a whale ship. Buzzby's grit and dry talk hold the tale together. It is one of the books that made Ballantyne's name for sea and ice adventure.
21852-folklore-as-an-historical-science:
Old tales and customs are treated as real evidence of the past in George Laurence Gomme's Folklore as an Historical Science, first published in 1908. Gomme argues that folk tales, local traditions, and even traditional law preserve facts that written history missed. His frontispiece shows the Pedlar's Seat in Swaffham Church, tied to the old Pedlar of Swaffham legend. Carved figures of the pedlar and his dog back the argument in wood.

Later chapters set out materials and methods, then the mental and social conditions behind tradition. Totem customs in Australia and their faint survivals in Britain get close study. Gomme writes as a founder of folklore study in England. The book asks historians to take the people's memory seriously, and shows how.
21885-the-ruinous-face:
Helen of Troy's beauty is the wound at the center of Maurice Hewlett's The Ruinous Face, published by Harpers in 1909. Ten years into the siege, most chieftains are dead and the rest are leaden-hearted. Menelaus alone still burns: for Helen, white-bosomed darling of gods and men, and for what he has lost. The corn-lands round Troy have known no plough for a decade.

Hewlett quotes Pausanias on a sanctuary in Rhodes of Helen of the Tree. Famous paintings of Helen, by Leighton and David among them, illustrate the volume. His prose is dense, archaic, and musical, more poem than novel. It retells the oldest love-and-war story in the West through the husband left burning on the plain.
21994-prince-ricardo-of-pantouflia-being:
Prince Ricardo, son of the too-clever Prince Prigio, takes up the fairy gifts in Andrew Lang's sequel of 1893. Lang dedicates it to Guy Campbell, who wanted more of Prigio, the lady Rosalind, and the firedrake. Ricardo finds the fairy presents thrown aside in an old turret chamber: the sword of sharpness, the seven-league boots, and the wishing cap among them. With these he delivers his country from a dreadful red-hot beast, the Firedrake.

Gordon Browne drew the pictures for the Bristol edition. Lang warns new readers that Prigio's own tale explains the family: a king of Pantouflia, fairies at the christening, and one gift too many. Ricardo's adventures teach the advantages of minding one's book, as the dedication jokes. It is Lang inventing fairy tales with a scholar's glee.
22063-the-trail-of-98-a-northland-romanc:
Robert W. Service, the bard of the Yukon, published The Trail of '98, a Northland romance, in 1910. Service had lived the gold rush's aftermath as a bank clerk in Dawson. His narrator opens in bitterness: the banquet of life is spread and the wonder-workers plan their pageants, yet there is no praise in his heart. He has seen, tasted, and tried; ashes and dust are all his gain.

From that confession the tale runs back to the stampede of 1898. The Chilkoot trail, Dawson's saloons, greed, love, and ruin fill the pages. Service's ballads had made the Klondike famous; this novel gave it a full-length story. It remains his one big prose monument to the rush.
22076-the-second-chance:
Nellie L. McClung, the Canadian writer and women's rights campaigner, published The Second Chance as a sequel to Sowing Seeds in Danny. The story returns to the Perkins family on their Manitoba farm. It opens with a shock: steady Martha, the family's rock, has asked her father for two dollars in cash. Thomas Perkins cannot believe his ears, and due bills on the store will not do.

Behind Martha's small request lies a tangle of family hopes and debts. McClung writes about prairie neighbours, courtship, money troubles, and second chances earned the hard way. Her humour is warm and her moral sense firm. The novel shows the prairie West that made McClung famous across Canada.
22079-the-brighton-boys-in-the-radio-ser:
Lieutenant James R. Driscoll wrote The Brighton Boys in the Radio Service in 1918, while the Great War still raged. The Brighton Boys series followed a group of American lads through different branches of wartime service. Radio here means wireless telegraphy, the new nerve system of armies and fleets. The story opens in Philip Burton's telegraph office with a young operator at his key.

Messages, codes, and sudden orders drive the plot. The boys' skill with the wireless set puts them where the danger is thickest. Driscoll mixes real technical detail with the usual series-book escapes. In 1918 such books let boys at home imagine themselves signalling under fire.
222-the-moon-and-sixpence:
Charles Strickland, a dull London stockbroker, abandons wife and job to paint. W. Somerset Maugham's Moon and Sixpence follows Strickland to Paris garrets and a Tahitian island, where art consumes him. A narrator who knew him pieces the life together.

Strickland's cruelty to friends and family shocks, yet his pictures gain a fierce power. Maugham based him loosely on Paul Gauguin, while denying a straight portrait. The novel asks what genius costs and whether it excuses ruin. It remains Maugham's most famous study of art. Maugham's portrait of obsession still sparks argument about art and decency.
22306-human-traits-and-their-social-sign:
Human Traits and Their Social Significance takes up a large question in plain terms. Its chapter on human traits and civilization opens the argument. Two factors, the writer says, have stayed constant through all of history.

One factor is the physical order of the universe, usually called Nature. The other is man's native biological equipment, usually called human nature. Against those constants, people have slowly remade their world to fit their desires. The book weighs what fixed traits mean for society and change. It offers readers an early, clear attempt to link biology, character, and civil life.
2243-the-merchant-of-venice:
Antonio, a Venetian merchant, borrows from the moneylender Shylock to help his friend Bassanio woo the heiress Portia. The Merchant of Venice turns on Shylock's bond, which demands a pound of Antonio's flesh if the loan fails, and on Portia's famous courtroom plea for mercy. Caskets, rings, and disguises drive the romantic plot alongside the legal one.

Shakespeare gives Shylock speeches of great force, making the play troubling as well as brilliant, and its treatment of Jews has sparked debate for centuries. Portia's wit and courage carry the trial scene to a startling close. Readers meet a comedy shadowed by prejudice, law, and revenge.
22530-from-place-to-place:
From Place to Place, published in 1920 by the George H. Doran Company, collects short stories. One central figure is Tobias Dramm, known as Uncle Tobe. He serves his town in a grim and unusual profession.

Tobe suffers a chronic heart affection that pales his skin. He is neat and prim in his personal habits always. Kind to dumb animals, he is tolerant of small children too. Money matters find him most prudent, saving, almost miserly. Yet an air of loneliness hangs about the old man. By profession, Uncle Tobe is a public hangman. That contrast gives Irvin S. Cobb's tale its pathos. Readers meet a gentle man doing a terrible job.
22565-from-farm-to-fortune-or-nat-nason-:
From Farm to Fortune, dated 1905, tells Nat Nason's strange experience. Nat is a farm boy under a harsh guardian, Abner Balberry. The opening scolding shows Nat's life in a few sharp lines.

Don't talk back, Abner orders the boy roughly at supper. Take your fish to the kitchen, then get to the barnyard. You've got to help me milk tonight, he adds with threat. Don't dare go fishing again without my permission, he finishes. From such a start, Nat's rise makes its Horatio Alger shape. Farm boys in these tales win fortune by grit and luck. Readers get a classic American success story in period dress.
22651-the-unsolved-riddle-of-social-just:
The Unsolved Riddle of Social Justice is Stephen Leacock's short book on the fairness of modern economic life, issued by the John Lane Company in 1920. The catalog record credits the publisher. Leacock, famous as a humorist, wrote here in earnest about wages, prices, and the working day, in the unsettled years after the Great War.

His sample argument chases a circle: shorten hours, and the price of the thing made rises higher still. Even high wages then fail to buy it, since each gain in pay seems only to feed the rise in prices. Leacock refuses easy answers from any camp. The book remains a crisp, readable statement of questions about work and reward that are still argued today.
22684-patent-laws-of-the-republic-of-haw:
Patent Laws of the Republic of Hawaii and Rules of Practice prints the short-lived republic's patent statute and the rules for using it. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. The Republic of Hawaii lasted only from 1894 to annexation in 1898, yet it ran a full legal order, including protection for inventors.

The law requires an inventor to apply in writing to the Minister of the Interior. He must file a description of the invention and of how to make and use it. The terms must be clear, concise, and exact. For a machine, the principle and its application must be explained. Such texts matter to legal historians tracing how American-style patent law spread across the Pacific. The volume is brief, dry, and complete: a working code from a vanished state.
22695-the-comedies-of-terence:
The Comedies of Terence presents the six surviving plays of the Roman comic poet Terence, in an edition sold by Harper and Brothers. The catalog record names no translator and gives no year. Terence, a former slave who became Rome's most polished comic writer, was a school author for centuries, prized for his pure Latin and humane wit.

His plays turn on young lovers, stern fathers, clever slaves, and foundlings restored at the last moment. Generations of students met Latin itself through these comedies, whose lines passed into proverb. The text here closes with the publisher's list of works for sale by all booksellers, a reminder that classics were also merchandise. Readers get Rome's drawing-room comedy in the dress American schools once used.
22743-ruth-fielding-and-the-gypsies-or-t:
Alice B. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding and the Gypsies, or The Missing Pearl Necklace, a 1915 volume in the long-running Ruth Fielding series for girls. Ruth, an orphan making her way with grit and good humor, was among the most popular series heroines of her day, years before Nancy Drew.

The sample opens at the old Red Mill, where the steady turning of the grinding-stones sets every board and beam a-quiver. The air hangs full of grain dust and fine stone dust. Around that mill, a missing pearl necklace and a band of Gypsies set the mystery in motion. Emerson writes brisk, wholesome adventure, with Ruth's friendships carrying as much weight as the plot. The book preserves girls' series fiction in its classic form.
22754-masters-of-space:
Masters of Space is a science fiction novel of the United States space navy and a mysterious alien power in deep space. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its officers talk pure service. Captain Sawtelle is old-school Navy brass who goes strictly by the book. A junior named Jarve is warned to keep on his own side of the line.

Karns insists the line be drawn razor-sharp, just where the Advisory Board's directive places it. Next time the captain crosses it, he says, kick his face in. Such counsel promises mutiny-grade friction aboard ship. Alien masters, human pride, and naval discipline collide in the pulp manner. The book is space opera with its boots in the wardroom.
22928-sacrifice:
Stephen French Whitman's Sacrifice, published in 1922, follows a wealthy woman through the pleasure routes of Europe. Wealth, the narrator notes, neutralized every hardship of her journeys. Even her money could not buy calm seas on every crossing, or clear skies over the Riviera on every visit. In Venice at midnight, gondoliers' soft, hoarse cries made her toss on her canopied bed.

Restlessness inside luxury drives the novel. Whitman sets his heroine's unease against hotels, trains, and bright coasts, asking what her comfort costs and what it hides. The title promises a price to be paid. Readers get a polished postwar society novel, observant about money and manners, with travel writing woven through its scenes.
23128-the-king-s-esquires-or-the-jewel-o:
A youth paces at Fontainebleau in The King's Esquires, or The Jewel of France. In a duty room adjoining the king's private apartments, a youth on the edge of manhood paces without rest. Now and then he glances from the low window across the Fontainebleau forest, where kings once loved to hunt.

George Manville Fenn, to whom this tale is credited, sets his esquires in the France of Francis the First, where a jewel draws boys into court intrigue. Pageantry, duels, and forest rides fill the chapters in Fenn's practiced manner. He wrote dozens of such historical adventures for boys. The Fontainebleau opening does his scene-setting in one window, a restless boy, a hunting forest, and centuries of kings behind the glass.
23153-the-big-bounce:
Walter S. Tevis tinkers in a chem lab in The Big Bounce. The narrator's project sounds modest. He wants a better eraser, one that soaks up graphite without wearing the paper. His other drafting inventions, a dimensional curve and photosensitive ink, already worked quite well.

An eraser that absorbs graphite without wear sounds harmless, until the bounce of the title arrives. Tevis, later famous for The Hustler and The Man Who Fell to Earth, began in the science-fiction magazines with inventions like this one. Small discovery, large consequences, told dry. The drafting-table setting keeps the wonder grounded in shop talk. Readers meet a major talent at the workbench, early and already exact.
23230-boys-their-work-and-influence:
Boys: Their Work and Influence is a book of guidance for boys, about conduct at home and beyond. Its advice is direct and practical. A boy should not be a bully, either to his brothers or his sisters. He should not be selfish, or claim all he can for himself.

Share and share alike, the book insists, should be the rule. Gentleness toward girls and little ones is pressed as a duty, not a favour. Even teasing a sister when they are left alone is named as a fault to avoid. Readers get a clear picture of Victorian ideas about manly kindness.
23266-janet-s-love-and-service:
Janet's Love and Service opens on a town at night, not yet fully asleep. Boyish voices drift from garret to garret across the narrow closes. Late home-comers' footsteps pass below, marked by the watchful ear of the narrator.

The spirit of slumber, the passage says, had not yet taken hold of the place. That wakeful hush sets up Janet's story of love and service. Readers get a period tale of devotion in a close-knit town, where young lives, duty, and affection are watched over by neighbours who miss very little.
23275-the-peasant-and-the-prince:
The Peasant and the Prince opens in the French countryside near Saint-Menehould. Not all the peasants are out on the roads. In the middle of a wood, a little north of the village, a traveller in the lane toward the ponds might hear the sound of a mallet at work.

That lane runs by the grounds of the Count de D—. The hidden worker in the wood gives the tale its quiet opening note. Readers get a story of rank and lowly life in old France. A prince's world and a peasant's world sit one wood apart. A chance meeting can join them.
2364-active-service:
Stephen Crane's Active Service follows a young American correspondent in the Greco-Turkish War, chasing a runaway bride and stumbling into real danger. The novel mixes romance and war reporting, with Crane's impressionistic prose turning battles into bursts of color and confusion. The hero's quest for a woman leads him through armies and intrigue.

Crane wrote from his own experience as a war correspondent, and the book's irony cuts against its romantic plot. It is less famous than The Red Badge of Courage but shows the same eye. Readers of Crane will find a fascinating second act.
2387-the-voice:
Margaret Deland's novel The Voice follows Dr. Lavendar, a beloved small-town minister, and the people of his parish as they wrestle with faith, love, and duty. The story opens with a visit to an Irvingite household and grows into a portrait of a community's spiritual life, told with Deland's warmth and humor. The voice of the title is conscience itself, speaking in different tones to different souls.

Deland writes the Old Chester world with affection and a keen eye for human weakness. The novel is gentle, thoughtful, and deeply humane. Readers of regional American fiction will find a comforting classic.
2391-bruce:
Albert Payson Terhune's Bruce tells of another Sunnybank collie, a dog of courage and devotion whose adventures rival Lad's. The stories follow Bruce through fires, rescues, and rivalries, with Terhune's warm, anecdotal narration. The dog's loyalty to his people anchors every tale.

Like the Lad books, Bruce blends real canine behavior with sentimental heroics. Dog lovers of every age have cherished Terhune's collies. This volume stands on its own as a tribute to a great dog. Bruce, like Lad, was based on a real collie from Terhune's kennels. The stories treat Bruce as a hero in his own right, not a copy of Lad.
2414-cliges-a-romance:
Chretien de Troyes's Cliges, a twelfth century Arthurian romance, follows a Greek prince who comes to Arthur's court and falls in love with Fenice, the wife of his uncle. The poem weaves tournaments, magic potions, and a lovers' plot that tests fidelity against marriage law. Chretien, the father of Arthurian romance, writes with wit and psychological subtlety.

The romance's treatment of love and adultery looks forward to Tristan and to later courtly tales. Modern translations keep its verse energy alive. Medieval literature lovers will find a key text. Chretien also wrote the first romance of Lancelot and of Perceval.
2417-okewood-of-the-secret-service:
Valentine Williams's Okewood of the Secret Service sends a British agent into the dangers of the First World War's shadow world. Okewood, a gentleman spy, moves through enemy territory, coded messages, and narrow escapes, with Williams's brisk plotting keeping the tension high. The novel belongs to the early school of spy fiction.

Its hero is brave, resourceful, and very much of his time. Readers who enjoy vintage espionage will find a lively period thriller. The book helped set the pattern for later secret service tales. Williams himself had served as a war correspondent before writing spy fiction.
2429-lost-face:
Jack London's Lost Face collects Yukon tales of survival, betrayal, and the old trail, including the title story of a trapper who buys his life with a joke. The stories return to London's gold rush world, where cold, hunger, and greed test every character. His prose is leaner here than in his novels, and the endings cut deep.

The volume captures London's short-story genius at its most economical. Fans of the Yukon tales will find it essential. Each story stands as a small, hard gem. The title story turns on a trapper who escapes death by making his captors laugh.
2497-put-yourself-in-his-place:
Charles Reade's Put Yourself in His Place is a novel of labor and invention, in which a working man faces a trade union's violence and a factory owner's greed. The story follows its hero through strikes, sabotage, and a fight for the right to work, with Reade's reforming anger driving the plot. The title states its moral: judge a man by his place.

The novel's industrial setting and its sympathy for the skilled worker make it a document of its age. Its melodrama carries a serious argument. Readers of Victorian social fiction will find a vigorous, earnest book.
2506-the-sleeping-car-a-farce:
William D. Howells's Sleeping Car is a farce set aboard a train's sleeping car, where passengers, porters, and misunderstandings collide through the night. The comedy turns on mistaken berths, snoring neighbors, and the small humiliations of travel, with Howells's realistic dialogue keeping the farce grounded. The play is short, brisk, and very much of its railway age.

Howells, better known as a novelist, shows his comic timing here. The farce's situations still amuse travelers. Theater readers will enjoy a light, period piece. Howells wrote several one-act farces for amateur and professional stages.
2531-an-accursed-race:
Elizabeth Gaskell wrote this short essay on the Cagots, a poor outcast people of the Pyrenees valleys, the Landes near Bordeaux, and Lower Brittany. For centuries their neighbors shunned them, barred them from trades and churches, and blamed them for ills they never caused, though no one could say why the hatred began.

Gaskell draws on old accounts and on Dr. Guyon, a surgeon who studied the Cagots and found their health, looks, and habits much like anyone else's. The essay is a plain plea against prejudice, showing how a whole people can suffer for a name. It still reads as a sharp early protest against the cruelty of inherited contempt.
2552-thankful-s-inheritance:
Joseph C. Lincoln sets this novel on the sandy roads and cranberry swamps between Wellmouth Centre and East Wellmouth, on the Cape Cod coast. Thankful, a plain spoken widow, comes into an inheritance that upsets her quiet life and draws the whole town's eye.

Lincoln fills the story with Yankee talk, seaside weather, and neighbors who mean well and meddle freely. Thankful must sort out kin, suitors, and her own pride while guarding what is hers. The book charms as a comedy of village life, told in the dialect and rhythms of the Cape he knew.
2571-peace:
Aristophanes wrote this comedy in Athens during the Peloponnesian War, when citizens longed for an end to fighting. A farmer named Trygaeus, sick of war taxes and ruin, flies to heaven on a dung beetle to free the goddess Peace, whom the gods have locked away.

With the help of farmers, sailors, and workers, he hauls her out of her pit and brings her home to Greece. The play bursts with jokes about generals, arms dealers, and war profiteers. It still plays as a bold anti war farce, and a reminder that peace must be dragged out by ordinary hands.
2628-the-rise-and-progress-of-palaeontol:
Thomas Henry Huxley traces the rise of palaeontology in this second essay from Science and Hebrew Tradition. The science, he says, began when the first person who dug a shell or a bone from gravel or rock paused to wonder what the thing was.

From that puzzled moment grew a discipline joining biology and geology, reading earth's history in fossils. Huxley tells the story with clarity and pride, honoring the collectors and thinkers who built it. The essay serves as a short, lively history of a science still young in his day.
2635-clarence:
Bret Harte follows Clarence Brant in this novel, president of the Robles Land Company and husband of the rich widow of John Peyton of the Robles Ranche. Clarence mingles with a theater audience in San Francisco, admired for good looks and good fortune, then slips into winter rain with trouble on his mind.

Harte untangles land claims, old marriages, and California fortunes, with his usual blend of romance and irony. The hero must prove himself more than a lucky husband, and the ranch country tests him. The book offers Harte's late California at its most polished, with plot twists worthy of a stage melodrama.
2685-the-way-to-peace:
Margaret Deland sets this novel in Kennebunkport, Maine, in August 1910, opening with Athalia Hall pausing for breath on a steep road above a covered bridge. Dawn air, bay scent, and dew drenched leaves fill the valley as night still hangs like gauze below.

Athalia's way to peace runs through family duty, love, and the quiet choices of a New England life. Deland writes with warmth and moral clarity, in the tradition of the village novel. The book offers a gentle story of a woman finding calm after storm, and of a town that watches her.
2706-the-bravo-of-venice-a-romance:
This romance of Venice, translated from the German by M. G. Lewis, comes with an introduction on Lewis himself. Lewis professed to have translated the tale out of German, much as Horace Walpole once framed his own romance, and the introduction weighs that claim with amusement.

The story follows a bravo, a hired swordsman, through Venetian canals, conspiracies, and midnight rescues. Daggers, masks, and noble villains crowd a city built for intrigue. The book delights as gothic melodrama, and as a sample of the tales that fed English readers' hunger for Italy.
2761-benita-an-african-romance:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this African romance from a tale he believed had a foundation in fact. Some twenty five or thirty years earlier, an adventurous trader heard from natives behind Quilimane a legend of treasure buried in the sixteenth century by a party of Portuguese.

Benita, a young Englishwoman, is drawn into the search, with love, danger, and a ghostly past guiding her steps. Haggard writes with his usual African color and supernatural hints. The novel offers a treasure hunt with a heroine at its heart, and a past that refuses to stay buried.
2793-flip-a-california-romance:
Bret Harte sets this romance where the Los Gatos road climbs like a fiery rocket's trail into the blue shadows of the Coast Range. Near the summit lies an embayed terrace hedged by dwarf firs, wistfully eyed by every traveler on the heat laden road.

Flip, a wild girl of the mountains, meets a stranger from the world below, and love grows between freedom and convention. Harte writes with pastoral charm and a light hand. The novella offers a California idyll, where a girl as free as the hills must choose her road.
2911-justice:
John Galsworthy's Justice follows William Falder, a junior clerk in a solicitor's office, whose forgery and love for Ruth Honeywill lead him to prison. The cast includes the solicitors James and Walter How, their managing clerk Cokeson, a judge, advocates, a prison governor, a chaplain, a doctor, and warders. The action moves from office to courtroom to cell.

The play's force lies in its attack on a system that breaks the men it punishes, as Ruth describes a fate hanging over Falder. Her advocate asks whether her danger and unhappiness affect his balance, his control, and even his reason, and she answers yes. Justice helped change British attitudes toward solitary confinement and remains Galsworthy's most influential play.
298-the-market-place:
A financier sits alone after a sweeping victory, sensing its shapeless scale. Harold Frederic's Market-Place opens with a victor who holds his enemies at mercy and wonders when to stop grinding their faces. Vistas of conquest stretch in every direction.

The novel follows market battles, ruined rivals, and the moral weight of winning without limit. Frederic, who also wrote Theron Ware, studies ambition in the age of trusts. The opening's fascinated pain sets the book's tone. It remains a sharp novel of money and power. Frederic died before finishing his market novel's full design.
300-united-states-declaration-of-indepen:
When a people must dissolve political bands, decency requires them to declare their causes. The Declaration of Independence, adopted in 1776, opens with that claim and the self-evident truths of equality and unalienable rights. Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness head the list.

Governments derive just powers from the consent of the governed, the text argues, and a destructive government may be altered or abolished. A long list of grievances against the king follows. The Declaration founded American political language. Its sentences still anchor debates on rights. Jefferson's draft, revised by Congress, became America's founding creed.
3096-beatrice:
Haggard published this novel in 1893. Its heroine, Beatrice, moves through love, faith, and family pressure. Chapter titles trace her course: a mist wraith, a confession of faith, appointments, appeals, and a night of storm. Geoffrey, Lady Honoria, and Elizabeth circle her, arranging and resisting while she tries to choose for herself.

Vows carry the plot. What Beatrice dreamed, what she swore, and what she will stand by once the cost is plain decide everything. The scenes shift between country houses and London rooms. A woman's word becomes the hinge on which the whole story swings.
3097-the-wanderer-s-necklace:
H. Rider Haggard wrote The Wanderer's Necklace, first published in 1914, as a romance of ninth-century Byzantium, dedicated to Sir Edgar Vincent. An editor's note claims the recovery of a bygone life ending in the early ninth century, fixed by the part played by the Empress Irene. The narrator, a Northman at court, serves as captain of the Augusta's guard.

Martina's favor brings him a commission worth more than random kisses, and he reads it in a little private room on the palace wall, struggling with Greek. He is made governor of a province, and the story follows war, love, and exile across the Byzantine world. The novel shows Haggard's late taste for historical romance told through reincarnation's frame.
3187-christian-science:
Mark Twain divides this volume into two books. Book One holds matter written about four years earlier, never before published in book form, and now corrected where judgment or fact had erred. Book Two, written at the start of 1903 and new in print, presents a character portrait of Mary Baker Eddy, drawn from her own writings.

Twain's target is Christian Science as a system and Mrs Eddy as its prophet. He quotes her at length, then applies his own logic to her claims about mind, matter, and healing. The book is polemical Twain at full power: funny, relentless, and convinced that a popular faith deserves the same plain scrutiny as a popular fraud.
3281-cy-whittaker-s-place:
Joseph C Lincoln sets this Cape Cod novel around Cy Whittaker's place. The perfect boarding house opens the chapters, with the wanderer's return and a fixing over. Bailey Bangs's experiment, a front door caller, and icicles and dust follow. Captain Cy proves delinquent, and the cow lady, politics and birthdays, and a letter and a visitor keep the village busy.

A bargain off, town meeting, and the repulse lead to a clue, with Debby Beasley to the rescue and a remarkable drive. Lincoln writes his village with a native's ear for talk and a humorist's eye for pride. Boarding houses, town meetings, and plans that rarely survive contact with neighbors: Lincoln's village at ease.
3364-dr-breen-s-practice:
William D Howells published this novel in 1881 around a woman doctor at a seaside resort. A hotel perches at the edge of a bold headland, facing southeast across open sea to the horizon. Behind the hotel spreads a great woodland that, two centuries on, has reclaimed the barren shore the first Pilgrims seized from it.

The forest has begun to efface the inroads made in recent years by bold speculation, Howells adds, and the hotel stands between wild nature and new money. Dr Breen's practice, professional and personal, unfolds in that border country. A doctor claiming a man's profession, in a place still deciding what to allow: Howells's new woman at work.
3390-my-mark-twain-from-literary-friends:
William Dean Howells remembers his friend Mark Twain in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. It was in the little office of James T Fields that Howells first met his friend of now forty-four years. The office stood over the bookstore of Ticknor and Fields at 124 Tremont Street, Boston. There Howells met Samuel L Clemens, and a lifetime's friendship began.

Fields was then editor of the Atlantic Monthly, and Howells his proud and glad assistant. Howells held a pretty free hand as to manuscripts, and an unmanacled command of the magazine's slush, as he recalls it. The memoir that follows traces a friendship across a lifetime: two humorists, one from the West and one from the East, meeting in Boston and never parting in print. It is the warmest portrait Twain ever received from a fellow writer.
3391-a-belated-guest-from-literary-frien:
William Dean Howells recalls Bret Harte in this memoir essay from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. Harte's journey east from California in 1871 drew wide attention, almost like the progress of a prince. Howells met him on the Atlantic shore at the start of that fame. The essay looks back from a later time, when both men are older and the excitement has cooled.

Howells writes about memory itself as much as about Harte. He notes how pleasant it is to sit by the fire and call back names, looks, and tones from the past. Famous friends lend a glow to the person remembering them, and he basks in it for a time. The piece suits readers interested in American literary circles and in how writers remember each other.
3392-cambridge-neighbors-from-literary-f:
William Dean Howells remembers Cambridge neighbors in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. He went to make his home in Cambridge as a wholly literary spirit. In that mood, he writes, he could hardly have been more content if he had found himself in the Elysian Fields, with an agreeable eternity before him. At twenty-nine, indeed, one is practically immortal.

At that age, time had for him the effect of an eternity in which he had no pressing business. The memoir that follows peoples that eternity: Lowell, Longfellow, and the Cambridge circle, seen by a young man who had come to live among his heroes. Readers get literary Cambridge as a young writer saw it: golden, leisurely, and already passing even as he enjoyed it.
3393-studies-of-lowell-from-literary-fri:
William Dean Howells paints a personal portrait of James Russell Lowell in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. He first met Lowell at Cambridge in 1860, when he came east from the West on a literary pilgrimage, and he knew him better after moving to Cambridge in 1866. The essay covers the years up to Lowell's death, with long evenings of talk in Lowell's study.

Howells warns that his Lowell may look different from other people's Lowell. He records suppers at two o'clock dinners, walks, and conversation rather than a formal life history. The value lies in the close view of a leading American poet, critic, and diplomat as a friend saw him, warm, talkative, and deeply rooted in New England.
3395-oliver-wendell-holmes-from-literary:
William Dean Howells remembers Oliver Wendell Holmes as a Boston figure of a special kind in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. Where writers elsewhere might rise from obscure corners, Boston writers, Howells says, often came from known families and dropped, as he puts it, from the skies. Holmes belonged to that settled world of law, science, and letters.

The essay sketches Holmes in conversation and in society rather than listing his books. Readers meet a witty doctor and poet who could hold a table with talk and verse. Howells also notes how Boston itself was changing, so the piece doubles as a farewell to an older city where a few families set the tone for its culture.
3397-roundabout-to-boston-from-literary-:
William Dean Howells traces his own road to Boston in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. As a young man he lived in Venice with literary hopes always present, sending poems to magazines across the English speaking world. Nearly all came back, except three pieces that editors kept, one for the Atlantic Monthly, one for Harper's, and one for the New York Ledger.

Defeat in verse pushed him toward prose, since he had to earn a living by some sort of writing. The essay follows that slow turn from rejected poet to working editor and novelist. It gives an honest view of a writing life: repeated failure, small breaks, and the steady work that finally builds a career.
3461-essays-on-life-art-and-science:
Samuel Butler, author of Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, gathers essays on life, art, and science in this volume, edited by R A Streatfeild and published in 1908. Contents include Ramblings in Cheapside, How to Make the Best of Life, Art in the Valley of Saas, Thought and Language, and The Deadlock in Darwinism. One essay defends a Holbein drawing in Basle against those who call it a copy.

Butler writes as an independent thinker, willing to quarrel with experts on art and on evolution alike. His essays mix travel notes, family sketches, and sharp argument, all in a clear, personal voice. The book suits readers who like Victorian essayists who think aloud and who refuse to follow fashion in science or art.
3487-augustus-does-his-bit-a-true-to-lif:
George Bernard Shaw writes a wartime farce about Lord Augustus Highcastle, a well meaning aristocrat who believes he is serving his country. The play was first performed by the Stage Society at the Court Theatre in London on January 21, 1917. Shaw's preface recalls his own trip toward the Flanders front, where passports and official favors made him think about how war work really gets done.

Augustus blunders through offices and interviews, convinced that his rank and good intentions count as duty. Shaw turns the comedy on patriotic cant and on the gap between talk and action. The piece is short, brisk, and very much of its moment, suiting readers who like Shaw's satire at its most direct.
3489-fabre-poet-of-science:
Georges Victor Legros writes a life of Jean Henri Fabre, the French naturalist famous for his studies of insects. The book draws on Fabre's letters and on long conversations with the author, and Fabre himself allowed his friend to speak for him in many passages. Legros calls the early chapters a biography of a solitary student, tracing how a poor boy became a scientist.

The life follows Fabre from school teaching to his field in Provence, where he watched wasps, beetles, and spiders for decades. Legros shows both the man and the method: patient watching, simple tools, and writing that made insects vivid to ordinary readers. The book suits nature lovers and anyone who wants to know the person behind the Souvenirs entomologiques.
3641-who-cares-a-story-of-adolescence:
Cosmo Hamilton writes a story of adolescence about a boy and a girl, as his own playful preface puts it. When asked what the novel is about, Hamilton answers only that it is about a boy and a girl. When asked if they marry or are happy, he replies that all love stories are happy if it is love. The book itself follows a girl who writes that she is miserable, with nothing to live for, since her mother married again.

Hamilton treats the pains of growing up with sympathy and humor: first love, family change, and the feeling that adults do not understand. The novel suits young readers and adults who remember adolescence, in a light, early twentieth century romance that takes young feeling seriously.
3676-the-firefly-of-france:
Marion Polk Angellotti writes a wartime melodrama set in France during the First World War. The story begins, as the author puts it, in the restaurant of the Hotel St Ives, an odd spot to serve as stage wings for a melodrama pure and simple. The narrator has survived shell fragments taken by a French surgeon from his head, and a British officer at Gibraltar who held up his papers.

The tale follows spies, soldiers, and a heroine called the Firefly through dangers in wartime France. Angellotti writes with speed and color, in the style of 1918 adventure fiction. The book suits readers who enjoy old fashioned war melodrama, with narrow escapes and a brave woman at its center.
3708-an-introduction-to-chemical-science:
Williams wrote this school textbook to lead beginners into chemistry through plain facts and homely tests rather than through theory alone. It works through the common elements and their compounds, with gases, acids, salts, and metals each getting clear notes on how they act and how they can be shown at a bench. Short trials let a pupil see a result with his own eyes before the book states the rule behind it.

The middle chapters give plain safety sense as well, such as testing well air with a lowered candle before going down, since heavy gases can pool unseen and kill. Mine damp, volcanic fumes, and the gases of breath all serve as live cases. The book still reads as a window on how science was taught a century ago, when care, sight, and smell stood beside the balance and the flask.
372-prince-otto-a-romance:
Robert Louis Stevenson sets this romance in the small German state of Grunewald, ruled by the dreamy Prince Otto. Otto, more poet than king, drifts from his clever wife Seraphina and falls into plots hatched by courtiers and rebels. A count, a farmer's daughter, and a band of schemers push the small court toward crisis.

Stevenson mixes court jest with real peril, as Otto must at last act like a prince or lose all. The prose is light and often comic, yet the stakes grow grave. The book shows an early Stevenson trying a new form, with wit, grace, and a keen eye for weak rulers and strong wills.
3745-the-road-to-providence:
Maria Thompson Daviess gathers a set of linked village tales around the doctors Mayberry, mother and son, of a Tennessee country town. Mother Mayberry rules the kitchen with a light hand for risen biscuits. Her son Tom runs the barn and the practice, and together they answer every call on the road to Providence. A singer lady, a peony girl, a little raven with a covered dish, and a tag gang of small helpers fill the chapters.

The stories run warm and funny, with deacons, sick neighbors, and weddings crowding the lanes. Daviess writes in local speech that stays readable, and her people help one another without fuss. Readers who like gentle community tales will find Providence a pleasant place to linger, with kindness treated as a daily habit rather than a sermon.
3758-the-gates-of-chance:
Van Tassel Sutphen links a dozen New York tales of chance, crime, and detection through a single curious thread. The book opens with a visiting card thrust into the narrator's hand, penciled with an evening call at a Madison Avenue address for a Mr Esper Indiman. From there the stories turn on a red duchess, a queen of spades, and an opal button. A brass baggage check and an upset apple cart join them, each a small object with a large secret.

One later tale finds a woman's rooms ransacked by detectives and a letter hidden beyond their reach, while her captors rage at their failure. Sutphen writes with a light, urbane touch, and New York's streets, clubs, and crossings frame every puzzle. Readers who like short mysteries with wit will find a book best taken one gate at a time.
3759-fridthjof-s-saga-a-norse-romance:
Esaias Tegner retells an old Norse saga as a verse romance, and this translation by Thomas and Martha Holcomb keeps its ringing dialogue. Fridthjof, a hero of the north, loves Ingeborg, the sister of kings, but her brothers Helge and Halfdan bar the match. Honor binds him to a quest for gold owed to King Angantyr, and the lovers must part while Fridthjof sails to claim it.

The middle scenes stage the parting as a debate, with Ingeborg pleading and Fridthjof vowing to return, sword at his side. Sea voyages, kings' halls, and pagan rites fill the later cantos. Readers who enjoy epic love stories will find a tale of loyalty tested by pride, exile, and the hard code of the Viking age.
380-weir-of-hermiston-an-unfinished-roma:
Robert Louis Stevenson left this Scots romance unfinished at his death, and it stands as his most praised late work. Archie Weir, son of a harsh hanging judge, is cast out to a lonely farm after defying his father. There he meets Kirstie, and love, pride, and family doom tangle in the moorland parish.

An opening note sets the scene at a cairn where a Covenanter once died, a place of old blood and silence. Stevenson's Scots prose is stern and musical, full of moor, mist, and law. Though cut short, the book grips as a tragedy of father and son, and of a young man caught between duty and heart.
384-the-lost-prince:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells of Marco Loristan, a boy in dingy London who plays at a secret game with his father. Marco and his friend, known as the Rat, drill a squad of boys, guard a lamp signal, and dream of Samavia, a far land torn by strife. What starts as play turns grave when Marco must carry a real message across Europe.

Burnett mixes adventure with a warm tale of loyalty, as two boys brave cities, frontiers, and spies. The lost prince of the title proves closer than Marco dreams. The book charms young readers with its blend of game and peril, and its faith in honor kept in secret.
393-the-blue-lagoon-a-romance:
H. de Vere Stacpoole follows two castaway children, Dick and Emmeline, in this island romance. A shipwreck strands them on a lush Pacific isle, where they grow from children to young lovers with no guide but nature. A kind old sailor dies early, leaving them to learn food, shelter, and love on their own.

Later books bring a schooner, a child, a cyclone, and a strange visitor who seeks the isle's secret. Stacpoole writes the lagoon in rich, bright detail, from reefs to palms. The novel charms as a tale of innocence and first love, set far from all laws but those of sea and sky.
4005-herb-of-grace:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's novel opens its eighth chapter on a studio door left ajar, where a sweet voice sings a lullaby and a young man named Malcolm peeps in rather than knock. A line from Maeterlinck sets the theme: wherever you travel, you meet only yourself on the road of fate.

The story follows Malcolm and the household around him through love, work, and the search for a worthy life. Carey writes in the plain, kindly manner of late Victorian family fiction, with studios, gardens, and sickrooms as its stages. Readers who like gentle domestic novels with a moral thread will find the book easy company and quietly moving.
4041-conscience:
A short story about conscience follows George, a man who keeps brushing aside small warnings that a duty is not a trifle. Weeks pass with no acknowledgment of money owed, until a letter asks Mr. Pratt to pay two hundred dollars promised some weeks before to Mr. Reid.

Reid is a poor man, to whom two hundred dollars is an important sum, and the delay weighs on him. The tale turns on how a small evasion grows into a moral debt, and on what it costs to set it right. Readers who like plain moral fiction will find a brief, pointed story about promises, money, and the voice that will not stay quiet.
4062-gaston-de-latour-an-unfinished-roma:
Walter Pater left Gaston de Latour unfinished, a romance of French youth in the age before revolution. A general of 1789 judged French young men of quality behindhand, urging king and nobles to care better for their education.

Enlightened and moral, Pater's young clerics and nobles might know their duties and abuse their privileges less. The fragment follows Gaston through courts, churches, and salons, with Pater's fine prose lending grace to every scene. Readers who love Pater will value this beautiful torso, even where the story breaks off. Its grace survives in every scene.
4090-from-ritual-to-romance:
Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romance argues that the Grail legends grew from old vegetation rites. A chapter on Tammuz and Adonis looks at how Aryan forefathers faced nature's ordered sequence of birth, growth, and decay.

By prayer and supplication, they threw themselves on the mercy of the god who granted or withheld rain and river water. Weston links dying gods, seasonal rites, and the Grail quest into one bold thesis, famous for shaping T. S. Eliot's Waste Land. Readers interested in myth, folklore, and the roots of romance will find a short, provocative classic.
4251-the-life-everlasting-a-reality-of-r:
Marie Corelli subtitled this romance A Reality of Romance. Its contents trace a heroine's spiritual story from a fairy ship and an angel of a dream. They pass through memories, visions, and doubtful destiny. Later chapters bring a love-letter and the house of Aselzion. A magic book, dreams within a dream, and a passage into the light follow.

Corelli opens with a prologue on voices in the wilderness. Such voices, she warns, are usually ignored. Her heroine then learns by vision and love rather than by argument. Readers who enjoy Corelli's blend of romance and mysticism will find her mix here: a love story used for ideas about the soul and life after death.
4296-friarswood-post-office:
Charlotte M. Yonge, author of The Heir of Redclyffe, wrote this children's story around a village post office at Friarswood. It opens with Ellen King scolding a tramp who has come in to buy a loaf, calling him a pig and wishing the police would keep such folk out of decent shops. The scene sets the village tone at once.

Later chapters bring hay-making, a new friend, and the strange lad of the first chapter into the children's circle. Yonge writes for young readers with a moral eye, showing kindness tested by prejudice. The 1909 edition carries colored pictures by A. G. Walker, and the tale suits family reading aloud.
4365-supplementary-copyright-statutes-us:
The United States Copyright Office put these extra notes on the law in one text. The items include paper 3 on notice, paper 15 on renewal, and paper 15t on longer terms. Paper 22 covers high points of changes in the law from the Uruguay Round trade deal. The WIPO treaty on the rights of authors is in the set as well.

The opening note explains that a notice is no longer needed under the law of the United States, though it is often of use. Each paper is set off by a page break and a row of stars. The set serves as a shelf of notes for readers who need the office's own words on notice, renewal, and treaty changes.
4598-the-story-of-creation-as-told-by-th:
T. S. Ackland, once a fellow of Clare College, Cambridge, and vicar of Wold Newton, wrote this short book to set the Bible's creation story beside modern science. He argues that the creation history is not a side piece of revelation. It is its foundation, since it states how man stands to God as maker, and to the world made for his home.
