Many readers, he notes, claim that this history cannot be squared with facts science has found.

Five chapters state the case, then face difficulties in geology, astronomy, and physiology, before closing with science as a help to interpretation. Ackland writes for readers troubled by the clash, and he tries to show a way through it without giving up either faith or fact. The book suits anyone curious about Victorian attempts to read Genesis and science together, in plain, earnest argument.
4633-philip-steele-of-the-royal-northwes:
James Oliver Curwood published Philip Steele of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police in 1911. It opens with a chapter called The Hyacinth Letter, in which Steele writes a letter he may never mail, to lessen his loneliness in a log cabin. Outside, wind drives sleet off the lake like shot, surf beats driftwood on the rocks, and tall pines whistle and wail as they straighten after each blast. Tomorrow, he expects, will be a desolation of snow.

Later chapters bring a face out of the night, a skull and a flirtation, and a silken scarf. They go on to a beauty-proof hero, a pretty face followed, a tragedy in the cabin, another letter, a trail taken up, and Isobel's disappearance. Readers get a brisk northern romance of police work, love, and pursuit, with Curwood's snow, storm, and lonely cabins, and a hero who must choose between duty and desire.
4638-california-1849-1913-or-the-ramblin:
L. H. Woolley, member of the Society of California Pioneers and of the Vigilance Committee of 1856, wrote California 1849 to 1913. Its subtitle is The Rambling Sketches and Experiences of Sixty-four Years' Residence in that State. He says the year 1849 holds a thrilling sensation for a California pioneer, not felt by those who came later. His purpose is not publication or praise, but to deposit his recollections in his descendants' archives.

He left the Green Mountains of Vermont to cross the plains to California, the El Dorado, the Land of Gold. By way of Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Independence, Missouri, he joined the first mule train of Turner, Allen and Company's Pioneer Line. Forty wagons, a hundred and fifty mules, and about a hundred and fifty passengers left the frontier on May 14, 1849. Readers get a pioneer's plain, first-hand California memoir.
4703-flower-of-the-north-a-modern-romanc:
James Oliver Curwood published Flower of the North in January 1912. He dedicates it to his comrades of the great northern wilderness, and especially to the Jeanne d'Arcambal who will find herself the heroine. The book opens with Gregson praising a girl's hair, eyes, and colour to Whittemore, swearing she was the handsomest girl he ever saw. She would not give him a look, yet he plans a full-page cover of her for Burke's magazine.

From that artist's admiration grows a modern northern romance of love, pursuit, and wilderness adventure. Curwood writes the long silent trail, its joys and hardships, with his usual vigour. Readers get a popular Canadian romance, with a strong heroine at its centre, for readers who like love stories set against snow, rivers, and rough frontier life.
4770-work-a-story-of-experience:
Louisa May Alcott, author of Little Women and Little Men, published Work, A Story of Experience, at Boston in 1901. A Carlyle epigraph stands at its head: endless significance lies in work, and in idleness alone lies perpetual despair. Alcott dedicates the book to her mother, whose life has been a long labour of love, inscribed gratefully by her daughter.

Contents follow Christie through servant, actress, governess, companion, and seamstress, then through the mist and a cure for despair. Mrs. Wilkins's minister, beginning again, a strawberry bed, and Christie's gala lead to waking up, which, midsummer, and mustered in. The colonel, sunrise, little heart's-ease, and at forty close the tale. Illustrations by Sol Eytinge show Christie, Aunt Betsey, Mrs. Stuart, Hepsey, and others. Readers get Alcott's novel of a woman earning her living, with work as dignity and hope.
4792-in-freedom-s-cause-a-story-of-walla:
G. A. Henty wrote In Freedom's Cause, A Story of Wallace and Bruce, addressing his readers as dear lads. He says few figures in history have exercised such influence on events as William Wallace and Robert Bruce. He argues Scotland owed her freedom from English domination to their courage, perseverance, and energy.

Contents follow the story from Glen Cairn and Leaving Home, through Sir William Wallace, the capture of Lanark, and a treacherous plot. The Barns of Ayr and a cave in the Pentlands follow. The council at Stirling, the battle of Stirling Bridge, and the battle of Falkirk lead to Robert the Bruce, the battle of Methven, and the castle of Dunstaffnage. Colonsay, a mission to Ireland, and an Irish rising carry the war on, through the siege of Aberfilly, a prisoner, and an escape from Berwick, to Edinburgh and Bannockburn. Readers get a stirring boys' adventure.
4923-king-midas-a-romance:
Upton Sinclair's King Midas opens in the two joyful months of spring when poets have the woods and waters to themselves, from the first bloodroot to the fading wild rose. In that season the romance follows a young poet and the wealthy world that tempts him, recasting the Midas legend for a modern age.

Gold, art, and love contend in the story, as the hero learns what his gift is worth when money enters the bargain. Sinclair, better known for social protest, here works in a lyrical register. Readers get an early Sinclair romance about the price of turning everything one touches into wealth, and what remains when the glitter fades.
493-falk-a-reminiscence:
Joseph Conrad tells of Falk, a taciturn tug captain with a dark past, in this sea story framed as a dinner tale. Seamen dining near the Thames recall a voyage where Falk's ship, food, and love for a captain's niece tangle in strange ways. Hunger, pride, and a long-kept secret drive the plot.

Conrad writes in his slow, probing style, letting the tale unfold through talk and memory. Falk proves both brutal and tender, a man shaped by the sea's harsh law. The story stands as a compact study of desire, guilt, and the bonds that hold seamen together.
4956-the-duke-s-prize-a-story-of-art-and:
A story of art and heart in Florence, this romance invites the reader on a fancy voyage across the Mediterranean to the Tyrrhenian Sea. The narrator touches at Gibraltar, Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily, praising storied shores that have been the poet's theme for ages, before reaching the city of art itself.

In Florence, love and ambition contend around a duke's prize, as artists and lovers weigh beauty against reward. The catalog entry is anonymous. Readers get a romantic tale of Italy, lush with scenery and sentiment, in the tradition of novels that treat Florence as a school for the heart.
496-the-little-lame-prince:
Dinah Maria Craik, writing as Miss Mulock, tells fairy tales for children in this volume, opening with the title story. A beautiful prince of Nomansland, lame from a cruel trick, learns courage and kindness in a lonely tower. His godmother's gifts, a magic cloak, and a traveling cloak help him see his kingdom truly.

Shorter tales follow: an invisible prince, Prince Cherry, the prince with the nose, the frog prince, and Clever Alice. Craik writes with warmth and plain moral sense, never scolding. The book endures as a gentle classic, where a lame child's heart proves stronger than his legs.
4995-true-to-himself-or-roger-strong-s-s:
Roger Strong, a boy paid by Widow Canby to watch her orchard, catches Duncan Woodward stealing pears in this boys' story of standing one's ground. Duncan, only son of Darbyville's wealthiest merchant, sneers at Roger and tells him to mind his own business, but Roger answers that minding the orchard is exactly his business.

The trouble in the orchard opens a tale of Roger's struggle for place, as a poor boy defends honest work against rich-boy bullying. Authorship is left unnamed in the record. Readers get a straightforward moral adventure, where courage means doing a small job well even when the thief outranks you.
5062-the-winds-of-chance:
Rex Beach's Winds of Chance opens with a shell game on a folding table, as Mr. Lucky Broad places a crisp ten-dollar bill in an eager palm and proclaims that the gentleman wins and the gambler loses. The eye is quicker than the hand, he announces, while he rearranges three worn walnut shells and conceals a pellet the size of a small pill beneath one.

The pellet's erratic comings and goings summon and hold his audience, and the novel follows fortune's winds from such small cons to larger gambles in the North. Beach writes the gambling frontier with gusto. Readers get an adventure of chance and character, where luck itself becomes a player in the story.
5170-poems-of-experience:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's Poems of Experience gathers lyrics on faith, endurance, womanhood, and the life of feeling. The collection was published in London in 1917 after several reprintings. Its contents run from The Empty Bowl and Keep Going to a Battle Hymn of the Women, a tribute to the actress Clara Morris. Poems on science, the city, and the voice of the voiceless appear among them.

Wilcox writes in plain, musical verse meant to comfort and encourage, and her popularity rested on that direct appeal. Readers will find here the optimistic, moral voice that made her one of the most widely read poets of her day, in poems short enough to read aloud and remember.
530-driven-from-home-or-carl-crawford-s-:
Horatio Alger Jr. follows Carl Crawford, a boy of sixteen driven from home with thirty-seven cents, in this success tale. Carl, son of a doctor at Edgewood Center, trudges country roads with a gripsack, a good education, and strong arms. Resting under an oak, he plans how to conquer fortune alone.

Alger tracks Carl through jobs, rivals, and kind strangers, praising pluck and honesty at each turn. The boy's fine handkerchief hints at a better past he will not beg upon. Young readers will find a brisk, hopeful story where a cast-out lad earns his way by work.
5338-mark-rutherford-s-deliverance:
Mark Rutherford's Deliverance, in the 1913 Hodder and Stoughton edition, follows a man's struggle toward intellectual and spiritual freedom. Its chapters run from newspapers and M'Kay, through Miss Leroy and a necessary development, to Drury Lane theology, holidays. The Latin-titled chapters come next, on the way through the sea and the scourge that shall not approach the tabernacle.

Rutherford, the pen name of William Hale White, writes a semi-autobiographical novel of doubt, work, and deliverance from narrow creeds. The book offers readers a quiet, thoughtful portrait of a Victorian mind finding its own faith, in prose that values honesty above display.
547-baron-trigault-s-vengeance:
Émile Gaboriau continues the tale of Pascal Ferailleur in this sequel to The Count's Millions. Ruined by slander and a vile plot, Pascal hides under a false name, torn between despair and a hunger for vengeance. Baron Trigault, a schemer of wealth and wit, offers him a path to strike back at his foes.

Gaboriau writes with melodramatic sweep, from Paris salons to hidden lodgings. Love for Marguerite, lost by a fatal letter, drives Pascal's grief. The novel charms fans of French sensation fiction, where honor, fortune, and revenge tangle in a web of plots.
5726-the-fairy-land-of-science:
Arabella Buckley invites young readers into science through a series of lectures called The Fairy Land of Science. Lectures begin with how to enter, use, and enjoy this fairy land. They then turn to sunbeams and their work. Later lectures treat the aerial ocean in which we live, a drop of water on its travels, and water and ice as two great sculptors. Voices of nature and further wonders follow.

Buckley treats science as a story to be watched, not a list to be memorized, using fairy language to make physics and natural history vivid. Readers learn how sunlight, air, and water shape the world, through images a child can picture. The book suits families, teachers, and young readers who enjoy Victorian science writing that still feels fresh in its wonder.
5825-the-courage-of-the-commonplace:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews explores everyday courage in The Courage of the Commonplace, opening at Durfee with a girl and her chaperon in a desirable second-story window looking down on a tree. Brant, a senior and a Bones man, holds a leading place in college life, and the story that follows tests what courage means outside battlefields and grand crises. Ordinary choices, loyalties, and losses carry the weight.

You get a quiet, earnest tale of young people learning to face disappointment, duty, and love without applause. Andrews writes with warmth and moral clarity, favoring character over sensation. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century stories of college and home life, and anyone who believes the hardest bravery is often the least noticed.
5998-waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since:
Walter Scott's Waverley, or 'Tis Sixty Years Since, appears in an 1893 edition with an introductory essay and notes by Andrew Lang. Scott dedicates the collection to the king, hoping his fiction may amuse hours of relaxation or relieve languor, pain, and anxiety, and so add in small measure to his people's happiness.

The chapter list points to Rose Bradwardine and her father, repentance and reconciliation, a more rational day, Waverley domesticated at Tully-Veolan, and a creagh, or cattle raid. The tale sets a young visitor among Scottish lairds and their households. Its subtitle marks the distance of sixty years from the events.
601-the-monk-a-romance:
Matthew Gregory Lewis tells a gothic tale of lust, sorcery, and damnation in this notorious romance. Ambrosio, a famed Madrid monk, falls from pride to sin through Matilda, a demon in disguise, while Agnes and Raymond suffer in dungeons and convents. Ghosts, magic, and a bleeding nun haunt the plot.

Lewis writes with lurid, fevered prose, mixing horror with moral warning. A preface in Horatian verse jokes about the book's fate in shops. The novel shocked readers of its day and endures as a landmark of gothic fiction, where a holy man learns that pride opens every door to hell.
6011-the-little-lady-of-lagunitas-a-fran:
Richard Henry Savage sets a Franco-Californian romance against gold-rush California, forty-two years after its golden star first glittered in the American flag. The state's checkered history begins with the rush of 1848 and 1849, when cosmopolitan free lances swept away defenceless Indians and robbed the great native families, the old Dons.

Mad riot and wild excess marked those early days, while society slowly made headway against motley adventurers. Savage places his little lady of Lagunitas amid French and Californian claims, treasure, and old family pride. The introduction frames a romance of a land still settling its fortunes.
6078-louis-agassiz-his-life-and-correspo:
Elizabeth Cary Agassiz edits the life and correspondence of Louis Agassiz, warning that the book lacks both full personal narrative and close scientific analysis. She began by weaving facts, letters, and journals into narrative to prevent the loss of scattered papers of unquestionable family value.

As the work grew, she felt the story of an intellectual life marked by rare coherence and unity of aim might serve a wider use, as stimulus and encouragement to others. The European part of Agassiz's life is little known in America, she notes, while its American period is unfamiliar in his native land. The volume bridges both.
6115-the-long-chance:
Peter B. Kyne opens The Long Chance at sunrise on the Colorado desert, as dawn's advance guard pauses on snow-encrusted peaks before charging down to rout night's lingering shadows. A coyote leaves his den in the tumbled malpais, points his nose skyward, and voices his morning salute to the Hosts of Light.

Far in the waste, seven dark objects detach from shadows and crawl toward the mountains. Like motes in a beam of light, they come out of the Land of Nowhere where greasewood meets horizon blue. A desert call for help, three fires by night and three smoke columns by day, signals the tale. Kyne writes desert adventure with a wide eye.
6139-marvels-of-modern-science:
Paul Severing, with Theodore Waters as editor, looks at wonders of new science in 1910. He starts with flying craft: early tries, the airship, Langley's tests, the Wright brothers, Count Zeppelin, and new flight records. Wireless follows, with the Marconi set and waves through the air.

Radium, moving pictures, tall towers, ocean liners, and strange new plants fill out the book. Parts deal with Becquerel and the Curies, Edison's film viewer, Lumiere's camera, New York's tall blocks, and huge ships. Severing writes for plain readers keen to grasp new powers. He keeps each marvel short, clear, and full of zest.
6242-parables-of-a-province:
Bronzed pipes hang on the side of Margath Mountain, tall and perfect, said to be the organ played by some son of God when the world was young. Hepnon the cripple says golden music still comes from them at sunrise and sunset, and no one laughs, for his dark, dreaming eyes make belief easy. Nine parables follow, among them a guardian of the fire, the singing of bees, a white omen, sojourners, and a forge in the valley.

Parker writes these as short fables of a province, each built on a single image and a moral felt rather than preached. A tent of purple mat, a little city, and a place called Peradventure give the set its range, from wonder to warning. The prose is simple and pictorial, inviting the reader to hear, as Hepnon does, music in ordinary hills and work.
6304-without-prejudice:
Israel Zangwill gathers miscellaneous work from four or five years, mostly first printed month by month in the Pall Mall Magazine, under the title Without Prejudice. He has left out pieces that hang on other people's books, plays, or pictures, seeking unity in a set that can stand alone. The result is a book of essays and fancies, witty, digressive, and fond of turning a familiar saying on its head.

Topsy turveydom is not so easy as it looks, he warns, for the trouble lies not in inverting but in finding what to invert. Language holds ancient saws, but only a real humourist knows which can stand on its head without falling. Zangwill writes on travel, morals, and modern life with the same trick, asking readers to feel their surroundings again rather than rush past them. The essays reward a slow, amused attention.
6308-hypatia-or-new-foes-with-an-old-fac:
Charles Kingsley warns that a picture of fifth century life must hold much that will pain readers. The age was hideous and great at once, with virtues and vices side by side in the same persons. In the year 413, some three hundred miles above Alexandria, the young monk Philammon sits on inland cliffs above a desert waste. Tombs, quarries, and half cut pillars sink in sand around him.

Alexandria itself is the novel's stage. Hypatia, philosopher and counsellor to Orestes, faces Cyril and his followers. Goths move through a dying world, and Miriam, a day in the city, and a new Diogenes fill the chapters. Philammon, watching monks curse Hypatia and Orestes to torment, asks whether these are ministers of a gospel. Kingsley writes a fierce, learned romance of faith, philosophy, and power in a city losing its old gods.
6333-public-speaking-principles-and-prac:
Irvah Lester Winter designs this book for students of public speaking, to set out the main principles of effective platform delivery and to supply ample material for practice. It can form a separate course or a training thread inside another course, and it honours Charles William Eliot, who taught by example the power and beauty of perfected speech. Principles come first, then practice in many forms.

Part one discusses tone, vocal flexibility, word formation, emphasis, feeling, picture, and action, then platform practice: formal address, public lecture, informal discussion, argument, after dinner speech, and occasional poem. Part two gives practice pieces, from Burns and Byron to Shakespeare, Kipling, and Patrick Henry's Virginia speech of March 1775. Winter writes a working textbook, not a theory alone.
6351-red-fleece:
Will Levington Comfort, writing in 1915 and dedicating his book to the hour when troops turn home, opens with a woman and an exile. Peter Mowbray first sees her at the corner of Palace Square nearest the river, not a starer by nature, his mind on work and the trickery of events. Their eyes meet full and leisurely, in a stirring silence before self and convention rush in, and he hopes at first for some flaw to break the pull.

The chapters that follow are stark in title: a court of execution, a house of amputations, a bomb proof pit, a skylight prison, a field of helmets, and the green of cedars. Russian soldiers lie unticketed, faces bandaged beyond recognition. Mowbray searches cots until midnight, asking what they do with the dead. Comfort writes war as exile and witness, where a glance in a square leads to a field hospital.
6364-warlock-o-glenwarlock-a-homely-roma:
George MacDonald opens in a rough, wild glen on the debatable land between highlands and lowlands, where the family took its name and gave back much of its character. Most folk speak both Scotch and Gaelic, mingling Celt and Teuton traits. The country grows more barley than wheat, more oats than barley, more heather than oats, more boulders than trees, and more snow than anything, thinly peopled, with bare hills and small streams.

Castle Warlock, the kitchen, the drawing room, an afternoon sleep, and the school lead the chapters, with Grannie's cottage, dreams, home, and a student to follow. Cosmo conducts a lady to the stable in the frontispiece, and a laird, Lady Joan, and Lord Mergwain, fond of his bottle after luncheon and dinner, fill the house. MacDonald writes a homely Scottish romance of glen, kin, and quiet wonder.
6523-the-post-office:
Tagore sets his play in the house of Madhav, who has taken in a sick child named Amal and now dreads the day the boy must leave. A doctor speaks in old medical terms of bile and palsy, while Madhav begs for plain help, not book lore. Around them gather a flower girl, a dairyman, a watchman, and a gaffer, each with a small part in Amal's narrow world.

Amal waits for the king's letter, and the post office itself becomes his hope of a wider life beyond his room. The play is short and tender, with speech that feels both simple and full of meaning. The Post Office asks what a child can dream when illness keeps him indoors, and how grown folk answer that dream.
6948-the-secrets-of-the-german-war-offic:
Armgaard Karl Graves, with Edward Lyell Fox, claims to open the secrets of the German war office on the eve of general war. The publishers note the manuscript had lain in their hands since June 1, 1914, before Europe was plunged into war, and they date their foreword August 7, 1914. Graves needs no further praise of his sources, they say, since the chapters speak for themselves.

The first chapter tells how he became a secret agent. It opens on June 12, 1913, when a Liberal member rose in the Commons to demand the secrets of the strange case of Armgaard Graves. From Parliament to the hidden world of spies, the book mixes memoir with exposure. It reads as a wartime warning from a man who says he saw the machine from inside.
7054-world-s-best-histories-volume-7-fra:
Guizot and Madame Guizot de Witt carry their history of France into volume seven, covering the Consulate through the Russian campaign. Chapter seven treats the Consulate of 1799 to 1804, chapter eight glory and success, chapter nine glory and conquest, and chapter ten the home government. Glory and illusions in Spain and Austria, the divorce of 1809 to 1810, and glory and madness in Russia close the volume.

The narrative opens with France, after ten years of shocks and sufferings, seeking a free and regular government to secure rights gained through tribulation. Monarchy overthrown, republic tried, and three constitutions accepted and rejected, France still struggled single handed with Europe. Only this seventh volume's span is described here.
7119-the-dolliver-romance:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Dolliver Romance survives in only three chapters the author lived to complete, with scenes and fragments beside them. An introductory note explains the romance would have given final form to his elixir of life theme, for which Septimius Felton was the preliminary study. Having abandoned that study and seemingly forsaken the scheme in 1862, Hawthorne renewed his meditation the following year.

The plan having developed to his satisfaction, he accepted a publisher's proposal. The story would begin as a serial in the Atlantic Monthly for January 1864, his first attempt at such a mode of publication. The fragments that remain hint at an old man, a draught of life, and a house haunted by time. The volume preserves a great romance cut short by death.
7183-doctor-grimshawe-s-secret-a-romance:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Doctor Grimshawe's Secret reaches print through his son Julian, who edited it with a preface and notes and dedicated it to George Parsons Lathrop and his wife. Julian admits the risk plainly. Friends of great writers often drag raw work from a closed desk with more zeal than judgment. A man in life tends to publish only what readers have time to read.

That honest preface frames a posthumous romance, offered not as a finished masterpiece but as a tale worth seeing in the light. Hawthorne's name promises his usual mix of mystery and moral shadow, and the editor's care lets readers judge the fragment for themselves. The book stands as a glimpse of work left behind at his death.
7227-mornings-in-florence:
John Ruskin begins his mornings in Florence at Santa Croce with a firm guide's claim: if a visitor cares for old art at all, Giotto is the artist to examine first. Florence, Giotto's birthplace, shows his pictures of every date and kind, from small panels to vast walls, painted from age twelve to sixty. Assisi and Padua hold fine work too, but neither gives the full range.

Ruskin urges the reader to start with Giotto at his best time and in his best kind, then to learn the city through his eyes. The book walks church by church, turning looking into a discipline of attention. Ruskin's prose mixes art history with direct address, as if a learned friend stood beside the reader in the chapel.
7259-shock-and-awe-achieving-rapid-domin:
Harlan K. Ullman and James P. Wade wrote Shock and Awe: Achieving Rapid Dominance for the National Defense University Press in December 1996, with L. A. Bud Edney, Fred M. Franks, Charles A. Horner, Jonathan T. Howe, and Keith Brendley. The text came from the Command and Control Research Program of the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense, where its pages counted as public information.

Its title names a doctrine of swift, overwhelming effect, meant to shape an enemy's will as much as his forces. The book lays out that idea in the sober prose of military study, with a foreword and prologue framing the argument. Readers meet a 1990s attempt to rethink dominance for a new age of war.
7278-horace:
Theodore Martin's Horace, from the series Ancient Classics for English Readers, follows the Roman poet from birth and schooling. His campaign with Brutus and Cassius, return to Rome after Philippi, and early poems come next. Martin then traces the introduction to Maecenas, the journey to Brundusium, the first book of Satires, and the gift of the Sabine farm.

Life in Rome, Horace's famous bore, and the extravagance of Roman dinners fill the later chapters. Love poetry, poems to friends, praise of contentment, astrology, views of a hereafter, and relations with Maecenas close the survey. Martin writes a clear, friendly life for English readers, letting Horace's wit and moderation shine through.
7307-the-precipice:
Ivan Goncharov's Precipice, Obryv in Russian, comes here in a condensed translation whose translator is not named. Its preface places Goncharov among the great circle of Russian writers gathered around the Contemporary under Nekrasov, beside Turgenev, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Belinsky, and Herzen. Goncharov, born in 1812, lacked the marked genius of the first three, the preface admits, yet his obscurity in the West owes something to a life with nothing sensational in it.

The novel's power lies instead in steady observation of Russian society, love, and moral falling, told without scandal's aid. This condensed text keeps the story's shape while shortening its long, patient scenes. Readers get a classic Russian novel in a briefer, still serious form.
7364-the-albany-depot-a-farce:
W. D. Howells's Albany Depot, a farce published by Harper and Brothers in 1892, sets its action in Boston, in a ladies' room opening from a public hall. Mrs Edward Roberts enters laden with proofs of an afternoon's shopping and studies the room with a searching gaze. She finds suburban shoppers on settees with bags and packages, old ladies in rocking chairs, and a chorewoman mopping the floor between expresses.

Mrs Roberts appeals to the chorewoman in anxiety: her husband was to meet her at ten minutes past three, yet no gentlemen seem to be about. From that small missed meeting Howells spins a one-act comedy of manners, misunderstandings, and married talk. The farce plays briskly, all talk and timing in a waiting room.
787-the-man-between-an-international-rom:
Amelia E. Barr wrote this international romance about Ethel Rawdon, a woman whose beginnings the narrator admits she hardly knows, so many picturesque ways are there to introduce her. The tale moves between America and Europe, where love, money, and social rank pull Ethel in different directions, and a man stands between her and her hopes.

Barr writes with warmth for her heroine and a keen eye for society on both sides of the Atlantic. The novel turns on choices of heart against duty, and on the price of a good match. It offers readers a late Victorian romance of manners, full of feeling and of the world its people inhabit.
809-holiday-romance:
Charles Dickens wrote this holiday tale in four parts, each told as if by a child. William Tinkling, Esq., edits the set, and insists that the opening part is real, not made up, so that readers may grasp how the rest came to be written. The children tell of holidays, games, and small romances in their own voices.

Dickens delights in the child's view, with its solemn rules and sudden fancies. The tale is slight, but it shows his humour and his ear for young speech. It makes a pleasant short read, and a window on how Victorians imagined childhood at play, told by children who take their games very seriously indeed.
82-ivanhoe-a-romance:
Norman lords rule Saxon England a generation after the Conquest, and old hatreds still burn. Sir Walter Scott's Ivanhoe follows the disinherited knight Wilfred back from the Crusades in disguise. Tournaments, sieges, and outlaws fill his road home.

Ivanhoe aids King Richard, loves Rowena, and rescues the Jewish healer Rebecca from trial and fire. Robin Hood's men, the Black Knight, and the Templar Bois-Guilbert cross his path. Scott's notes defend his blend of history and romance. The novel set the pattern for historical fiction in English. Scott's blend of Saxon and Norman conflict gave later writers a model for national romance.
854-a-woman-of-no-importance:
Oscar Wilde wrote this play about Mrs Arbuthnot, a woman of no importance in society's eyes, and her son Gerald, a young man on the rise. Lord Illingworth, a witty lord, offers Gerald a post, while Mrs Arbuthnot hides a secret: Illingworth is Gerald's father, who wronged her years before. The truth breaks at a country house party.

Wilde's epigrams glitter, but the play turns grave on a mother's shame and a son's choice. First printed in 1894, it shows Wilde moving from pure comedy to moral drama. The play remains a powerful study of respectability, sin, and the price women paid for men's freedom.
880-my-garden-acquaintance:
James Russell Lowell wrote this essay about the birds and beasts that visit his garden, and about the books that taught him to love them. White's Natural History of Selborne, a delight of his father's library, gains charm with years, he says, as he learns the simple secret of its pleasure: close, patient looking.

Lowell sketches robins, orioles, and other garden guests with humour and learning, mixing natural history with personal memory. His prose is urbane and witty, the essayist at ease outdoors. The piece delights readers who keep a garden, or who love the older tradition of nature writing that watches before it judges.
935-self-help-with-illustrations-of-cond:
Samuel Smiles wrote this famous Victorian manual on self-help, with illustrations of conduct and perseverance drawn from the lives of engineers, inventors, and workers. He quotes Shakespeare's counsel to be true to oneself, and he argues that character, thrift, and steady work matter more than birth or luck.

Smiles tells brief lives of men who rose by effort, from humble shops to great works, and he draws lessons for readers of every rank. His tone is earnest and encouraging, the voice of an age that believed in improvement. The book shaped a generation, and it remains a landmark of Victorian moral advice.
943-misalliance:
George Bernard Shaw wrote this play about misalliance, the clash of classes, ages, and ideas in love and marriage. A country house party brings together parents, daughters, and suitors, and Shaw turns their talk into a debate on sex, money, and freedom, with his usual wit and paradox.

Shaw's characters argue as much as they love, and the play's famous long scenes test every convention of courtship. His spelling and punctuation, kept as printed, add to the flavour. Misalliance is a bold Shaw comedy of ideas, for readers who like theatre that thinks as hard as it laughs.
978-the-yates-pride-a-romance:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman wrote this romance about the Yates pride, centred on Miss Eudora Yates's old colonial mansion. Opposite stands the perky modern Queen Anne house of Mrs. Joseph Glynn, whose daughter Ethel and unmarried sister Miss Julia Esterbrook love to talk, with many callers who like to hear them.

Freeman sets old pride against new money in a New England village, where family honour, gossip, and love pull neighbours apart and together. Her prose is precise and wry, with a keen ear for village talk. The novel charms readers who enjoy Freeman's New England, where a house can hold a family's whole history.
993-malbone-an-oldport-romance:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson wrote this romance of Oldport, the old name for Newport, Rhode Island, opening with a prelude and an arrival. A drive on the avenue, Aunt Jane, and the place aux dames follow, as the tale moves through society, love, and loss in a seaside town of old families and new wealth.

Higginson quotes Thoreau on nature, asking what nature is unless an eventful human life passes within her, with joys and sorrows as its lights and shadows. His romance is gentle and literary, full of sea air and social nuance. Malbone delights readers who love old Newport, in a tale of manners and feeling.
a-belated-guest-from-literary-friends-an:
William Dean Howells reflects on the duty of remembering the famous dead in this piece from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. It is sweet at first, he writes, to sit by the fire and recall names, looks, and tones from the past, and to bask in borrowed lustre. But the pleasure soon becomes a grievous obligation, as more shades claim their right to be recorded.

The belated guest of the title arrives late into Howells's company of memories and takes his place among the writers of an older America. Howells sketches talk, character, and the rooms where they met. The essay is literary history at its most personal: a survivor's roll call, written with affection and honest weariness.
a-little-tour-in-france:
Henry James travels slowly through provincial France and writes up what he sees, town by town. He begins at Tours and works through the Loire country of châteaux, then east and south to places such as Bourges, Dijon, and the old cities of Provence. Churches, inns, markets, and pictures fill his days.

James writes as a novelist on holiday: alert to manners, light, and the look of streets, and honest about boredom where he finds it. He compares French provincial life with American and English life as he goes. The sketches are easy in manner and exact in observation, and they have kept their place as a model of the literary travel book.
a-sicilian-romance:
Ann Radcliffe wrote A Sicilian Romance as a Gothic tale framed by a found manuscript. A traveller admires the ruined castle of the house of Mazzini on Sicily's northern shore, and a friar offers him the family's recorded history. tells how luxury and vice brought that proud house to ruin and left its halls to decay.

Inside the manuscript, the Marquis Mazzini rules his castle and daughters with cold cruelty, and lights and sounds in the deserted apartments suggest someone hidden within the walls. Julia Mazzini's flight from a forced marriage drives escapes, pursuits, and revelations through convents, wild country, and dungeons. Radcliffe helped fix the Gothic recipe here: terror, scenery, and a heroine in flight.
a-strange-disappearance:
Anna Katharine Green's detective novel begins with talk of sudden vanishings, as the young detective called Q agrees to tell of a case stranger than most. A young woman has disappeared from a wealthy New York house, and no one will speak plainly about her. The contents promise clues in a bureau drawer, a bit of calico, and a few golden hairs.

Twenty chapters follow secrets in Mr. Blake's studio, a house at a crossroads, a capture, and long explanations. Green builds her case from small physical clues and guarded witnesses. The book is an early American detective story, written before the genre had settled rules, and it shows her gift for slow, careful suspense.
a-woman-of-no-importance:
Oscar Wilde's play is set at Hunstanton Chase, a grand country house, and later at Mrs. Arbuthnot's home nearby. The title page of this edition notes the play was first printed in 1894. Guests trade sharp talk about love, marriage, and society while a hidden past waits offstage. Mrs. Arbuthnot guards a secret about her son Gerald and the man who fathered him.

Across four acts the polite party talk gives way to shame, anger, and a hard choice about honor. Wilde mixes bright epigrams with a serious attack on rules that punish women and excuse men. The ending refuses the easy pardon the guilty man expects.
abc-s-of-science:
Charles A. Oliver sets out the ABCs of science for young readers in a short primer of seven chapters. The book aims at beginners, as its title promises, and keeps its lessons elementary. It introduces the natural world in simple language meant for a child's first steps into the subject.

Short chapters and plain statements carry the whole design; there is no apparatus of notes or advanced terms. The primer belongs to the age when popular science for children was a new and hopeful trade. Read today, it shows what a young reader of its time was first taught about how nature works, and in what order the wonders were presented.
active-service:
Stephen Crane sends a young newspaper correspondent, Rufus Coleman, to cover the war between Greece and Turkey. Crane had reported that war himself, and the novel draws on what he saw: bad information, big talk in cafés, and danger that arrives without ceremony. Coleman goes to rescue a professor and his family caught behind the lines.

The rescue becomes a tangle of cavalry, comic opera soldiers, and a running fight. Through it Coleman carries on a duel of pride with the professor's daughter. He had once courted her at home. Crane writes the war scenes with his sharp, color-struck eye and treats the heroics with irony. The book mixes adventure, satire of journalism, and a hard-edged romance.
an-accursed-race:
An Accursed Race is a short work of 1855 by Elizabeth Gaskell, the English novelist often called Mrs Gaskell. Gaskell, best known for her novels of Victorian society and her biography of Charlotte Brontë, here turns to a stranger subject: the Cagots, a despised outcast people of the Pyrenees region. Her piece asks how a whole group could be shunned for centuries without a known crime.

She gathers what history and tradition say about the Cagots: the separate church doors, the badges, and the bans forced on them. The tale is part inquiry and part protest against inherited prejudice. It shows Gaskell's social conscience at work on a small, haunting case, told with the detailed sympathy that marks her fiction.
an-introduction-to-chemical-science:
Rufus P. Williams wrote his textbook, by his preface, for the average high school: simple, practical, experimental, and inductive, not a cyclopaedia of chemical information. He insists above all on the writing of equations, which he calls the multum in parvo, the much in little, of chemical knowledge. Questions throughout call attention to what the pupil should observe.

Chapters build from first experiments with air, water, and common substances toward the metals, acids, and organic compounds, with an appendix of tables. The book belongs to the years when laboratory teaching was entering American schools. Its clarity and order made it a standard beginner's chemistry for a generation of students.
augustus-does-his-bit-a-true-to-life-far:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Augustus Does His Bit, a short wartime farce first performed by the Stage Society at London's Court Theatre in January 1917. Shaw's preface explains his target: Lord Augustus Highcastle, a well-meaning, patriotic, self-important official. Government departments, Shaw says, knew the type well. Their problem was winning the war with Augustus on their backs.

Lord Augustus sits in a mayor's parlor in Little Pifflington, heels on the writing table, reading his newspaper. A mysterious lady visitor and a clerk named Horatio Floyd Beamish draw him into intrigue over secret papers. Augustus blunders through every exchange while believing himself indispensable. Shaw squeezes a full satire of wartime bureaucracy into one act. Readers get a brief, sharp comedy about the governing class at its most confidently useless.
baron-trigault-s-vengeance: Baron Trigault's Vengeance, Émile Gaboriau's novel. The baron's revenge. This book preserves that tale. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. Its place in history is secure. Kept for study. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
beatrice: Beatrice, H, rider haggard's novel, her tale. This book preserves that romance. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
benita-an-african-romance:
H. Rider Haggard sets this African romance on the Zambesi, where Portuguese gold was said to lie hidden for three centuries. His opening note describes treasure buried near the river in the sixteenth century and a child's trance account that led searchers to a few old coins. The heroine, Benita Clifford, has the gift that found them: under mesmeric trance she sees what is hidden.

Benita sails for Africa on the mail steamer Zanzibar, and the story follows her into the ruins where the gold is believed to rest. Haggard mixes treasure hunting with her unwilling second sight, which draws fortune seekers toward her as much as toward the gold. Love, greed, and the dead hand of the old Portuguese builders drive the plot to its end among the ruins.
brandes-main-currents-2-the-romantic-sch:
French Romantic writers take the stage in the second book of Brandes's Main Currents, here in English. Hugo, Lamartine, and Musset lead a revolt against the stiff classical rules of the old stage and page. Brandes writes of them with heat and flair.

He paints the Romantics as fighters for freedom of the mind. Their poems, plays, and novels broke forms open and let raw feeling in. Brandes tells literary history like a gripping story, with heroes and foes. Readers meet the French movement through a critic who loved bold art and hated dull obedience.
brandes-main-currents-3-the-reaction-in-:
Writers who fought back against the French Revolution fill the third book of Brandes's Main Currents, here in English. Catholic and royalist voices raised altar and throne against the new ideas. Brandes, a liberal, gives even these foes a fair and vivid hearing.

He tracks how fear of chaos fed faith, order, and longing for the old world. Strong minds on the losing side get sharp, honest portraits. The volume shows Brandes at his most generous as a critic. To grasp the century, he insists, one must grasp the reaction as well as the revolt.
bruce:
Albert Payson Terhune dedicated Bruce to his ten Sunnybank collies, the best friends of his famous dedication, and the novel follows a collie family at his New Jersey kennels. It opens with Rothsay Lass, a beautiful collie bitch marked down as a second because her ears prick up instead of tipping as show fashion demands. Her son Bruce inherits her brains and courage rather than her fault.

Chapters carry Bruce through puppy trouble to service as a war dog, with episodes titled When Eyes Were No Use and The Werewolf. Terhune tells dog stories as biography, crediting his collies with loyalty, humor, and moral sense. Readers of Lad will find the same Sunnybank world here, deepened by a harder, stranger tale.
burke-reflections-revolution-france:
Edmund Burke published his Reflections on the Revolution in France in November 1790, while the revolution was still young. The book is framed as a letter to a young French friend who had asked his views. Burke, a Whig statesman, shocked old allies by attacking a cause many of them cheered.

Burke warns that tearing up a whole society by abstract rights ends in chaos and tyranny. He defends slow reform, inherited custom, and respect for church and crown. His praise of Marie Antoinette and his dread of paper money made the book famous at once. Paine's Rights of Man answered it, and the two books still argue across the centuries.
california-1849-1913-or-the-rambling-ske:
L. H. Woolley's California, 1849-1913 records sixty-four years of one pioneer's residence. Woolley, a member of the Society of California Pioneers and of the Vigilance Committee of 1856, wrote for his descendants. He left the Green Mountains of Vermont for the El Dorado in 1849. His train left Independence, Missouri, on the fourteenth of May.

Forty wagons, one hundred and fifty mules, and as many passengers made the Pioneer Line's first train. Woolley tells of wild mules, burnt bacon, and a cook dancing furious around the fire. Plains hardships give way to mining camps, vigilance days, and settled life. The sketches ramble as his title promises, anecdote after anecdote. Such plain memoirs are the ore from which California history is refined, and Woolley knew their worth.
cambridge-neighbors-from-literary-friend:
William Dean Howells wrote Cambridge Neighbors as part of Literary Friends and Acquaintance, his memoir of American literary life. Howells arrived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at twenty-nine to work on the Atlantic Monthly. Poets and scholars filled his days. He recalls feeling practically immortal among them, with endless hours to read and dream of writing.

Francis J Child, the Harvard ballad scholar, opens his gallery of portraits. Howells describes Child's refined face, gold-rimmed spectacles, and unfailing sweetness. Other neighbors from Harvard and Boston literary circles follow. Howells writes freely because most of his subjects had died by publication. Readers get warm, precise recollections of the generation that made Cambridge a center of American letters, recorded by a younger writer who loved them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abstinence:
Abstinence means abstaining from food, and the entry traces the history of church legislation on it and the motives behind that legislation. Its first instance under law is Genesis 2:16-17, where a mandate taught the moral head of humanity dependence on the Creator. Fasting laws chiefly fix the quantity of food allowed on fast days, while abstinence laws fix its quality. Fridays of Lent are days of both fasting and abstinence, while ordinary Fridays bind to abstinence alone.

From that starting point the long entry works through abstinence in the Old Testament and the early church, then through councils, theologians, and later discipline. It examines why the church shaped the rule as it did and how custom and desuetude bear on obligation. Sources run from the Fathers and Duchesne to Hefele, St. Thomas, and Thomassin on fasting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acceptance:
In canon law, acceptance means taking a thing with approval. A benefice's collation stays incomplete until the person accepts it. Acceptance links benefice and benefited. It grounds a right in the thing itself. Acceptance is likewise needed to make an election valid.

Acceptance is also of the essence of a gift, a free gift of property. For goods, giving with words of gift suffices, and for land a deed is mostly needed. Acceptance of a law, however, is not needed to impose submission to it. Even where people vote, they may not refuse laws once made and published. Otherwise the power to make laws would be a mockery. Custom and disuse can end duty only for merely church law, never against natural or divine law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accomplice:
An accomplice is a partner in some form of evildoing, one who cooperates in the wrongful act of another counted as the principal. Moral theology does not judge every such association unlawful at once. It first distinguishes formal from material cooperation. Formal cooperation shares the perverse frame of mind of the principal, as in persuading another to skip Sunday Mass without reason. Material cooperation shares only the physical act, as in selling a revolver in an ordinary deal to a man who then kills himself.

Cooperation is also proximate or remote, by closeness to the principal's act. Formal cooperation can never be lawful, since it presupposes a sinful attitude of will. The entry also treats restitution among partners. It covers the constitution of Benedict XIV, which bars a priest who shared a sin against the Sixth Commandment from validly absolving that person, except in danger of death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actual-grace:
Actual grace is treated here as distinct from sanctifying grace, a distinction seldom drawn before Trent but made necessary by modern disputes. Grace in general is God's supernatural gift to men and angels for eternal salvation, whether by salutary acts or a holy state. Actual grace is the transient help to act, while sanctifying grace is the permanent state of grace. This article treats only actual grace.

The name actual comes from Latin actualis, toward an act, since the grace is granted for performing salutary acts and is present and gone with the action itself. Its opposite is not possible grace but habitual grace, which makes for holiness, so the two relate as action to state, not as act to potency. The entry examines its nature and properties, then grace and liberty, and closes on the heathen who cooperates with vocation's grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altarpiece:
An altarpiece is a sacred picture on the wall or framed behind the altar, or statuary grouped on the altar. In the Middle Ages some churches used embossed silver or gold, enamelled and jewel-set work, instead of picture or group. Sometimes the piece stood upon the altar itself, rather than behind it, for all to see.

Where the altar stood free in the choir, visible from behind just as from before, both sides bore painted work. The decorated screen, retable, or reredos also carries the name of altarpiece today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amice:
The amice is a short linen cloth, square or oblong, blessed before use like other sacerdotal vestments, and first put on by the priest vesting for Mass. It covers the shoulders and originally the head. Many older orders still lay it first over the head, ends falling on the shoulders, then vest from alb onward. Only flax or hemp linen is permitted, as for the alb, and a little cross must be sewn to it.

Tracing its history meets the same difficulty as the alb's: early writers' expressions vary, and the word amictus shifts meaning. The amice thus opens the vesting, a plain linen square with a long, tangled name history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-chu:
The Apostolic Church Ordinance is a third-century collection, falsely claiming apostolic authorship, of moral and hierarchical rules drawn mainly from ancient Christian sources. Initially published in Ethiopic by Ludolf in 1691 with a Latin translation, it served as a law code among the Egyptian, Ethiopian, and Arabian churches. It rivalled the Didache, the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, under whose name it sometimes passed. Though of undoubted Greek origin, it survives chiefly in Coptic, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Syriac versions.

Bickell of Marburg first published it in Greek in 1843 from a twelfth-century Vienna manuscript and gave it its usual German name, Apostolische Kirchenordnung. After a short introduction inspired by the Letter of Barnabas, it falls into two parts, the first adapting the Didache's first six chapters. The entry introduces a code that governed eastern churches while wearing apostolic dress it never owned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assessor-of-t:
The Assessor of the Holy Office is a functionary of the Congregation of the Inquisition, also called the Congregation of the Universal Inquisition. Its present functions are to watch over matters of faith and examine suspected tenets of persons or books. The office-holder ranks next after the congregation's cardinals, and is a secular churchman or an honorary chamberlain of the pope.

His duty is to make the report of the Holy Office in a particular case. When consultors alone meet, he presides and then lays their ballots before the cardinal inquisitors. When the congregation decides, he reports the result to the pope that same evening, if the pope has not presided. He must attend all four meetings of the congregation, and on Saturdays he examines matters laid before the Holy Office with four fellow officials.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-association-o: The Association of Priestly Perseverance is a priests' association founded in 1868 at Vienna and first confined to that archdiocese. In 1879, mainly through its journal La Correspondance, it extended into other dioceses and countries. In 1903 it counted 14,919 living members in 150 dioceses across Austria, Germany, Switzerland, and other countries. Its structure closely matches the Apostolic Union of Secular Priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avarice:
Avarice, from the Latin avarus, greedy, is the inordinate love for riches. Its special malice lies in making the getting and keeping of money and possessions a purpose in itself to live for. Such things, the entry insists, are worth only as tools for a rational and harmonious life, with due regard for one's social condition. Avarice forgets that limit and treats wealth as an end.

It ranks as a capital vice because many other sins are committed to gain or hold its object. It is more to be dreaded because it often cloaks itself as a virtue. It slips in under the pretext of decent provision for the future. Where it drives injustice in gaining or keeping wealth, it is often a grievous sin. In itself, as mere excess desire or pleasure in riches, it is commonly not a mortal sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avempace:
Avempace, also called Ibn Bajja or Ibn Badsha, was an Arabian philosopher, physician, astronomer, mathematician, and poet. He was born at Saragossa toward the end of the eleventh century and died at Fez in 1138. In 1118 he stood at Seville, writing treatises on logic, and later he moved to Granada and to Africa. Arabian accounts say rival physicians poisoned him.

He wrote on mathematics, medicine, and philosophy, and he commented on Aristotle's Physics, Meteorology, Generation and Corruption, and parts of his animal works. His philosophical books include logical treatises, a work On the Soul, The Hermit's Guide, a work on the intellect's union with man, and a Valedictory Letter. Most of his writings are lost or still undiscovered, though his logical treatises survive at the Escorial. Moses of Narbonne's account of The Hermit's Guide lets us trace its aim: the mind's union with the Active Intellect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benefice:
Benefice, a central term of church law, receives a long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. In strict use it means a permanent right granted by the Church to a cleric. That right lets him draw income from church property in return for a spiritual service, such as the care of souls. Popular speech often confuses it with the property itself or with the office alone.

Four marks define it: a right to revenue without ownership of its source, a twofold permanence in both income and holder, and a spiritual duty attached. The entry then works through kinds of benefices, how they are gained and lost, and who may hold them. It is a lawyer's map of how clergy were once paid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berenice:
Berenice, a titular see in Egypt, is the subject of this brief 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. It stood at the end of the Greater Syrtis, where Benghazi stands today, first named Euhesperides until Ptolemy III renamed it for his wife Berenice. A Jewish colony there helped make it an early Christian centre.

Its bishops appear in ancient records, including Ammonas, to whom Dionysius of Alexandria wrote in the third century. Another bishop, Daces, attended the Council of Nicaea in 325. The entry is a short note tying a classical town, a royal name, and a line of early bishops together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernold-of-co:
Bernold of Constance, a historian and theologian, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Swabia about 1054, he died at Schaffhausen in 1100 after study at Constance under Bernard of Constance. He was present at Rome's Lenten Synod in 1079, where Berengarius retracted his errors on the Eucharist.

Back in Germany he defended Bishop Gebhard's enforcement of Gregory VII's reform decrees and served as counsellor to King Herman at the battle of Bleichfeld in 1086. His chronicle and theological writings make him a key witness to the Gregorian reform. The entry presents a partisan scholar writing history as it happened.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bigamy-in-civ:
Bigamy in civil jurisprudence, marrying while a former marriage still stands, receives a long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Definitions from Bishop, Murray, and Coke agree that it is a species of polygamy, the having of two or more spouses at once. The entry surveys its punishment across legal systems.

Polygamy, though legal among some peoples, proves rarer than custom suggests: early Babylon, Assyria, and Egypt leaned to monogamy, and China forbade a second wife. The entry follows English and American law on the crime, its defences, and its proof. It is a comparative study of marriage law's oldest offence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candace:
Candace was the Ethiopian queen whose eunuch Saint Philip baptized. The name appears in a ruined pyramid near ancient Meroe. Another queen of the same name, named by Strabo and Dion Cassius, revolted against Rome. She was beaten by Petronius at Napata in 22 B.C.

Pliny reports that Nero's explorers, crossing Nubia, found a Queen Candace on the throne of the island of Meroe. Pliny adds that the name had long passed to all queens of that country. The Ethiopia of Candace is not modern Abyssinia, but the region of Meroe at the meeting of the Nile and the Taccasi. Pliny's queen may be the queen of the Acts, but no direct proof settles it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chalice:
The chalice ranks first among sacred vessels. By a figure of speech, the cup itself often stands for the Precious Blood. St. Paul calls it the communion of the blood of Christ. No reliable tradition survives about Christ's Last Supper vessel. In the sixth and seventh centuries pilgrims at Jerusalem were shown a chalice said to be the actual one. It was kept in the Holy Sepulchre with the sponge offered to the Saviour on Calvary.

Later claimants fared no better under scrutiny. Antoninus of Piacenza called the Jerusalem vessel onyx. Adamnan, less than a century later, called it a silver cup with two handles holding a Gallic sextarius. Two more vessels were later venerated as the Last Supper chalice: the sacro catino of Genoa, a green glass dish long taken for emerald, and an agate cup at Valencia. The article judges the tradition untrustworthy and late.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-mainte:
An entry on church maintenance, the support of church buildings, institutions, and clergy, always both a necessity and a problem. Since the Church is visible, with priesthood, worship, and temples, it must hold property, movable and immovable, and that requires generosity from the faithful. To strip the Church of all property, the entry argues, is both error and absurdity.

Under the Old Law the priesthood held towns through Israel and received firstfruits, tithes, and shares of sacrifices, while kings and people maintained the Temple and its treasury. In the New Testament, Christ and the apostles kept a common purse. The first Christians sold lands and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet, and Christ told His preachers to accept support from those they served. The entry follows that principle through later offerings, endowments, and laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-allegia:
Civil allegiance means the loyalty and obedience owed by a person to his State as citizen. The word comes from liege, a free man's service to his lord. Catholic teaching grounds that duty in nature and religion. As children owe dutiful conduct to parents, so citizens owe obligations to country and rulers: patriotism and obedience.

Patriotism asks esteem and love for one's country, interest in its history, and readiness to sacrifice life for the commonwealth. Obedience asks respect for rulers as God's ministers for the common good and observance of just laws. The article meets the charge that Catholics cannot be good citizens while obeying a pope who may be foreign. It answers that the Church is a separate spiritual society. The State has no competence in religion, and when it oversteps its bounds, obedience ends: God, rather than men, ought to be obeyed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-d-espe:
Claude d'Espence, a French theologian, was born in 1511 at Chalons-sur-Marne and died at Paris on 5 October 1571. He entered the College de Navarre in 1536 and became rector of the University of Paris in 1540, before his doctorate in 1542. Cardinal de Lorraine's court called him, and he saw propositions from his 1543 Lenten sermons referred to the Sorbonne. He joined the Melun consultation of 1544 on Trent and was sent to the council at Bologna in 1547.

At Poissy in 1561 he argued against Beza for tradition, the infallibility of the Church, and the Sacrament of Order. An anonymous work on image veneration, censured by the Sorbonne and believed his, forced him to subscribe the faculty's sixteenth article against Protestants. His collected works of 1619 include a treatise against the Predestinarians and an Institution of a Christian Prince. They also include a work on parents' consent in marriage and commentaries on Timothy and Titus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concupiscence:
John Ming's entry defines concupiscence broadly as any yearning of the soul for good. Strictly it means desire of the lower appetite against reason. The senses seek gratification, while reason seeks the good of whole nature in subordination to God. Left alone, the lower appetite chases sensuous pleasures without regard for higher faculties. Desires against reason's good may thus rise before the mind attends, then stir the body to pursuit. This clash is natural in man, an imperfection rather than corruption.

Paul's voice sounds the law: when he wills good, evil stands present. Christ's death freed mankind from sin's bondage. Sixteenth-century Reformers, above all Luther, taught anew that concupiscence itself is sin, the corrupt state of nature, and that original justice was due to man by nature. The Catholic Church condemns these views as erroneous or heretical, a line later drawn by Pius VI against Pistoja in 1794.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conscience:
John Rickaby's entry opens with the name. English doubled a Latin word: conscience for morals, consciousness for the universal field. Cicero leaves the ethical limit to context, valuing his own conscience above all men's talk. Hamilton weighed consciousness of outer objects, and German keeps Bewusstsein apart from Gewissen.

Origin follows in race and individual. Some anthropologists accept the Biblical account, others do not. Ethics means regulated life, beginning crudely in animal life as stimulus response, reflex action, and adaptation. Customary rules gain ethical character through principles and ideals. Conscience is no distinct faculty, but intellect judging right and wrong, aided by good will. History moves from pre-Christian testimonies through patristic Scripture and pagan classics, each Father characteristic without system, into scholastic times. Merit begins once duty stands fulfilled, goodness beyond duty meritorious too, virtue prized for itself and God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constance:
Michael Ott's entry on Constance, Latin Constantia, German Konstanz, Czech Kostnitz, presents a town formerly seat of a diocese. Very ancient, it sits where the Rhine leaves the Bodensee, in Baden's south-east. A lake-dwellers' village first, it gained Roman fortification in 304. Legionaries likely brought Christianity by the second century's end or the third's start. The see first stood at Vindonissa, now Windisch in Aargau, Switzerland, its erection date unknown.

Bubulcus, present at Epaon's Burgundian Synod in 517, stands as the first bishop history records. Diocesan limits were fixed in the seventh century, and decline began with the Reformation. The city won municipal rights in 780, became a free imperial city in 1192, and ranked among Germany's largest medieval cities. Chronicles from Merck and Neugart to Eiselein and Beyerle carry the record through war, property, and civic rights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-continence:
John Melody's entry defines continence as abstinence from even licit marriage gratifications. It forms part of temperance, though Aristotle denied it virtue's high character, since it involves conflict with wrong desires, an element foreign to virtue in the strict sense. Continence bears a narrower sense than chastity, which finds place within marriage. The abstinence discussed belongs to celibacy's state, though celibacy's notion does not necessarily involve continence.

Practice treats continence as a state of life. Even among peoples where early marriage rules, continence frequently appears. Two general objections face the state of continence, answered in turn. The entry closes by weighing social service. Critics may doubt such lives make desirable citizens, yet the example's service, given every person's duty of absolute chastity for longer or shorter periods, holds highest value.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-controversies:
Joseph Pohle's entry treats controversies on grace. How can grace's potent influence on the will, eliciting good works, reside with free will's simultaneous consent? Merely sufficient grace, gratia mere sufficiens, implies withheld consent, hence inefficiency, gratia inefficax. The question reduces to free will versus efficacious grace, gratia efficax, by which free will does grace's desire. The radical solution cuts the knot, setting aside supernatural grace with the Pelagians.

Heretical solutions follow, including Luther's theory: original sin so impaired free will that, like a horse, it acts only as ridden by God or the devil. Faith's sources protest free will's subjugation. Catholic systems start from grace or free will. Thomism rests on Saint Thomas, with premotion as Divine knowledge's medium for foreseeing. Objections press freedom's survival, the efficacious-sufficient distinction, sin's demand for first-mover predetermination, and premotion's infallibility. Linking two kinds of efficacious grace deepens difficulties, ending in mystery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornice:
Thomas Poole's entry defines the cornice as an entablature's uppermost division, the roof's representative within an order. It consists of projecting mouldings and blocks, usually divisible into bed-moulding, corona, and gutter. In classic architecture each order possesses its own peculiar cornice, distinct in profile and proportion from the others.

More widely, any moulded projection crowning or finishing the part it adorns counts as a cornice. Examples include a façade's coping, the moulding running round an apartment beneath the ceiling, and mouldings surmounting a door or window. The term thus spans both the strict classical member and every comparable crowning moulding in building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-co:
The Council of Constance, a partly ecumenical council held from 5 November 1414 to 22 April 1418, faced three tasks. It had to end the Western Schism, reform church government and life, and repress heresy. Pisa's council of 1409 had only added a third pope to the two it tried to remove, leaving Christendom with three claimants.

Across forty-five general sessions the council secured resignations and depositions, then elected Martin V, restoring a single head. Reform decrees and action against Wycliffite and Hussite teaching accompanied the settlement. Attendance and procedure receive their own closing survey in the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-fl:
The Council of Florence, the Seventeenth Ecumenical Council, continued the Ferrara assembly after plague forced its move to Tuscany, and behind Ferrara stood Basle, convoked in 1431. Eugene IV proclaimed the transferred council the lawful continuation, and its ecumenical standing rests on that claim. Greek and Latin differences, above all the Filioque, dominated debate.

On 6 July the union decree Laetentur Coeli was proclaimed in Florence cathedral, and the Greeks departed at once. Latin members stayed on to pursue reunion with Armenians, Syrian Jacobites, Mesopotamians, Chaldeans, and Maronites of Cyprus, ending at the Lateran in Rome. Papal supremacy emerged strengthened, winning back men like Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pius II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
The Councils of Aix-en-Provence span seven meetings, in 1112, 1374, 1409, 1585, 1612, 1838, and 1850, a long provincial thread rather than a single event. Each gathering answered its own century, from medieval discipline to nineteenth-century doctrinal defence, and the entry picks out the meetings with lasting marks.

In 1612 the fathers censured Edmund Richer's Gallican work on ecclesiastical and political power. In 1838 they asked Gregory XVI to add Immaculate to Conception in the Mass preface for the Blessed Virgin's feast, and he did. In 1850 they condemned rationalism, pantheism, communism, and arbitrary interpretation of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-credence:
A liturgical entry describes the credence, or credence table, a small table placed in the sanctuary near the Epistle side of the altar. It holds the cruets, acolytes' candles, and other utensils needed for the celebration of Mass. In solemn Masses the chalice, paten, corporal, and veil rest on it until the Offertory.

Size and covering follow the occasion: about forty inches long for ordinary use, larger when a bishop celebrates, and draped to the ground on very solemn feasts. For low Masses the rubrics allow a wall niche or bracket instead, though custom now favours a credence table. The entry cites the Ceremoniale Episcoporum and standard manuals of Mass celebration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daughters-of-:
A congregational entry traces the Daughters of Providence, founded at Paris by Madame Polaillon, born Marie de Lumague, a pious widow. In 1643, with letters patent from Louis XIII, she opened a home to protect and instruct young girls. Beauty, poverty, or parental neglect exposed them to loss of faith and other perils. She named the home the Seminary of Providence.

Seven women of religious vocation among the inmates formed a community under rules drawn by Saint Vincent de Paul at Archbishop Gondy's direction in 1647. Louis XIV's mother gave them the Hospital de la Sante in 1651, confirmed by royal letters in 1667. After two years' probation, members took simple vows of chastity, obedience, service, and perpetual stability, and houses spread to Metz, Sedan, and across Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-office:
The divine office, also called the Liturgy of the Hours, is the set of prayers said at fixed hours of day and night. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the name as a duty done for God, laid by church law on priests, religious, and clerics. It covers only the prayers of the Breviary, not the Mass or other liturgical rites. Other names for it include canonical hours, diurnal and nocturnal office, and simply cursus.

The entry traces the obligation of clerics to recite the office and the growth of the Roman Breviary. It cites the great histories of the Breviary and studies of the personal duty of recitation. For readers new to the hours, it offers a clear door into the daily round of prayer that orders clerical life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-provid:
Providence in general is foresight, the practical reason that fits means to an end. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry applies the word to God, in whom providence is the act by which his wisdom orders all events of the universe toward the end of creation. That end is that all creatures should show forth the glory of God, and that man in particular should glorify him, serve him in love, and reach eternal happiness in him.

The universe forms a system of real beings that God both made and guides, and his concurrence is needed for each natural working. The entry defends this ordering against chance and fate, drawing on the moral order of the world. It closes with a long shelf of writers on divine government, from Lacordaire to modern English theologians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divorce-in-ci:
Divorce in civil jurisprudence is defined as the ending or partial suspension by law of the marriage bond. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry distinguishes the absolute form, divorce from the bond itself, which ends the marriage wholly where the law allows it. Beside it stands a limited form, divorce from bed and board, which suspends common life for a time or without limit. Courts also grant decrees that declare a marriage void from the start.

Such marriages, never valid, leave the parties free as though no bond had existed. The entry surveys these forms across the states and the wider literature of marriage law. It points readers to the proceedings of the National Divorce Congress of 1906 and to a world bibliography of marriage and divorce, a guide for lawyers and moralists alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donation-in-c:
Donation in civil jurisprudence is the free transfer, or gift, of ownership of property. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the Latin munus meant a gift for a special occasion, such as a birth or marriage. The giver is called the donor and the receiver the donee. In law, donation rests on the basic right of each person to dispose of his property as he wills, a right long held fit for legal regulation and restraint.

Donation needs the consent of both sides, the donor to give and the donee to take. The entry draws on Story, Parsons, and the court reports to set out the rules. It serves as a compact guide to a simple act, giving, that the law has fenced about with care since Babylonian times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
An ecclesiastical province is an administrative district under an archbishop. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that provinces first took fixed shape in the Eastern Roman Empire. The great centers, Antioch for Syria, Ephesus for Asia, Alexandria for Egypt, and Rome for Italy, sent out missionaries and became mother churches of new Christian communities.

From the later second century, bishops within the same natural bounds met for common counsel in synods on weighty occasions. By the end of that century the bishop of the state capital commonly summoned these synods and presided over them. The entry cites Sieke, Werminhoff, and Phillips on the growth of the metropolitan system from those gatherings.

Ecclesiastical residence means abiding where one's duties lie, as a bishop in his diocese, a rector in his benefice, or a canon in his cathedral church. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets it against non-residence or absence. Residence exists to guarantee service and the fulfillment of duty, and mere bodily presence does not satisfy the law. Vigilance and solicitude must go with it, and only a laborious residence counts.

Residence differs from domicile, since domicile turns on the intent to remain. By a fiction of law, one lawfully absent fulfills the residence rule, while one unlawfully absent counts as present. The entry cites Trent, Urban the Eighth, and Benedict the Fourteenth on a duty that keeps shepherds with their flocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-ignati:
Edmund Ignatius Rice founded the Irish Christian Brothers, living from 1762 to 1844. Born at Callan, he grew rich as a Waterford merchant, known for honesty, charity, and piety. About to enter a convent abroad, he was stopped by the sight of ragged boys in the street. A friend challenged him: why bury himself in a cell when poor youths needed him at home?

He opened his first school at Waterford in 1802, and Bishop Hussey laid the stone of Mount Sion schoolhouse that June. His first paid helpers fled, but young men from Callan took their place, and more schools followed. The entry tells how a businessman turned his wealth and life to free schooling for poor boys, and how a small start grew into an order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egyptian-chur:
The Egyptian Church Ordinance is an early Christian set of thirty-one canons ruling ordinations, worship, and the main lines of church life. It takes its name from Egypt because the West first met it in languages tied to Egypt. In 1677 the Dominican Wansleben gave a short account of the canons as found in the Ethiopic Synodos, and in 1691 Ludolf printed a fragment with a Latin version.

Later finds filled out the text. Tattam printed all the canons in Bohairic, the lower Egyptian tongue, with English in 1848. Lagarde printed them in Sahidic, the upper Egyptian tongue, from a manuscript of 1006. In 1900 Hauler found a very old Latin version from the fifth or sixth century, prized because it keeps the liturgical prayers missing elsewhere. The lost original was doubtless Greek, and the work belongs to a chain of church-order books linked to Hippolytus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-essence-and-e:
