Essence and existence are transcendentals, so no strict definition of either is possible. Essence is properly described as what makes a thing what it is. Existence is what makes the essence actual in the order of being. The essence is the ground from which a thing's properties emanate. Essence is the abstract counterpart of the concrete entity, pointing to the reason why a thing is precisely what it is.

Answering the question What, essence is equivalent to quiddity: the essence is what a thing's definition expresses. As essence is what makes a thing what it is, nature is what makes it act as it does. Hence Saint Thomas says nature is the essence as it relates to its proper operation. Essence is also in a manner synonymous with form, since beings are sorted into species chiefly by their formal principle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-examination-o:
Examination of Conscience means looking back over one's past thoughts, words, and deeds to judge them against the moral law. It concerns the will above all, the good or bad aim behind each thought, word, and deed. The Stoics practiced such self-scrutiny, and Scripture enforces it, from God's word to Abraham to Jeremiah's call to search our ways. Saint Paul then commanded it before Holy Communion, saying a man must prove himself before eating the bread and drinking the chalice.

Early Christians, who received Communion often, made it a familiar exercise, and saints such as Anthony, Basil, Augustine, and Bernard made it a daily rule for their followers. The entry separates the devotional examen from the examen before confession. In the latter, the penitent reviews the Ten Commandments, the Church's precepts, the seven capital sins, and the duties of his state of life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-final-perseve:
Final perseverance means keeping the state of grace from the last conversion until death. The phrase comes from Matthew, chapter ten, where endurance to the end brings salvation. It differs from mere continuance in grace, since lost grace can be won back again. Theologians view it both as a power to persevere and as the fact of persevering.

Catholic teaching, shaped by Augustine and the Council of Trent, joins divine grace with human will. Neither grace alone nor will alone suffices; the two must work together, Trent held. The gift lies beyond certain knowledge and beyond strict merit, yet prayer can seek it. A good death crowning a life of well-doing is the normal form the gift takes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florence:
Florence stands on the Arno in Tuscany, at the foot of the Fiesole hills. Destroyed by Sulla in 82 B.C., it was rebuilt by Caesar in 59 B.C. as a military post. Its wealth began in the eleventh century, when it backed the papacy against the emperors. By 1155 it could shut its gates against Frederick Barbarossa.

The commune grew under consuls, then a podesta, with guild priors holding legislative power. Guelphs and Ghibellines, born of a broken engagement and a murder in 1215, split the city for centuries. In 1250 the people deposed the podesta and set up a Captain of the People with elders. Trade, guilds, and civic pride made Florence a great republican power in Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-france:
France is treated here in a vast survey article, one of the longest in the encyclopedia. It covers a country of 207,107 square miles with coasts on both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. It opens with descriptive geography, tracing the hexagon of France from Dunkirk to the Pyrenees and the Alps, its cliffs, dunes, river mouths, and mountain frontiers. It notes that France alone in Europe touches both seas.

From geography the survey moves through the nation's history, its church, religious orders, charitable and social organisations, and contemporary Catholic life. It closes with long lists of sources on French charity and religious movements. Readers looking for a single reference point on France's land, people, and Catholic institutions will find the article's scale matches its subject. Individual sections now read as history in their own right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gebhard-iii-o:
Gebhard III of Constance, a bishop of the Investiture struggle, defended papal rights against emperors for twenty-six years. Born about 1040 to Duke Bertold I of Zähringen, he served as provost at Xanten. He became a Hirschau monk and was consecrated bishop in December 1084 by the legate who became Urban II. An imperial anti-bishop, Otto, held the see by force.

An imperial synod at Mainz deposed Gebhard in 1085, but Otto's death in 1086 let him take his see. He reformed Petershausen, consecrated a new cathedral in 1089, and served with Passau's bishop as papal vicar for Germany. Driven out again in 1103, he returned with Henry V in 1105, freed the king from the ban, and, after a papal rebuke for siding with the emperor, withdrew to diocesan care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerace:
Gerace, a diocese in Calabria's Reggio province, stands on a height above the Ionian Sea near Cape Spartivento. Its importance rose from the ruin of Locri Epizephyrii, an early Greek colony founded by Ozolian Locrians about 684 to 680 before Christ and law-given by Zaleucus. Locri flourished by trade and culture, suffered under Dionysius the Younger and Pyrrhus, and passed to Rome in the Second Punic War, keeping Zaleucus's constitution as it decayed.

Before Locri's total ruin its bishop's see moved to Gerace in 709 under Bishop Gregory. Gerace likely takes its name from Saint Cyriaca, whose church Saracens wrecked in 915; they seized the town in 986 and Normans took it in 1059. The Greek Rite held until 1467, despite a Latin-Greek schism about 1250 to 1253. Barlaam II, bishop in 1342, taught Greek to Petrarch and Boccaccio. The see, suffragan of Reggio, counts sixty-nine parishes and 132,300 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ghost-dance:
The Ghost Dance was the rite of a Native American religion that arose about 1887 around Wovoka, also called Jack Wilson, a Paiute man in Nevada. In a vision he claimed to have spoken with God. God promised a new earth where dead Indians, buffalo, and game would return and white settlers would be pushed back across the ocean. A Catholic Encyclopedia article recounts the teaching and the dance meant to hasten it.

Believers held hands in a circle, sang ghost songs without instruments, and danced while priests brought dancers into trances. The faith spread to nearly all tribes east of the Missouri and stirred years of excitement, until set dates passed without result. In Dakota it fed the Sioux outbreak of the winter of 1890-91, marked by the killing of Sitting Bull and the massacre at Wounded Knee. Its doctrine of human brotherhood barred all warlike acts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-croc:
Giovanni Croce was a composer born at Chioggia near Venice in 1557, who died on 15 May 1609. Under Zarlino's tutelage at Venice he became one of the noted composers of the Venetian school. After entering the priesthood he served at Santa Maria Formosa. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him to the top post at St. Mark's.

In 1593 he took charge of the choir boys at St. Mark's as vice-director. On the death of Baltazzaro Donati in 1603, he succeeded him as choirmaster. He wrote much secular music, madrigals and canzonettas, but his chief works served the Church. Their marks are clarity of form and a devotional spirit, and three of his motets appear in Lueck's collection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace:
Grace is a teaching article in four parts: actual grace, sanctifying grace, the controversies on grace, and supernatural adoption. Actual grace is a help from God for good acts, granted through Christ's merits. A Catholic Encyclopedia article moves from first meanings to the schools that divided Catholics.

Sanctifying grace is treated with justification and its preparation. The controversies section covers the Reformers' and Jansenists' heresies and the Catholic solutions of Thomism, Augustinianism, Molinism, Congruism, and Syncretism. The closing part presents adoption as God's children, the gracious raising of man to share the inner life of the Most Blessed Trinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greece:
Greece is treated under seven heads. They cover the land and people, the Church before the schism, the Orthodox Church, the Church's constitution, the Catholic Church, Protestants and other sects, and the Church in enslaved Greece. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows Hellenism as a force unbroken for nearly thirty centuries.

The Greeks first appear as small states bound by language, religion, and civilization in the southern Balkans, the islands, and the Asia Minor coast. For three centuries they reached a perfection in civilization that gives them the first place in European history. Hellenism then spread over Asia, Egypt, and Italy. Greece swallowed the eastern Roman Empire from Constantinople for nearly ten centuries. At last, chiefly by the magic of her name, she shook off the tyrant to become free Greece again.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guardianship-:
Guardianship, the lawful care of someone too young, inexperienced, or weak in mind or will to act for themselves, is traced here from Rome through England to modern law. Roman tutela gave a tutor authority over a free minor, boys to fourteen and girls to twelve, with a curator to age twenty-five. The office could arise by will, by law among relatives, or by a magistrate's appointment.

English law added guardianship by nature for parents, feudal wardship that tied a landholding orphan to the lord of the fee, and socage guardianship kept deliberately from the next heir. A statute of 1660 let fathers name testamentary guardians. The lord chancellor stood as paramount guardian of all infants, with the Court of Chancery carrying out what the sovereign, as father of the country, owed minors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gulf-of-st-la:
Quebec's Vicariate of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, erected on 12 September 1905 from a prefecture of 1882, covers the province's north-east beyond the Diocese of Chicoutimi as a suffragan of Quebec. Eudist Fathers staff all its missions except the Montagnais, Naskapi, and Eskimo stations, which belong to the Oblates of Mary Immaculate.

Its first vicar apostolic, Gustave Blanch, born at Josselin in France in 1849 and ordained in 1878, took up residence at Seven Islands after his consecration at Chicoutimi in October 1905. The vicariate then counted 9,650 Catholics, including 2,000 Indians, served by 20 priests across 12 missions with residences, 28 stations, and schools teaching 950 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harbor-grace:
Newfoundland's Diocese of Harbor Grace, erected in 1856, gathers the northern bays from Conception to White Bay with the Labrador coast under Newfoundland's rule. Its coastline of five hundred miles is served by twenty-three priests for 29,000 Catholics. Forty-nine churches, eighty-five stations, five convents, and a hundred schools with 4,500 pupils fill that scattered charge.

John Dalton, its first bishop, built the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in a peaceful thirteen years, while his Italian successor Carfagnini doubled the clergy but battled faction near schism. Ronald MacDonald restored peace across twenty-five years and rebuilt the fire-ruined cathedral. John March, consecrated in 1906, opened a fund for church students as his first act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hector-boece:
Scottish chronicler Hector Boece, born at Dundee about 1465, helped found the University of Aberdeen and wrote the history that reached Shakespeare through Holinshed. A student and then professor at Paris's College of Montaigu. There he befriended Erasmus and joined Bishop Elphinstone from about 1495 in winning a bull for an Aberdeen university. King's College opened its teaching in 1505.

Boece served as principal, lecturing in divinity and medicine, and published Lives of the Bishops of Murthlack and Aberdeen in 1522 and his seventeen-book History of Scotland in 1527. Admired for grace, love of country, and love of freedom, he was attacked even by contemporaries for credulity about origins. Yet Bellenden's Scots translation of 1536 carried his tales into Holinshed and so into Shakespeare's plays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hendrik-consc:
Antwerp novelist Hendrik Conscience, born in 1812 to a French father and Flemish mother, became the father of Flemish prose literature. A cripple until seven, raised on his mother's fairy tales, self-taught by reading, he quit tutoring for six years as a private soldier, learning peasant life in northern Belgium at first hand.

Advised to write in Flemish, then scorned as too rude for letters, he failed with two romantic books. He then triumphed in 1838 with The Lion of Flanders, and never stopped, leaving more than a hundred volumes. Drawn from fatherland, family, and loyalty to the Church, his historical novels, village tales, and studies of manners won translation across Europe. Antwerp raised his monument weeks before his death in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-de-sain:
Carmelite theologian Henri de Saint-Ignace, born at Ath in 1630, was a learned moral theologian whose Jansenist leanings coloured a long controversial career. Professor of moral theology, he professed Augustine and Aquinas while favouring Baius and Jansenius. A long Roman stay under Clement XI saved his orthodoxy without cooling his lifelong antipathy to the Jesuits.

His chief work, Ethica amoris of 1709 in three volumes on human acts, laws and virtues, and sacraments, drew on a fellow Carmelite's Tempestas. It adopted novel views on the Eucharist that Rome forbade in 1714 and 1722 and Paris condemned, its venom earning it the nickname Ethica odii. A 1713 defence of efficacious grace provoked a Jesuit reply. His Molinismus profligatus of 1717 closed a life spent in doctrinal war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-william:
Henry William Wilberforce, born at Clapham in 1807, was the famous William Wilberforce's third son and Robert's younger brother. Entering Oriel College, Oxford, in 1826 as a pupil of Newman, he took a brilliant degree, studied law at Lincoln's Inn, and was persuaded by Newman to leave law for the Church. He took Anglican orders in 1834 and served as curate of Bransgrove, vicar of Walmer, and vicar of East Farleigh.

On 15 September 1850 Wilberforce and his wife entered the Catholic Church. He then turned to journalism, owning and editing the Catholic Standard, afterwards the Weekly Register, from 1854 until 1863. His books include The Parochial System of 1838 and Reasons for Submitting to the Catholic Church of 1851, which ran through several editions and stirred much controversy. Proselytism in Ireland, an essay on events before the English Reformation, and The Church and the Empires, published after his death in 1873, complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-alliance:
The Holy Alliance was a treaty signed on 26 September 1815 by Emperor Francis I of Austria, King Frederick William III of Prussia, and Tsar Alexander I of Russia. Though a political act, its wording is purely religious in character. After Napoleon's fall, the three monarchs resolved in gratitude to God to take Christian principles, justice, love, and peace, as the only rule of their rule, at home and abroad.

They declared Christian morality the best guide in public life, not only in private life. They pledged brotherly feeling, mutual support, and abstention from war with each other, and promised to guide subjects and armies in a fatherly manner. Christ, they said, remained the rightful Lord of nations. The entry traces the treaty's terms and its place in post-Napoleonic Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospice:
A hospice, from the Latin hospitium or guest house, was in early Christian centuries a shelter for the sick, the poor, orphans, the old, travellers, and needy people of all sorts. It dates back to Constantine's reign. Originally all hospices stood under bishops, who named priests to run their spiritual and temporal affairs.

About 436, a statute from Carthage's so-called Fourth Council ordered bishops to keep a small hospice near their churches. In time the general hospice gave way to special establishments for particular needs, and the term came to mean houses where travellers were harboured. Such hospices rose in wild regions and on mountain passes, run by hermits or monks, and multiplied as pilgrimages to the Holy Land, Rome, and Compostela grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-human-race:
This article asks whether mankind forms one race or several species. Some have treated human varieties as distinct species, while others defend human unity, judging the differences too small to split species. The apparently unlimited fertility of crossed races supports unity, and the gaps between darkest and lightest peoples are bridged by many intermediate stages.

Intellectual likeness between the most primitive peoples and the most cultured also supports unity, the entry argues. Various living types are only different races. Schwalbe proposed splitting an early Quaternary type, homo primigenius, with heavy brow ridges and chinless jaw, from homo sapiens, but Klaatsch's study of aboriginal Australian skulls challenged that split. The article surveys the evidence for unity against the case for division.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignorance:
To be ignorant is to lack knowledge about something, in a being that can know. Fundamentally it comes from the limits of our intellect or the obscurity of the matter itself. This article treats its ethical aspect and consequences. Only free, voluntary acts count as imputable, so ignorance that kills or weakens that freedom has to be reckoned with.

Here the word narrows to mean missing information that one ought to possess. Mere want of knowledge, without any requirement to possess it, may be called nescience. For fixing human responsibility the chief division is invincible versus vincible ignorance: invincible when a person cannot rid himself of it despite moral diligence, vincible when he could have removed it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-immanence:
Immanence comes from the Latin in manere, to stay within. It names the quality of an act that starts and finishes inside the agent. Living action counts as immanent in body, mind, and morals alike, since it flows from the spontaneity at the heart of a living subject and works out that subject's own powers. Such action begins and ends inside one being, like a closed system.

Yet is that system sealed off, able to stand alone and take in nothing from outside? Or can it grow by absorbing things around it, sometimes things it needs, just as food feeds the body's inward activity? Philosophies of immanence raise this question and try to answer it, for individual people and for the whole universe. The teaching itself arose as soon as people began to philosophize.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-injustice:
Moral theology gives injustice a narrow sense here, apart from its broad use for any breach of the virtue of justice. In this narrower sense it means breaking another person's strict right against that person's reasonable will. A right, the entry explains, is the moral power to hold, do, or claim something that serves one's own good.

Goods tied to the person stand apart from goods outside the person. The first kind includes life, limb, liberty, and good name. The second kind includes property of any kind. Harm to the first kind counts as personal injury, harm to the second as real injury. The entry sorts those cases and the forms of wrongdoing that follow, giving readers a working map of how moralists graded offenses against what others are owed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-armand-l:
Jean-Armand Le Bouthillier de Rancé, born in Paris in 1626 and dead at La Trappe in 1700, became abbot of Notre-Dame de la Trappe and its reformer. A child prodigy, he published an edition of Anacreon with Greek notes at twelve. His brother's death left him canon of Notre-Dame, abbot of La Trappe, and holder of rich benefices.

Ordained in 1651, Rancé lived at first as a wealthy man of the world, fond of feasting and hunting. Conscience at last turned him: he gave up his wealth and ease, took up strict monastic life, and remade La Trappe under a hard rule of silence, labour, and penance. That reform, born from his own conversion, shaped the Trappist way of life that still bears the abbey's name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeanne-mance:
Jeanne Mance, foundress of Montreal's Hôtel-Dieu, was born at Nogent-le-Roi in 1606 and died at Montreal in 1673. Daughter of the king's attorney, she lived with her father until his death in 1640, when she met Dauversière and first heard of New France and its mission women.

Sailing from La Rochelle in June 1641, Mance reached Quebec that August and nursed settlers all winter. In May 1642 she went upriver with Maisonneuve to Montreal, dressed the altar for its first Mass on 18 May, and founded a hospital in her own home that year. A larger hospital on Saint Paul Street followed in 1644, which she ran alone for seventeen years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-boyce:
John Boyce, writing as Paul Peppergrass, was an Irish priest, novelist, and lecturer who carried his countrymen's stories to America. Born in Donegal in 1810 to a wealthy hotelkeeper and magistrate, he studied at Navan and Maynooth. He was ordained in 1837 and labored eight years on the Irish mission before emigrating in 1845. From Eastport, Maine, he moved in 1847 to St. John's Church, Worcester, Massachusetts, where he stayed until his death in 1864.

His novels, Shanty Maguire, The Spaewife, and Mary Lee, or the Yankee in Ireland, show a keen observer's humor and pathos rather than his full scholarship. One was dramatized. He also wrote for the Boston Pilot and published sketches and criticism. He lectured in New York on the satisfying influence of Catholicity on intellect and senses, winning fame as an eloquent speaker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-chetwode:
John Chetwode Eustace was an Irish antiquary whose Classical Tour made him suddenly celebrated in 1813. Born in Ireland about 1762 to an English family, he was educated at Sedgley Park and the Benedictine house at Douay. He taught rhetoric at Maynooth and was ordained there. He then returned to England as tutor and chaplain, traveling through Italy in 1802 with three pupils and keeping the journal that became his famous book.

In 1805 he became tutor at Jesus College, Cambridge, to George Petre. That post was unusual for a Catholic priest. It drew charges of indifferentism from Bishop Milner, who accused him of laying aside distinctive priestly worship to please Protestant company. Friends insisted he never lost sight of his sacred character. Later tours took him to Greece, Sicily, Malta, and France. A final Italian journey ended with malaria at Naples, where he died in 1815, lamenting errors in his writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-ponce:
John Ponce was an Irish Franciscan philosopher and theologian of the Scotist school. Born at Cork in 1603, he entered the Irish Franciscans at Louvain young, studied philosophy at Cologne and theology at Louvain under Hugh Ward and John Colgan. He was called by Luke Wadding to Rome's new College of Saint Isidore in 1625.

Teaching philosophy and then theology at St. Isidore's, Lyons, and Paris, he won great repute for learning. His Course of Philosophy of 1643 drew opposition from Mastrius. He answered in 1645 by accepting Scotus's conclusions without adopting all his proofs, a reply Mastrius acknowledged as illuminating. His Complete Course of Theology of 1652 and his great Commentary on the Sentences of 1661 explain Scotist teaching with clearness and precision. He also aided Wadding's edition of Scotus and served Irish Confederate Catholics at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justice:
Justice, in the sense used here, is the cardinal virtue that perfects the will and moves it to give each person what belongs to them. Prudence perfects the intellect, fortitude steadies anger and daring, and temperance moderates appetite. Fortitude and temperance look inward; justice looks outward to others, sharing that field with charity. Charity gives from one's own stores to a neighbor in need; justice hands over what is already his.

Human beings hold God-given rights prior to the State, as free, intelligent persons made to know and love their Creator. Those natural rights, with rights from Church, State, or one's own work, form the object of justice. Justice therefore requires that everyone be left in free enjoyment of their rights. Claims like a needy man's call for help count here as charity, not justice, unless a strict right stands behind them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kielce:
Kielce is a diocese in the south of Russian Poland, covering the province of Kielce and part of Piotrkow. This entry describes its cathedral town, where the Assumption church, now the cathedral, dates to 1173, alongside a Holy Trinity church from 1646 and a St. Adalbert church on the saint's traditional martyrdom site.

First raised in 1807 by Pius VII and made subject to Cracow, the diocese was suppressed after its first bishop clashed with the Russians. Leo XIII restored it on 26 December 1882 as a suffragan of Warsaw. By 1910 it counted 944,604 Catholics, 242 parish churches, and 339 secular clergy. Its seminary had ten professors and 79 seminarians, and Sisters of Charity ran a hospital and ten houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lace:
Lace, from Latin laqueus, a noose, is hand-made openwork in two great families: needle-made and bobbin-made. Needle lace splits into lacis, stitches on knotted netting, linen lace by drawn or cut work, and punto in aria, lace worked in the air with no foundation at all.

Bobbin lace, made with bobbins on a pillow or by crochet, tatting, and knotting, takes three chief forms. First comes early peasant tape lace. Then finished sprays joined by brides or net ground. Last comes the all-in-one method of Mechlin, Binche, and Valenciennes. History reaches back to Egyptian knotted netting found in 1909 at Qurneh, covering vases beside a seventeenth-dynasty burial of about 1600 before Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lecce:
Lecce, in Apulia's Terra d'Otranto, is the capital of its province, seven and a half miles off the sea. It is an industrial and trading city of tobacco, grain, wine, oil, and woven goods, with marble quarries nearby. Megalithic ruins prove very ancient settlement, and ancients knew it as Lupiae, with a port Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius enlarged.

Under the Normans it became a countship, with famous counts like Tancred, who contested Henry VI for the Two Sicilies, and Gautier de Brienne. Charles V gave it new life, and its uniform baroque style endures: the cathedral of St. Oronzio, first built in 1114, the seventeenth-century St. Domenico, sixteenth-century St. Croce, and a 240-foot cathedral tower still serving as a lighthouse between Otranto and Brindisi. Its first named bishop appears in 1057.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leuce: Leuce was a Thracian see, known to no old writer on history or place. Yet its bishop Symeon sat at the Council of Constantinople. Lists of sees from the tenth to the thirteenth centuries put Leuce under Philippopolis. It is likely today's village of Copolovo, south of Philippopolis, or Plovdiv, in Bulgaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mace:
A mace is a short, richly ornamented staff, often of silver, topped with a knob or head-piece. It bears a coat of arms and is borne ahead of high church bodies, magistrates, and learned institutions as a sign of authority.

More strictly, the mace is the club-shaped beaten silver stick, mazza. Papal mazzieri, Swiss Guard vergers in papal chapels, and papal messengers, cursores apostolici, bear it at bishops' consecrations. Carried on the right shoulder with head upward, it descends from the twelfth century, when mazzieri, once servientes armorum or halberdiers, formed the pope's bodyguard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manifestation:
Manifestation of conscience was a practice in many religious orders, by which members told their superior the state of their conscience. The aim was close knowledge of each person, so the superior could guide spiritual growth. It belonged to domestic, paternal rule, needing no church jurisdiction, so even a lay or female superior might receive it.

Such knowledge let a superior judge how often a member should receive communion, what reading suited them, what penances fit, and what counsel met their doubts and temptations. Its first object was the member's own good, its second the institute's good. A superior could not use it to harm the member or betray the secret. Leo XIII's decree Quemadmodum of 17 December 1890 ended compulsory manifestation and barred superiors from pressuring members toward it. It required the decree to be read aloud once a year. Voluntary sharing for help stayed lawful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marianus-of-f:
Marianus of Florence was a Friar Minor and historian, born at Florence about the mid-fifteenth century and dead there on 20 July 1523. Little is known of his life, and his writings share that obscurity, not because they lack worth but because none was ever published and copies are hard to get.

His chief work, the Fasciculus Chronicarum, tells Franciscan history from the order's start to 1486. Writing three centuries after St Francis, he still merits trust, since he used original sources now lost, whose precious fragments reach us through him. He died of plague while giving last sacraments to Florence's stricken people. Besides the Fasciculus, he wrote a catalogue of over 150 famed women of St Clare's order. He also wrote histories of Mount Alvernia and the Tuscan province, a Rome itinerary, and a history of St Francis's habit moving to Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-de-fran:
Marie de France was a French poet of the twelfth century, known almost only by inference, since no biography survives. Her lays honour a King Henry, and her Ysopet a Count William, long a puzzle for scholars.

Careful study of her language settled both figures. She was Norman, writing in the pure Norman dialect of the later twelfth century, and her patrons were Henry II of England and his son William, Count of Salisbury. Her works comprise fifteen lays of the Breton cycle's love group, short octosyllabic tales of knights braving deeds for their ladies, told with rare feeling, simple grace, and clear brevity. Her Ysopet holds 103 fables from Henry Beauclerc's English version, and her Purgatory of St Patrick sends an Irish knight through a cavern of torments and joys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-master-of-the:
Master of the Sacred Palace, Magister Sacri Palatii, is the pope's theologian, an office always held by a Friar Preacher. St Dominic, appointed in 1218, was the first holder. Among eighty-four Dominican successors, eighteen later became cardinals, twenty-four archbishops or bishops, and six generals of the order. 

Dominic's work included teaching St Paul's letters to church leaders and their aides, who had idled gossiping in waiting rooms. The office's work continues today: by 1409 records show the Master lecturing on set days and answering questions at theological conferences. Before the Inquisition congregation of 1542 and Index of 1587, he condemned books and banned reading under censure, a task fading by 1604. Pius V made him canon theologian of St Peter's in 1570, though Gregory XIII revoked that bull. Since Rome's 1870 occupation he examines Italian bishop candidates and confers the doctorate from his Vatican apartment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice:
Maurice, Roman emperor from 582 to his death in November 602, was born in 539 to an old Latin family settled in Cappadocia. He began as a soldier and served well against the Persians under Tiberius II, who gave him his daughter Constantina in marriage and named him successor. Tiberius died almost at once, and Maurice took the throne peacefully.

He found the treasury empty from his predecessor's lavish spending and cut court costs with strict thrift. The thrift won him a name for stinginess, deep unpopularity, and in the end his fall. His twenty years saw the Persian war drag on for a decade, then a revolution that let Chosroes II beg Roman help to regain his throne. Maurice failed to turn that opening to the empire's gain, and decay continued under him as under his neighbours in time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-eusta:
Maurice Eustace, eldest son of Sir John Eustace of Castlemartin, County Kildare, was martyred for the faith in November 1581. Penal laws sent him to the Jesuit college at Bruges, where he longed to join the Society of Jesus. His father ordered him home, but after a brief stay he went back to Flanders. His teachers advised him to serve religion in the world instead.

Back in Ireland he became a captain of horse and won many of his men back to the faith. He never dropped his priestly dream and secretly took Holy Orders. His servant told his father, who had him jailed in Dublin. A younger brother, eyeing the estates, denounced him as priest, Jesuit, and friend of the queen's foes. Tried for high treason, he refused Archbishop Loftus's offer of a daughter's hand and a fortune, and died for his faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-negligence:
Negligence, from Latin for not picking out, is the condition of not heeding. More specifically it is the omission, habitual or not, of the care required for performing duties, or at least for their full adequate discharge. In Saint Thomas's teaching it marks the commission of all sins, and it also stands as a special sin in itself.

Its particular deformity is the imputable lack of such solicitude as is here and now demanded for meeting obligations. Thomas therefore sets prudence as the virtue directly opposed to it. The same applies to actions not of precept, once undertaken. Negligence is at first a lack of promptness of will, distinct from torpor or slipshod execution. It is commonly no more than venial, except when it omits something indispensable for salvation, or when remissness wholly extinguishes love of God in the soul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-negro-race:
This 1911 article, retained in the online edition for historical reasons only, surveys the peoples then grouped under the term negro, derived from Spanish and Latin words for black. Strictly the term covers certain peoples and tribes of Central Africa and their descendants elsewhere, though it is often loosely applied to a large portion of mankind. Blumenbach's fivefold division treats them first under Ethiopian, embracing Kafir, Hottentot, Australian, Alforian and Oceanic groups.

Pritchard and Latham protest against equating negro with African, since dark-skinned peoples of various types live across the tropics. The article insists that not all members of the group share common traits. It quotes Professor Dowd that lumping all Africans as one race with one character is as unscientific as lumping all Europeans and Americans. It surveys physical traits, languages, customs and history, in the period's anthropological terms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nice:
Nice comprises the Department of Alpes-Maritimes. Restored by the Concordat of 1801 as suffragan of Aix, its countship belonged to Sardinian States from 1818 to 1860, when the see became Genoa's suffragan. Annexed to France in 1860, Italian parts left for Vintimille, and in 1862 Nice returned to Aix. In 1886 Grasse's arrondissement left Frejus for Nice, which now unites the former dioceses of Nice, Grasse and Vence.

Tradition says Saint Barnabas, sent by Saint Paul, or Mary Magdalen, Martha and Lazarus evangelised Nice, and makes Saint Bassus, martyred under Decius, its first bishop. The Gallic see existed in 314, sending delegates to Arles, and its first historically known bishop, Amantius, attended Aquileia in 381. Nearby Cimiez, famed for Saint Pontius's martyrdom about 260, held a see under Saint Valerianus, united to Nice by Leo the Great's rescript after 450.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-novice:
A novice, in canon law, is a person admitted to a religious order and prepared through exercises and tests for profession. Romans used the word for a newly bought slave, Greeks called the beginner archarios, and the church now applies it to entrants who have usually passed a postulant's probation.

No age limits bind admission, though children below puberty need parents' consent, and parents hold a year to reclaim a child entered without it. Trent fixed sixteen as the earliest age for profession, so a one-year novitiate implies entry at fifteen, and the entry details impediments, training, and vows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obedience:
Obedience, from the Latin for hearkening, is treated here as a settled virtue, not a single act of compliance. It means carrying out a superior's order with the exact aim of fulfilling the injunction, a habit Aquinas roots in the natural and positive subordination of the world.

Against post-Reformation claims that subjection clashes with freedom, the entry argues that lawful command serves human nature and God's prescriptions. Obedience also colors every virtue, since each virtue executes some precept, yet as a special virtue it stands apart by its focus on command itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oblate-sister:
The Oblate Sisters of Providence, a congregation of Black nuns founded at Baltimore, taught Black children when no schools served them. French refugee priest Jacques Joubert, charged with Black Catholics at Saint Mary's chapel, found sermons forgotten for want of teaching.

Encouraged by Fathers Babade and Tessier, Joubert joined four Black women who ran a small private school and hoped to consecrate their lives. With the archbishop's approval, they began a novitiate and made vows on 2 July 1829, Elisabeth Lange becoming first superior. Sister Mary Elisabeth Lange was chosen superior of the first four sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occurence:
Occurrence, in liturgy, means two offices falling on the same day, while concurrence means one office's second Vespers meeting the next office's first Vespers. Moving Easter and the shifting Dominical Letter cause most clashes, since fixed feasts collide with feasts that wander through the calendar.

An accidental occurrence, like Corpus Christi landing on Saint Augustine's day in 1891, is settled for that year by the diocesan ordo. A perpetual one, like a patron's octave day always meeting a fixed feast, needs Rome's lasting change, moving the office to the first free day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-omnipotence:
Omnipotence, God's power to effect whatever is not intrinsically impossible, is defined here without implying any limit on God. A power reaching every possibility must be perfect, and the impossible means only the self-contradictory, whose parts cancel into nothingness.

Aquinas therefore calls it more exact to say the impossible cannot be produced than to say God cannot produce it. The entry rejects views that make absurdity an object of divine intellect, and sets Hugh of Saint Victor's formula beside it: God is almighty because he cannot be powerless. Vorstius, the Calvinist, included the contradictory within divine power, a view the entry rejects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peterspence:
Peter's Pence, called Romescot by the Anglo-Saxons, was an annual tribute to the Holy See, a penny from each householder holding land of a set value. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces a payment almost confined in the Middle Ages to England and a few northern peoples, and certainly English in origin. Vague tales crediting Ini of Wessex in 727 give way to firmer ground with Offa of Mercia.

Offa promised 365 mancuses a year, confirmed to papal legates at Chelsea in 787. The money served the Roman poor and church lights, though later chroniclers tied the gift to the Saxon school in the Borgo. Ethelwulf, after visiting Rome with his son Alfred about 855, ordered 300 mancuses yearly, whether as a new grant or a confirmation nobody can say. The entry follows the tribute through later centuries and peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-physical-effe:
The physical effects of abstinence, in this Catholic Encyclopedia entry, concern partial abstinence from flesh meat, not vegetarianism. Friday fish observance, vigils, Lent's forty days, and Ember Days form the Catholic practice at issue. Man, the entry argues, is naturally omnivorous, as teeth and digestive chemistry show, with flesh food largely entering his natural diet.

What then does periodic abstinence do to the body? Effects vary as widely as causes: family history, age, personal history and infant feeding, education and environment, climate, occupation, and present state all shape the outcome. Later sections weigh fasting's influence on digestion, nerves, and general health, judging the Church's discipline against physiology rather than piety alone. The study treats a bodily question in bodily terms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-simon-:
Pierre-Simon Laplace was the French astronomer and mathematician often called the Newton of France. He was the son of a small farmer near Caen, born in 1749. He won a Paris professorship at eighteen with a letter on mechanics. He rose through the Revolution, the empire, and the Restoration, serving briefly as minister of the interior in 1799.

His fame rests on celestial mechanics, the mathematics of the heavens. In 1773 he showed that the average motions of the planets do not drift. That result secured the long-term steadiness of the solar system. His System of the World of 1796 and his five-volume Celestial Mechanics of 1799 to 1825 also advanced the theory of probability and the mathematics of gravitational attraction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pilgrimage-of:
The Pilgrimage of Grace was the great Catholic rising in northern England in 1536 against Henry VIII's religious changes. It was led by Robert Aske, a London barrister of Yorkshire family. It drew on anger at the suppression of monasteries, the seizure of first fruits, church taxes, and the power of Thomas Cromwell.

Breaking out on 13 October after the failed Lincolnshire rising, Aske marched nine thousand men into York. He restored expelled monks and nuns to their houses and gathered thirty to forty thousand at Doncaster. He won a royal promise of pardon and a parliament at York, but the promise was broken, a fresh rising followed, and Aske and other leaders were executed for treason.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-au-princ:
Port-au-Prince archdiocese covers western Haiti, with about 668,700 people, mostly Catholics, scattered over some 3,080 square miles. Most know their religion only slightly. Created by bull of 3 June 1861, it has had an almost entirely French clergy. Dominicans served the territory in the eighteenth century, and after the Revolution unworthy clergy held it until the 1860 Concordat drove them out.

Five archbishops served in turn: Testard du Cosquer, Guilloux, Hillion, Tonti, and Conan. In January 1906 Conan held Haiti's first provincial council, approved in August 1907, and fourteen diocesan synods had published their acts. The senior seminary sits in France, at St Jacques in Finistère, while Port-au-Prince holds a seminary-college under the Holy Ghost Fathers with five hundred pupils. St Louis de Gonzague teaches about as many boys, and two girls' schools, Ste Rose de Lima and Notre Dame du Sacré-Cœur, complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-precedence:
Precedence, from Latin praecedere, to go before another, is the right to enjoy a mark of honour ere other folk. It means the best place in a march, rite, or assembly. It also means the right to speak, vote, or sign ere others, or to fill the most honoured posts. Civil and church law both rule them. In canon law rank follows place in the hierarchy of rule and of order. Where rank ties, age of foundation decides: qui prior est tempore, potior est jure.

With colleges, rank turns on the worth of the person to whom the college clings. The order runs: the pope first, then cardinals, patriarchs, archbishops, exempt bishops, suffragan bishops, titular bishops, and prelates nullius. Within these ranks, date of ordination and promotion decides, and for bishops or archbishops the date of first rise to that rank. Custom or privilege may bend the rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preface:
The preface, Latin praefatio, is the first part of the Eucharistic prayers, the Anaphora or Canon, in all rites, now split from the rest by the Sanctus's singing. Thanks forms the heart of the service, so all liturgies open the Anaphora by thanking God for His gifts.

The thanks prayer lists the gifts, starting with creation, running through nature and grace, and touching much Old Testament history. It crests in Christ's Incarnation, Life, and Passion, where the Last Supper's tale leads to the words of institution. It ever opens with a call to the folk: Lift up your hearts, then a call to give thanks to the Lord our God. The folk answer with words from the earliest age: It is meet and just. The celebrant takes up their word and starts the preface ever: Truly it is meet and just.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prescription-:
Some form of prescription under some name is said to belong to each civilized nation's municipal law, save the Jewish. Devas calls the doctrine, in economics as in politics, essential to social welfare. Public policy holds that ownership of things the law deems ownable should not stay forever unsure, and that suits should not outlive suitors, who are mortal, while title deeds perish.

In old Roman law, usucapio let a Roman citizen's holding of a bodily thing for a lawful span ripen into full ownership, dominium. Cicero notes that a farm can be left by a father, but usucapio of a farm, the end of worry and of suits, comes not from a father but from the laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prose-or-sequ:
A long encyclopedia survey traces the Sequence, also called the Prose. It is the chant sung at Mass on feasts, between the Gradual and the Gospel. Unlike a Breviary hymn, where every stanza shares one metre and tune, an early sequence gives each pair of verses its own shape and melody. Many open with a free line or an Alleluia. The survey follows the form from its roots in the Alleluia jubilus through its later, more regular phases.

Readers meet two great epochs of sequence writing. The first age is loose and varied. The second age is tidier, and its Whitsuntide and Requiem pieces reach full symmetry across all verses. Names, dates and manuscript sources fill the later pages. A closing bibliography points to the great collections edited by Dreves, Blume and Bannister at Leipzig.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prudence:
Prudence, from the Latin prudentia, ranks among the four cardinal virtues. The word is a shortening of providentia, seeing ahead. This encyclopedia entry gathers definitions from Aristotle onward. It prizes his brief formula, right reason applied to practice, in Father Rickaby's rendering. Fuller accounts call prudence an intellectual habit. It is the knack of seeing, in a concrete situation, which course is virtuous and which is not, and how to reach the one and shun the other.

Though prudence in some sense rules the moral virtues, it perfects not the will but the intellect, pointing out the golden mean here and now. The entry weighs how this virtue guides choice amid messy circumstances, drawing on Saint Thomas Aquinas, Rickaby and Lehmkuhl. Readers studying ethics meet here a clear account of why good intentions still need a sharp eye for the right act at the right moment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-obe:
Religious obedience is the submission religious vow to God and promise their superiors, who guide them towards perfection under their order's purpose and constitutions. Lessius defines it as letting oneself be governed through life by another for God's sake. It has three elements. The first is giving up independence in outward actions. The second is the motive of personal perfection, joined as a rule to works of mercy and charity. The third is an express or implied contract: the order undertakes to lead the member to that end.

The entry defends the practice on grounds. Community life offers example and counsel under a rule the Church vouches for, and orders exist for their members' perfection and for spiritual and corporal works of mercy. Such shared work needs a union of efforts only obedience secures, just as an army's campaigns depend on military obedience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhythmical-of:
A rhythmical office is a liturgical hour prayer, a canonical hour of the Breviary. In it, psalms and lessons aside, every part shows metre, rhythm, or rhyme. Antiphons to each psalm, to the Magnificat, Invitatorium, and Benedictus, and responses and versicles after each of the nine lessons take rhythmic form. Benedictions before the lessons and antiphons to the minor hours do the same. The old name was Historia, with or without rhytmata or rimata, a label later writers misunderstood.

The entry praises varied stanza structure. Refined language matches rich, deep contents, and the parts join into a striking picture of its saint or mystery. Its example is Archbishop Pecham of Canterbury's Office of the Trinity, whose first Vespers opens with antiphons praising the Son with the Father in the seraphic cry. The office thus turns the hour into a rhymed portrait of its subject.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ricoldo-da-mo:
Ricoldo da Monte di Croce was a Florentine Dominican whose travels and polemical writings made him a leading Western voice on Islam. Born at Florence about 1243, he joined the Dominicans in 1267 and taught in Tuscan convents. After a pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 1288, he spent years as a missionary in western Asia, based chiefly at Baghdad. He then returned to Florence and rose to high office in his order.

His Itinerarium, written around 1288-91, served as a guide for missionaries and describes the Eastern lands he visited. Five letters lamenting the fall of Acre in 1291 followed. His best-known work, Contra Legem Sarracenorum, written at Baghdad, became a widely used polemical source against Islam and was often reprinted. He also wrote against Jewish errors, on Eastern nations, and in defence of Thomas Aquinas, and he started rendering the Koran about 1290. He died at Florence in 1320.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-isaac-:
Robert Isaac Wilberforce was a Tractarian theologian who followed Newman toward Rome but died before ordination. Born at Clapham in 1802, second son of William Wilberforce and younger brother of Samuel, Bishop of Oxford, he entered Oriel College in 1820. Graduating with a double first, he became a fellow of Oriel in 1826 alongside Newman, Pusey, Keble, and Froude.

After Anglican orders he served as rector of East Farleigh and Burton Agnes, then as canon of York and Archdeacon of the East Riding from 1841. His wide reading made him influential among Tractarians. Twice widowed, he became a Catholic at Paris on All Saints' Day 1854, a heavy loss to the High Churchmen. On Manning's advice he entered the Accademia at Rome to study for the priesthood. He died at Albano in 1857, having received only minor orders. With Samuel he had written their father's life in five volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-wace:
Robert Wace was a Norman poet of the twelfth century, author of the Brut and the Roman de Rou. Born at Jersey about 1100 to a noble family, he was sent young to Caen for schooling and then to Paris. Returning to Caen between 1130 and 1135, he became reader to King Henry I. Short of money, he began writing to increase his income.

His earliest surviving works are lives of St Nicholas and St Margaret and the Brut, or Geste des Bretons, finished about 1155 and presented to Queen Eleanor. In 1160 he began the Roman de Rou, dedicated to Henry II. He attended the king at Fecamp in 1162. He was made canon of Bayeux between 1160 and 1170, on his own testimony. When he began the Rou in 1160 he called himself a clerk of Caen; in its later part he records a Bayeux prebend from the king. He died at Bayeux in 1174.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrifice:
Sacrifice, identical with the English offering, means the offering of a sense-perceptible gift to the Deity. It is an outward manifestation of veneration, aiming at communion with Him. Strictly, the offering becomes a sacrifice only when a real change is effected in the gift, by slaying, shedding blood, burning, or pouring out. No theory of sacrifice can rest on a priori methods; every theory must fit pagan systems, especially Judaism and Christianity.

Pure Buddhism, Mohammedanism, and Protestantism have no real sacrifice. The entry considers pagan, Jewish, and Christian sacrifice, then theory. Among Indians, ancient Vedism was above all a sacrificial religion linked to Agni and Soma. A Vedic saying calls sacrifice the world's navel. Originally a feast for the gods, sacrifice gradually became a magical agency for influencing the gods. This appears in the formula do ut des.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanctifying-g:
Sanctifying grace, from the Latin gratia and the Greek charis, is treated in this long doctrinal entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It means God's supernatural gift to thinking creatures for their eternal salvation. Salvation itself means heavenly bliss from seeing the Triune God face to face, who dwells, in Paul's words, in light no one can approach without grace. Grace stands as the pillar of the whole Christian edifice.

Among the three great ideas of sin, redemption, and grace, grace serves as the God-given means that frees people from sin through Christ and leads them to heaven. Before Trent, schoolmen rarely said actual grace, preferring terms like special help and divine motion, and they did not sharply separate actual grace from sanctifying grace. The entry then defines sanctifying grace as the lasting state of holiness in the soul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sentence:
In canon law, a sentence is the decision of a court on an issue brought before it. This short entry sorts sentences into kinds. A definitive sentence settles the main question in dispute. It acquits, condemns, or declares that a crime was committed whose penalty follows by the act itself. An interlocutory sentence settles some side point during a trial. Some interlocutory sentences carry the force of a final one, as when a court declares itself incompetent.

A final sentence must be definitive and unconditional. It must be given by the judge in court, before the parties or their agents, in writing or dictated for the minutes. It must match the charge and state the law behind any punishment. Once pronounced, it cannot be revoked by the same court. Merely interlocutory sentences need no special formalities and may be revoked by the judge who gave them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silence:
Silence, as writers on the spiritual life present it, is a practice commanded under pain of total failure. Yet no rule meets more complaint from beginners. Scripture warns of the tongue's perils, with death and life in its power. The New Testament calls the man who never offends in word perfect. Pagans knew the danger too. Pythagoras imposed strict silence on his disciples, and vestal virgins kept severe silence for years.

Silence works from three sides. It aids good, since we keep silence with men to speak better with God, while mere abstaining without that aim is the idle silence Ambrose condemns. It prevents evil, guarding against sins of speech. It also serves as a means of union with God. Monastic rules, above all Saint Benedict's, give the practice its classic form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simplicius-fa:
Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrice were martyrs at Rome in the Diocletian persecution of 302 or 303. The brothers Simplicius and Faustinus were cruelly tortured for their Christian faith, beaten with clubs, and finally beheaded, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber. Their sister Beatrice drew the bodies from the water and buried them.

For seven months she lived with a pious matron named Lucina, and with her help she aided persecuted Christians day and night. At last she was found and arrested. Her accuser was her neighbor Lucretius, who coveted her lands. She boldly told the judge she would never sacrifice to demons, being a Christian, and was strangled in prison. Lucina buried her beside her brothers. Soon divine punishment struck Lucretius, so the legend says, at a feast. Their feast is 29 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Providence of Montreal, more exactly the Daughters of Charity, Servants of the Poor, began on 25 March 1843. Bishop Bourget founded the community with Emilie Gamelin, born Marie Emélie Eugénie Tavernier. Their work covered shelter for children and the aged, visits to poor and sick homes, care for the infirm and homeless, dispensaries for the needy, and teaching the young.

Leo XIII gave final approval to their rule on 12 September 1900. By then the community counted about 1,600 religious in more than eighty houses. Its chief Montreal works included the mother-house, the Gamelin Asylum, the Longue-Pointe Refuge, the Hospital for Incurables, and a home for deaf children. Foundations also spread to seven provinces, from Quebec to Washington, Montana, and Oregon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-di:
The name Sisters of Divine Providence covers several distinct congregations surveyed in this entry. The Saint Vincent de Paul branch began at Molsheim in the Diocese of Strasburg under Vicar Ludwig Kremp. It reassembled at Bindernheim after the Revolution and won church and civil approbation in 1807. Its Mainz mother-house later counted 76 branch houses with 730 members.

A Lorraine congregation founded by Jean-Martin Moye in 1762 worked for Christian education of rural children and care of the sick. It later reached Belgium and the United States. Six sisters from Mainz founded the Pittsburgh branch in 1876, numbering about 200 sisters running schools in Pittsburgh, Wheeling, and Columbus. A Kentucky provincial house at Newport grew from the Lorraine congregation, and an 1842 Münster foundation under Eduard Michelis cared for poor and neglected children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-pr:
The Sisters of Providence of Saint Mary-of-the-Woods grew from the French congregation of Ruillé-sur-Loir, founded in 1806 by Jacques-François Dujarié, curé of Ruillé in Sarthe. After a struggling start, the society found firmer footing. Bishop Gabriel Bruté of Vincennes sent his vicar general, de la Hailandière, to France for priests and teachers, and the new bishop obtained a colony of sisters for Indiana.

Six sisters under Mother Theodore Guérin reached America on 22 October 1840. Hardships followed, from climate, poverty, and isolation to a seven-year misunderstanding with the bishop, who informed her he had deposed her and dismissed her. Her death came on 14 May 1856, and steps toward her beatification began at Rome. By 1910 the sisters counted 937 members running 68 parochial schools, 15 academies, and teaching 20,000 children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-sa:
The Sisters of Sainte Anne of Providence began at Turin in 1834, founded by Marchesa Julia Falletti de Barolo for the care of children and the sick. The Holy See approved the order on 8 March 1848. Its mother-house stands at Florence, with daughter houses at Bagnoria, Castelfidardo, and Assisi, where the sisters run the industrial school of San Francesco, founded in 1902.

In Rome the sisters kept two infant asylums, Saint Anne and Sacred Heart, sheltering three hundred children. At Secunderabad in the Diocese of Hyderabad, India, they ran a convent educating European and Eurasian girls, plus a school at Kazipet. In Italian Eritrea they kept a home for children redeemed from slavery, carrying the Turin foundation's care for the young across three continents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
An offshoot of the Sisters of Providence founded by Jean-Martin Moye in 1762, the Sisters of the Institute of Charity owe their present form to Antonio Rosmini, whose institute they truly join. In 1831 four uneducated young women from the Val d'Ossola came to Portieux for religious training, then returned to a Locarno community meant as novitiate and poor school. Poor management led Rosmini to intervene, reform their rule, and take full responsibility for them.

From then on they stood as a distinct body, called Rosminiane in Italy. The order is mainly contemplative but undertakes teaching girls and young children, visiting the sick, and instructing in Christian doctrine when needed. Italy counted about 600 sisters and 60 novices in 1908 across 64 houses. The English branch began in 1843 through Lady Mary Arundel at Loughborough, whose convent school was the first poor day school in England taught by nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-sa:
Founded at Paris in 1642, the Society of Saint Sulpice trains directors for seminaries. At Olier's death in 1657 the society stood approved by religious and civil authority, with the Paris seminary and three provincial seminaries open to young clergy. Successor Alexandre Le Ragois de Bretonvilliers drew up its constitution, aiming to labour under the bishops for the education and perfection of clergy.

Members take no vows but renounce all prospect of church dignities, and a superior general with twelve lifelong assistants governs the society. Olier had longed to work in Canada, and in 1657 he sent four disciples to Villemarie, now Montreal. In 1663 the associates of Notre-Dame ceded the Island of Montreal to the Sulpicians, who became its owners and lords. The society reached the United States in 1791.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-space:
Space, from the Latin spatium, is one of philosophy's most stubborn puzzles. This entry works through what the word actually means. In everyday speech it means empty extension occupied by bodies. It is the room in which local motion happens, and the distance between things. That idea is so tied to emptiness that space is set against bodies as containing none.

That popular picture assigns space no limits, though not strictly infinite ones. The entry moves from this common notion into deeper disputes among philosophers and psychologists over space's nature. Readers who want a clear map of a question that has preoccupied thinkers for centuries will find the terms defined first, and the disagreements laid out after.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-squillace:
Squillace was a suffragan diocese of Reggio in Calabria, its city standing near the Ionian Sea between two branches of the River Alessi, a centre of wine, olive. And silk work with lead and iron mines and earthenware shops. This entry traces the ancient Scyllaceum, whose harbour is now a marsh, founded, says Cassiodorus, who was born there, by an Athenian colony.

Saracen invasions in the ninth and tenth centuries, a Turkish landing in 1595. And the earthquake of 1783 brought ruin, yet the diocese kept the bodies of many saints, including St Achatius in the cathedral and St. John Terrestre of Stilo. St. Bruno founded two Carthusian houses nearby, and the entry joins civic disaster to enduring devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-boniface:
St. Boniface, or Winfrid, Wynfrith, was apostle of Germany, martyred on 5 June 755, or 754. This entry follows a native of England, though some authorities have claimed him for Ireland or Scotland. His birthplace is not known, though it was probably the south-western part of Wessex, with Crediton in Devonshire given by more modern authors. The same uncertainty exists about the year of his birth, though it seems safe to say he was born not before 672 or 675, nor as late as 680.

Descended from a noble family, he showed great ability from his earliest years and received a religious education. His parents intended him for secular pursuits, but missionary monks who visited his home inspired him with higher ideals, and Winfrid felt called to a religious state. His father's permission came only after much difficulty, and he went to the monastery of Adescancastre, and the entry follows him to Germany and martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-canice:
St. Canice, or Kenny, whose feast falls on 11 October, was born in 515 or 516 at Glengiven, in today's County Derry, Ireland. He died at Aghaboe in 600. This entry follows a boy descended from Ui-Dalainn, a Waterford tribe dwelling on an island now identified as Inis-Doimhle in the Suir. His father was a noted bard who made his way north and settled at Glengiven under its chief. His mother was called Maul, and her name lives in the church of Thomplamaul in Kilkenny.

Canice spent his early years watching his chieftain's flocks. Then God called him to higher aims, and in 543 we find him at Clonard under St. Finian, a fellow pupil of St. Columba. In 544 he studied at Glasnevin with St. Kieran of Clonmacnoise and St. Comgall of Bangor, under St. Mobhi. Ordination as priest followed in 545 at the Llancarvan monastery in Glamorganshire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eustace:
Eustace, second abbot of Luxeuil, carried Columbanus's work forward after his master's banishment. A monk of Bangor in Ireland and one of Columbanus's first companions, he helped spread the Gospel across central and southern Europe. When Columbanus was exiled from Burgundy for rebuking King Thierry's morals, he urged his community to choose Eustace as successor. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 29 March 625.

Three years after his appointment, Clothaire II, now ruler of the triple Frankish kingdom, sent Eustace to Bobbio in Italy to recall Columbanus. The exile declined in a letter to the king, asking instead royal protection for Luxeuil and its brethren. During the twelve years that followed, Eustace ruled the house Columbanus had founded, holding its community through a founder's absence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-felix-of-c:
Felix of Cantalice, a Capuchin friar who died in 1587, spent his working life as shepherd and farm labourer before he wore a habit. Born to peasant parents on the Abruzzi border, he was hired at nine to a farmer at Cotta Ducale and stayed over twenty years, first tending sheep, then labouring on the farm. Leisure went to prayer in harsh or solitary places. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Rome to 18 May 1587.

A friend's reading of desert fathers' lives stirred a longing for the hermit's life, tempered by fear of living without a superior. Prayer resolved him toward the Capuchins. Art shows him holding the Infant Jesus, from a vision in which Mary placed the child in his arms. The entry honours holiness formed in fields and farmyards before the cloister claimed it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-isabel-of-:
Isabel of France, sister of Louis IX, refused emperors' sons to found a Poor Clare house at Longchamp. Daughter of Louis VIII and Blanche of Castile, born in March 1225, she showed extraordinary devotion, modesty, and virtue from childhood at court. Innocent IV's bull of 26 May 1254 let her keep Franciscan fathers as special confessors, and she loved the order even more than her royal brother. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Longchamp to 23 February 1270.

She broke an engagement with a count and refused Conrad, son of Emperor Frederick II, though pressed by everyone, even Innocent IV, who later praised her fixed resolve to remain virgin. Wishing to found a Clare convent, she watched Louis begin buying land in the Forest of Rouvray near Paris in 1255. The first stone of its church was laid on 10 June 1256. The entry follows a princess whose no outlasted kings and popes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lawrence:
Lawrence, deacon and martyr of 258, was the last of Rome's seven deacons to die under Valerian. At August's start the emperor ordered all bishops, priests, and deacons put to death at once, in Cyprian's quoted Latin. On 6 August Pope Sixtus II was seized in a catacomb and executed forthwith, with four deacons. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates Lawrence's death to 10 August 258.

Two more deacons, Felicissimus and Agapitus, died the same day as Sixtus, and the fourth-century Roman calendar keeps their feast with his. Four days later Lawrence, last of the seven, suffered martyrdom. His anniversary falls on 10 August, and his fame soon outgrew the brief record. The entry gives the persecution's machinery in Cyprian's own words, then the deacon's death, four days after his pope's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-leonard-of:
Leonard of Port Maurice, Franciscan preacher and ascetic writer, turned a ruined stomach into a preaching career. Born on 20 December 1676 at Porto Maurizio to Domenico Casanova and Anna Maria Benza, he studied brilliantly with Rome's Jesuits, then joined the Riformella, an offshoot of the Reformati Franciscans. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Rome's S. Bonaventura to 26 November 1751.

He took the habit on 2 October 1697, made his novitiate at Ponticelli in the Sabine hills, and finished studies at S. Bonaventura on the Palatine, remaining there as lector, or professor. He hoped for the Chinese missions, but severe gastric haemorrhage sent him home to Porto Maurizio's Observant monastery in 1704. Restored after four years, he began preaching in Porto Maurizio and nearby, and Cosimo III de' Medici soon handed him a monastery for his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-maurice:
Maurice, leader of the Theban Legion, heads a short entry on a mass martyrdom in Roman Gaul. As primicerius, or first officer, he commanded a legion said to be wholly Christian, summoned from Africa to crush a revolt of the Bagaudae. Ordered to sacrifice to the gods, the soldiers refused, and after two decimations the whole legion was massacred at Agaunum, about 287.

The entry points readers to fuller treatments of Agaunum and the legion for the value of the legend. Maurice is pictured as a knight in armour bearing a standard and palm, and he became patron of soldiers, swordsmiths, dyers, and clothmakers, invoked against gout and cramps. His feast falls on 22 September, and towns across Switzerland, Piedmont, France, and Germany claim him as protector.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-substance:
Substance, the first of Aristotle's categories, means being that exists in and by itself and underlies change. This entry builds the idea from ordinary cases: wood stays wood whether hot or cold, flat or upright, yet once burned to ashes and gases it is wood no longer. Some changes touch only the surface, while others destroy the thing itself.

Behind surface change must stand something lasting, a base that carries secondary realities, and that base is substance. Scholastic writers split the notion into primary substance, the single thing itself, and secondary substance, the shared essence found in genus and species. Later sections sort complete and incomplete substances, and a full bibliography of scholastic sources closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-surplice:
The surplice is a large-sleeved tunic of half length, made of fine linen or cotton and worn by all clergy. Its wide sleeves set it apart from rochet and alb, and unlike the alb it is shorter and never girded. Hem and sleeves carry embroidery or lace, though lace wider than fifteen inches is barred, since ornament must not swallow the vestment itself.

Most used of all liturgical garments, it serves as choir dress and procession dress. It is also the official dress of lower clergy for sacraments, blessings, and Benediction. There it stands in for the alb, which present custom reserves for Mass and a few functions. A bishop blesses it when giving the tonsure, with words about the new man created in righteousness. Its history runs from eleventh-century England and France to general use in the thirteenth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taenarum-gree: Taenarum was a titular see in Greece, suffragan of Corinth, lying five miles north of Cape Taenarum, now Cape Matapan. It held temples of Demeter and Aphrodite, and today it is the village of Kyparrisos. After escaping Spartan rule, the maritime Laconians formed a confederation and founded a capital called Caeneopolis, new town. Inscriptions show that this new city was really Taenarum under its old name, though two close cities may have existed. No bishop of Taenarum appears in the episcopal lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-temperance:
Temperance, from Latin temperare, to mingle in due proportions, is treated here as one of the four cardinal virtues. It is the righteous habit of governing natural appetite for pleasures of the senses by reason's norm. In one sense it marks every moral virtue. For St Thomas it is also a special virtue, bridling concupiscence, the yearning for pleasures that most attract the heart. Those pleasures preserve the individual, perpetuate the race, and ease human life.

Its subordinate virtues are abstinence, chastity, and modesty. Abstinence restrains food and drink, with a measure varying by person and purpose. It opposes gluttony and drunkenness, which damage health and so are intrinsically wrong. Gluttony is seldom a grievous sin, but drunkenness is when complete, destroying reason's use for a time. Chastity governs sensual pleasures tied to propagation, against lust. Temperance ranks last among the cardinal virtues, after prudence, justice, and fortitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-terce:
Terce, like Sext and None, dates to Apostolic times. Romans, Greeks, and Jews divided day and night into four three-hour parts. Terce was the day's second division, from nine until midday. The New Testament names the sixth and ninth hours, and records the Holy Ghost descending at Pentecost at the third hour. These texts show the three hours chosen for prayer by Christians, probably from Jewish custom. Third-century Fathers mention the three as daily prayer hours.

Tertullian says we should always pray, with no prescribed time. Yet he adds that the common hours, third, sixth, and ninth, deserve no lax observance, since Scripture marks them more solemn. Clement and Tertullian speak only of private prayer then. The Canons of Hippolytus agree. On station days, Wednesday and Friday, and on Sunday, these hours were recited in common. The entry follows Terce through later breviaries to modern use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abbey-of-:
The Abbey of Bonne-Espérance stands near Binche in Hainault, Tournai, Belgium. It owes its founding to William, only son of Rainard, Knight of Croix. Seduced by Tanchelm's heresies, William returned through St Norbert's persuasion, and his parents gave land to Norbert for an abbey at Ramignies, while William followed him to Prémontré. Ramignies proved unsuitable, so Odo, the abbot, led the colony elsewhere.

Legend says Odo cried Bonæ spei fecisti filios tuos, Thou hast made Thy children to be of good hope, on seeing the spot. Others credit the statue of Our Lady of Good Hope venerated there. Either way his confidence proved sound, and the abbey grew, sending out learned priests. Odo's successor Philip the Almoner wrote books published in Migne. The abbot, Bonaventure Daublain, saw the abbey pillaged by French Republicans in 1792 and 1794, and its survivor gave it to Tournai for a seminary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-college-d:
France's free college for higher learning, founded by Francis I, is the institution traced here. Planned as early as 1517, it took shape only in 1530 under Budé and Jean du Bellay's spur. Paris University taught neither Hebrew nor Greek. Francis set up chairs in both tongues, hiring the best teachers: Paradisi and Vatable for Hebrew, Danes and Toussaint for Greek, paid from royal coffers.

Free lectures drew students and roused Paris professors, who lived on fees, to rivalry. Noël Beda accused the Royal Lectors before Parliament, claiming the Vulgate would lose authority if Hebrew and Greek were taught in public. Marcillac defended them and won. Later charges of Calvinist leanings brought bans on reading and interpretation, yet the college endured and grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-evangelic:
Protestants of many churches, joined in the Evangelical Alliance of 1846, are the fellowship described here. First meeting's resolution aimed to let Christians realise and show others that a living, everlasting union binds all true believers in the Church's fellowship. Nine points of belief, the Basis adopted at the first conference, sum the Gospel as members hold it.

Scripture's divine inspiration, authority, and sufficiency head the Basis, with private judgment in interpretation. Godhead's unity and Trinity of Persons, human depravity from the fall, and Incarnation, atonement, mediation, and reign of the Son follow, with justification by faith alone and the Spirit's work. Conferences, branches, and evangelical cooperation follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-holy-lanc:
John chapter 19, verse 34, opens this entry: after Christ's death a soldier opened his side with a spear, and blood and water flowed at once. Of that weapon nothing certain is known until Antoninus of Piacenza, visiting Jerusalem in 570, reports seeing crown of thorns and lance together in the basilica of Mount Sion.

Later claims multiply and clash. A Syriac manuscript of 586, lit by Rabulas at Florence, gives the piercing scene high prominence, with the name Longinus written above the soldier in Greek letters. Rival lances at Antioch, Constantinople, Rome, and Vienna follow, each with its champions. The entry sorts relic from legend with a sceptical eye.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-renaissan:
Rebirth of ancient learning and art, and the modern spirit it carried, form the two faces of the Renaissance examined here. In the general sense it means achievements of the modern spirit against the medieval mind. In the particular sense it means revival of classic, above all Greek, learning and recovery of ancient sculpture, painting, and architecture, lost for a thousand years in Western Christendom.

Ecclesiastical history moves in periods matching secular revolutions: Fathers to 476, Middle Ages through tumult, then the new age from the late fourteenth century. Influences good and evil, traceable to pagan letters and remains, are summed in relation to the Church. Humanism, art, and the papal court each take their turn in a wide survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-sacrament:
Forgiveness after baptism, granted through priestly absolution, defines the sacrament examined here at great length. Penance stands as a sacrament of the New Law, not a mere ceremony, because Christ instituted it as an outward sign imparting grace. Penitent's actions, presenting himself, accusing himself of sins, and priest's actions, absolving and imposing satisfaction, together make the sign.

Confession names the whole procedure, and tribunal of penance fits it well, since the penitent plays accuser, accused, and witness at once while the priest judges and sentences. Grace frees from guilt and, for mortal sin, eternal punishment, reconciling the sinner with God. Matter, form, history, and practice follow in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Valence was erected as a university on 26 July 1452 by letters patent from the Dauphin Louis, later Louis XI, who loved the town. Pius II approved the erection in a bull of 3 May 1459.
