In February 1541 Canon Pierre Morel set up a college for thirteen poor students. During the sixteenth century Valence won fame for law, taught by Italian professors or by men trained in Italy.

The Portuguese jurist Govea taught there in 1554 and 1555, the French jurist Cujas from December 1557 to 1559, and François Hotman from late 1562 to August 1568. At Hotman's urging Bishop Montluc won from Charles IX the edict of 8 April 1565 uniting Grenoble and Valence. Cujas returned to a chair at Valence from August 1567 to 1575. The entry sketches a law school famed across France for a generation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valence:
Valence, in the Drôme department of France, was restored as a diocese by the Concordat of 1802. It was formed from the old Diocese of Valence, minus the portion placed in the new Diocese of Viviers. It also took parts of Die, Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, Vienne, Orange, Vaison, Gap, and Sisteron. From 1802 to 1821 it answered to Lyons, and since 1821 it has depended on Avignon.

The old diocese traces Christianity at Valentia to three missionaries sent from Lyons by St Irenaeus: the priest Felix and the deacons Achilles and Fortunatus, all martyrs. That tradition dates from the early sixth century. The Chronicles of the Bishops of Valence, probably compiled about the middle ages, carries the story onward. The entry follows the see's bishops, councils, and modern life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venice:
Venice is presented as a northern Italian city built on 117 small islands joined by 378 mostly stone bridges. Its houses rise on rows of piles driven into the shallow lagoon floor, its canals include the S-shaped Grand Canal. Gondolas and small steamers carry its traffic, while a long rail bridge links it to the mainland.

The lagoon itself splits into dead marshes and living shallows, guarded from the Adriatic by the Lido. Beyond topography the entry follows Venice's long political arc, from lagoon settlement to maritime republic, its leagues and wars against Genoese, Turks. Mainland rivals, its defence of Crete, and its commerce in the Black Sea and beyond. Churches, government, and trade all figure, but the spine of the piece is how an island city held a sea empire together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vice:
Vice is defined here not as a single wicked act but as a settled habit inclining a person to sin. Formed by repeated sinful acts of one kind and then itself becoming their cause. Its character in any case comes from the virtue it opposes, and calling an individual act a vice is, the entry insists, entirely improper.

A man may therefore have vices yet at times commit no sin, and isolated sins do not make him vicious; guilt attaches to the act, not the habit. Aquinas holds that, absolutely speaking, sin surpasses vice in wickedness, and even when sin is forgiven the vice may remain. Rooting out a habit of sinful indulgence takes unrelenting vigilance and contrary acts over a longer or shorter time, as the vice is more or less inveterate. Infused virtues return only through God's free gift.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-violence:
Violence, from Latin vis, is defined here in moral philosophy as an impulse from outside forcing a person to act against choice, without any concurrence on his part. The moving cause must come from without, since no one can do violence to himself. The person compelled not only fails to assist the force but resists it as far as possible; mere indifference is not violence.

Violence cannot touch the will's own elicited acts directly, since unfreedom contradicts the very notion of a willed act. Acts the will commands through other faculties, inward or outward, can be coerced when those faculties are impeded. Such commanded acts are still called voluntary, so violence makes them involuntary to that extent and frees the agent from responsibility. Irresistible coercion removes blame for the outward act, while violence that can be resisted limits freedom in proportion to its vehemence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-russe:
William Russell Grace was an Irish-born merchant, philanthropist, and the first Catholic mayor of New York. Born at Cork in 1832, he died at New York in 1904. His father sailed for Peru in 1850 and came home empty-handed, but young William stayed, joined John Bryce at Callao, and built Grace Brothers and W. R. Grace and Company, with offices across the west coast of South America and New York and San Francisco.

Grace founded the New York and Pacific Steamship Company and married Lillias Gilchrist in 1859. During the Irish famine of 1878 and 1879 his firm gave a quarter of the Constellation's relief cargo. The gift lifted him to the mayoralty in 1880 and again in 1884, the first Catholic in the post. Each mayoral morning he attended Mass at Saint Agnes before work. In May 1897 he founded the Grace Institute, offering training to women in dressmaking, shorthand, typing, bookkeeping, and home science.
charlotte-s-inheritance: Braddon gave her heroine an inheritance with strings attached. Charlotte's fortune comes wrapped in secrets. The sensation plot twists. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The book preserves that Victorian novel. Its pages add to the record of the past.
christian-science:
Mark Twain published this book on Christian Science in 1907, and his preface divides it honestly. Book I, written some four years earlier and corrected for this printing, is a comic narrative. Book II, from 1903, attempts a character portrait of Mrs. Eddy drawn solely from her own acts and words. It also gives an account of the monarchy she built and the laws she wrote to govern it.

Book I opens in Vienna in 1899 with a fall from a cliff and a heap of broken bones. A Christian Science practitioner sends absent treatment and the assurance that nothing is the matter. The joke sustains a serious inquiry into the church's claims, finances, and discipline. Book II drops the clowning. Twain's verdict on Mrs. Eddy mixes admiration for her genius with alarm at her power.
clarence:
Bret Harte began Clarence with a rich man sitting lonely in a San Francisco theatre as news of civil war arrives from Washington. Clarence Brant, president of the Robles Land Company, has married the older widow of his old patron Judge Peyton, and her half-maternal rule of the house has curdled into tyranny. The novel flashes back to Clarence's youth as the Peytons' protégé and his love for their adopted daughter.

Harte moves between California ranch society and the coming war, testing a gentle, intuitive hero against pride, suspicion, and old obligations. Clarence is among his longest fictions, less a mining tale than a novel of manners with the war gathering behind it. The theatre scene's hollow home sets the key: wealth everywhere, welcome nowhere.
cliges-a-romance:
Chrétien de Troyes wrote Cligès in twelfth-century France, and L. J. Gardiner translated this prose version, published in 1966. The romance begins with Alexander, a Greek emperor's son who wins glory and love at King Arthur's court, then follows his son Cligès. Cligès loves Fenice, the wife of his uncle the emperor Alis, and the lovers are trapped between desire and loyalty.

Fenice, aided by her nurse's potion, feigns death rather than share her body with two men, and the plot turns on tombs, swoons, and discovery. The introduction praises Chrétien's modern, self-debating heroines. Among Arthurian romances Cligès is the clever one: part love story, part argument against the Tristan legend it keeps rewriting.
confidence:
Henry James wrote Confidence, published in 1879, one of his early novels of Americans in Europe. Bernard Longueville, a painter with easy charm, is asked by his friend Gordon Wright to judge the woman Gordon means to marry, Angela Vivian. Bernard meets Angela in Siena and finds her clever, proud, and hard to read. His report, meant kindly, helps break the match.

Years later the three meet again, with fresh pairings forming and old feelings in the way. James builds the tale from drawing-room talk, letters, and small shifts of trust among a tiny cast, moving between Italy, France, and Baden. The title points at its true subject: what friends owe each other in candor, and what a confidence kept or shared can cost.
conscience:
Eliza Lee Cabot Follen's Conscience, an American book of moral tales for children published under her byline as Mrs. Follen, opens in a family parlor in early spring. Mrs. Chilton spends the twilight hour reading stories aloud to her boys Frank and Harry, who have just asked for chalk money without saying why. The frame tale turns on that small secrecy: a trifle, the chapter title says, is where conscience begins its work.

Inside, the stories Mrs. Chilton reads teach honesty through errands, coins, and small temptations rather than sermons. A tale of a necklace and other household incidents show how tiny concealments grow into habits. Follen, a Boston abolitionist and children's writer, trusted narrative more than scolding. Readers meeting the book today get a clear specimen of nineteenth-century American Sunday reading, gentle in tone and exact about the moment a child first decides whether to tell the truth.
cy-whittaker-s-place:
Joseph C Lincoln placed Cy Whittaker's Place in Bayport, his fictional Cape Cod village of sea captains, gossips, and town politics. Retired Captain Cy Whittaker comes home after years away and settles into the old house that gives the book its title. His return stirs neighbors who remember him well. Bailey Bangs and clerk Asaph Tidditt supply much of the local talk.

Chapters follow Cy as he fixes up the house, faces a front-door caller, and gets drawn into village schemes. A letter, a visitor, and a bargain that falls through complicate his quiet plans. Town meeting politics and Congressman Everdean raise the stakes. Lincoln tells the tale in salty dialect and gentle humor, celebrating small-town loyalty while laughing at its vanity.
darwin-and-modern-science:
A C Seward edited Darwin and Modern Science in 1909 to mark the centenary of Darwin's birth and fifty years since the Origin of Species. Darwin's own words on the mental qualities behind his success open the book. An introductory letter from Sir Joseph Hooker, Darwin's oldest scientific friend, follows.

Essays survey the theory's state: Arthur Thomson on Darwin's predecessors, August Weismann on selection, Hugo de Vries on variation, and William Bateson on heredity in modern lights. Cell structure, mimicry, and Muller's once-opposed hypothesis get detailed treatment. Cambridge published the volume as its verdict on Darwinism at a moment when Mendel's genetics was remaking the theory from inside. It remains a rich snapshot of biology in transition.
doctor-grimshawe-s-secret-a-romance:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Doctor Grimshawe's Secret is a posthumous romance, edited with preface and notes by his son Julian Hawthorne. Julian admits that dragging a great writer's unfinished work into print is not always wise, since surviving friends often show more zeal than discretion.

Hawthorne himself published during his lifetime as much as the public had time to read, Julian notes, and critics may fairly doubt what an author left in his desk. Yet this romance, dedicated to the Lathrops, offers Hawthorne's late imaginings on secrets, inheritance and old houses. Readers of Hawthorne will value it as a fragment, atmospheric and tantalising rather than complete.

domestic-peace:
Honore de Balzac set Domestic Peace in November 1809, when Napoleon's fugitive empire touched its apogee after Wagram. Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell translated the tale. Paris, contemporaries said, never saw such entertainments; kings orbited the emperor like stars. Into a great ball Balzac sends the beautiful, mysterious Countess to whom the sketch owes its tension.

Officers and coquettes hiding behind fans trade gossip with malicious old Madame de Lansac. Monsieur de la Roche-Hugon is ruined, they say. Meanwhile a husband hunts the wife he has not seen since marriage. Balzac, dedicating the piece to his niece Valentine Surville, compresses a whole adultery plot into a novella of glances. It belongs to his Scenes from Private Life.
dr-breen-s-practice:
William Dean Howells published Dr Breen's Practice, a short novel, in 1881. Grace Breen is a young woman physician, trained in an era when many patients doubted women doctors. She takes up practice near Jocelyn's, a fading seaside resort on a bold headland. The hotel there stands amid young birches reclaiming failed building lots. Her patients are mostly summer boarders.

Illness, gossip, and courtship test Breen's judgment through twelve chapters. A difficult case forces her to weigh pride against a patient's safety. Colleagues and admirers press their own views on her career. Howells treats her ambition seriously while showing the social cost she pays. Readers get an early American novel about a professional woman, handled with Howells's quiet realism and close attention to manners.
driven-from-home-or-carl-crawford-s-expe:
Horatio Alger Jr sends sixteen-year-old Carl Crawford onto the road in Driven from Home, his pockets holding thirty-seven cents and a small gripsack in his hand. A stepmother has made home impossible, and his father has let him go. The grave, strongly built boy must now earn his own living.

Carl finds work, faces dishonest men like the bullying Stark, and protects his earnings against schemes that tempt weaker boys, including a companion who steals from a drunken man's wallet. Alger rewards Carl's honesty and steadiness in the usual way, with patrons, promotion, and a restored home. The tale is a clean example of his rags-to-respectability formula for nineteenth-century boys.
essays-on-life-art-and-science:
Samuel Butler's Essays on Life, Art and Science collects pieces left at his death, edited by R A Streatfeild and published in London in 1908. Butler wrote most of them for the Universal Review in 1888, 1889, and 1890. Two began as lectures. Their subjects range widely, as Streatfeild admits in his introduction. Butler's curiosity refused narrow bounds.

Ramblings in Cheapside and a family sketch of an aunt, her nieces, and a dog open the volume. Travel pieces describe a shrine at Montrigone and art in the Saas valley of Switzerland. Thought and Language tackles how words shape thinking. The Deadlock in Darwinism attacks weak points in evolution theory, Butler's lifelong quarrel. A guide to making the best of life sums up his practical creed. Readers meet Butler the essayist at his most various and contrarian.
fabre-poet-of-science:
Georges Victor Legros wrote Fabre, Poet of Science, a biography of the French naturalist Jean-Henri Fabre, translated by Bernard Miall. Legros, a devoted disciple, drew on Fabre's letters and long conversations with him. Fabre himself supplied a preface, dated at Sérignan in November 1911. He praises the book as the memoir he was too ill to write.

Chapters trace Fabre's poor childhood, his teaching in Corsica and at Avignon, and his slow rise as an observer of insects. Legros explains Fabre's methods, ideas, and discoveries alongside the life. The famous garden laboratory, the Harmas, anchors the later chapters. Evenings at Sérignan and a quiet twilight close the story. Readers get both a life and a guided tour of the work, told by a friend determined to correct legends about his master.
fairbanks-first-philosophers-greece:
Arthur Fairbanks edited and translated this sourcebook of the earliest Greek philosophers in 1898. It gathers the surviving fragments of thinkers from Thales to the Pythagoreans. Ancient testimony about their lives and teachings stands beside the fragments.

These pre-Socratic thinkers first asked what the world is made of. Thales named water, others named air, fire, or number. Almost everything they wrote is lost except quoted scraps. Fairbanks arranges the scraps so readers can watch philosophy being born. The material is brief but dense with first ideas. Students of Greek thought still start from collections built on this plan.
falk-a-reminiscence:
Joseph Conrad framed Falk as a reminiscence told among seafaring men dining at a small hostelry on the Thames. The narrator recalls Hermann, captain of the German barque Borgmester Dahl, and Falk, the taciturn Scandinavian tug skipper at an eastern port. A damaged ship, a towage bargain, and Hermann's niece draw the two men together.

Falk carries a terrible secret from his time aboard a drifting, starving ship, and it governs both his courtship and his price for the tow. Conrad keeps the horror mostly unspoken, building pressure through manners, money, and silence at the dinner table. The novella ranks among his finest shorter works, a study of appetite, shame, and survival.
false-evidence: False Evidence, E. Phillips Oppenheim's novel. The false trail unfolds. This book preserves that mystery. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. It holds its historical place. Those who study the era will use it.
flip-a-california-romance:
Bret Harte places this California romance on a hidden terrace in the Coast Range above the Los Gatos road. The air there is so laden with spice and resin that travellers called the spot Gin and Ginger. No hunter or surveyor has ever worked out its secrets. The man who finally penetrates it is Lance Harriott, a gambler and outlaw riding under a stagecoach to escape the sheriff of Monterey County.

The terrace's only settlers are a charcoal burner and his daughter, and Harte builds the tale around the outlaw's arrival among them. The girl of the title, Flip, is as wild as the place and quicker than any of the men hunting or hunted in it. A diamond found in the hills turns the hiding place into a prize others will kill for.
flower-of-the-north-a-modern-romance:
James Oliver Curwood dedicated Flower of the North, in Detroit in January 1912, to his comrades of the northern wilderness. One comrade, Jeanne d'Arcambal, would find herself the heroine of the story. The novel opens in a lamp-lit cabin where the artist Gregson raves about a girl. Such hair, such eyes, such colour, he swears.

Philip Whittemore, Gregson's bronzed friend, listens with amusement at yet another discovery. The two had adventured together in South America less than three years before. Now the Canadian wilds hold a beauty neither can explain. A modern romance follows, of a trading venture, a hidden past, and the flower of the north herself. Curwood writes his usual mixture of wilderness hardship and sentiment, with Jeanne's honour at the centre of the plot.
friarswood-post-office:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote Friarswood Post Office as a village novel about faith, illness, and quiet duty. The story centres on the King family, who keep a small shop and post office after the father's death. Ellen King helps her widowed mother run the business. Her younger brother Alfred, once the merriest boy in the parish, now lies crippled and in pain.

Much of the book stays close to Alfred's couch and the daily work of the shop. A ragged travelling lad draws scorn from Ellen, yet Alfred sees a fellow sufferer in him. Through visitors, letters, and small kindnesses, the Kings learn patience and sympathy. Yonge tells a gentle story about how a household bears loss and finds worth in ordinary care.
fridthjof-s-saga-a-norse-romance:
Esaias Tegner, Sweden's national poet and a bishop, retold an old Icelandic saga as Fridthjof's Saga, a long poem in varied verse forms. Thomas and Martha Holcomb translated the Swedish into English for American readers. Fridthjof, a bold Norse sea hero, grows up beside Ingeborg, a king's daughter. Their love drives the whole poem.

King Bele's sons refuse Fridthjof their sister's hand, since he holds no royal rank. Sent away on a hard errand, he returns to find Balder's temple burned and blame fixed on him. Exile turns him viking, raiding and winning gold while his name blackens. Ingeborg is married off to an aging king, and Fridthjof's grief sharpens into wandering. At last he comes home, helps rebuild the burned temple, and wins pardon, peace, and Ingeborg. Swedish schoolchildren once learned the poem by heart; readers still come for its sea fights, feasts, and code of honor.
from-ritual-to-romance:
Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romance argues that the Holy Grail romances grew out of ancient fertility ritual. Weston says in her preface that Frazer's Golden Bough first set her on the road to the Grail castle. Jane Harrison's Themis and talks with Professor von Schroeder sharpened the question: could such rites also lie behind medieval romance? The book answers yes, and spends its chapters proving the chain.

Inside, the Fisher King, the waste land, and the Grail procession are read as survivals of vegetation ceremonies older than Christianity. Weston connects the romances to mystery cults, seasonal kingship, and the symbolism of fish and lance. Her test of a theory is how many facts it explains. Readers get the study that later fed modern poetry its waste land imagery, a work of comparative religion that treats King Arthur's knights as priests in disguise.
from-the-memoirs-of-a-minister-of-france:
Stanley John Weyman wrote From the Memoirs of a Minister of France as twelve tales told by the Duc de Sully, minister of Henri the Fourth, in old age. His contents promise the clockmaker of Poissy, the tennis balls, the lost cipher, the cat and the king, and Fontainebleau. The narrator begins by foreseeing that enemies will call his memoirs self-serving.

The tales mix court intrigue with provincial adventure: mayors of Bottitort, a governor of Gueret, and talents the minister discerned before an assassin's crime ended his master's schemes at one blow. Weyman, the English master of the historical short story in his day, ventriloquizes Sully's dry pride convincingly. Each tale is a small machine of honor, policy, and swordplay.
gaston-de-latour-an-unfinished-romance:
Walter Pater's unfinished romance Gaston de Latour opens at the Château of Deux-manoirs in La Beauce, the corn country of central France. The Latour family house, largely Gaston's own work, was left incomplete at his death around 1594. Gaston himself, a young clerk in orders, moves through a France divided by the wars of religion. The chapter list promises Our Lady's Church, Modernity, and Suspended Judgment among its stations.

Inside, Pater follows his hero's education in seeing: churches, sermons, new learning, and the court of the last Valois kings. Peach-blossom and wine, a lower pantheism, and the shadows of coming events give the chapters their sequence of moods. The romance breaks off unfinished, as its title admits, leaving Gaston suspended in Pater's favorite posture of judgment delayed. Readers get Pater's only sustained historical fiction, a Renaissance portrait gallery built around one watchful young Frenchman.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAGreece_CIA_G:
George Papadopoulos led the colonels who seized Greece in 1967, and this article names him the CIA's front man. It traces his rise through the Greek state: his path to the premiership, the regency, and the presidency of the junta's Greece.

Papadopoulos had worked with American intelligence for years before the coup, which made his regime a standing charge against the CIA in Europe. The article's author and publication are not identified in the text, but its argument was a common one in the period. The piece is preserved as Cold War journalism on America's man in Athens, held without endorsement.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ChurchCommittee:
Laurence Stern reported on January 29, 1976, on the Church Committee's findings about domestic spying, and the headline gives the scale: Domestic Spying Abuses Said to Cover 40 Years. The Senate committee traced the abuses from J. Edgar Hoover's appointment in 1924 onward.

Among the endpoints named is the FBI's monitoring of the 1964 Democratic convention, where agents had spied on political figures for the White House. Stern covered the committee as it dismantled the Bureau's claim to have policed only crime. The article is first-rate contemporary reporting on the oversight revolution, preserved from the Washington Post's pages.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HalperinMaurice:
An unnamed reviewer takes up Maurice Halperin's book The Rise and Decline of Fidel Castro, issued by the University of California Press. Halperin subtitled his work an essay in contemporary history. The book follows Castro from revolutionary victory to the harder years that followed, written while the story was still current.

A rise-and-decline frame asks where a revolution turns, and Halperin wrote as a scholar of Cuba watching events closely. The review gives readers a period judgment on his answer. It preserves how the book was received by critics measuring Castro's Cuba in real time.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-IssermanMaurice:
An unnamed writer advises Maurice Isserman on a practical problem: asking the FBI for its files. The letter warns of the disadvantages of requesting field office files. Among them are processing delays long enough to endanger a book-contract deadline, a real cost for a working historian.

Freedom of Information requests were a research tool with a clock problem. Files arrived slowly, in pieces, sometimes after the book they were meant for had closed. The letter passes on hard-won strategy about where to ask and what to expect, the kind of advice researchers traded in this period.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RECE_RECE: A masthead is the printed nameplate of a periodical, and this one belongs to RECE. RECE was the periodical of the Representación Cubana del Exilio, a Cuban exile organization based in Miami, Florida. Its editor was Jorge Mas Canosa, who became the most powerful voice of the exile community. A masthead fixes a publication's name, its sponsoring body, and its editor. This one preserves those facts for an exile paper of the Cold War years.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SchillerLawrenc:
The premiere issue of a magazine called 'Prevailing Winds' is preserved here. Its featured pieces include one on a CIA massacre, one on strange new weapons, and Peter Dale Scott's 'Oswald Framed?' The publisher is not identified. A first issue is a magazine's manifesto, and this one's table of contents announces its territory at once.

Small magazines carried the intelligence debate of the 1970s and 1980s. Scott, a former diplomat and poet, was among the field's most serious writers, and his presence dates the venture's ambitions. The issue gathers the era's subjects in one cover: secret wars, secret weapons, and Dallas. It preserves the editorial bet that readers wanted all three in the same pages.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
DINA was the secret police force that served General Augusto Pinochet after his 1973 coup in Chile. One declassified American description, quoted in this posting's title, called it a Gestapo-type police force. The National Security Archive page gathers that record of how United States officials saw DINA.

That comparison matters because it came from inside the government, not from later critics. It shows American officials understood DINA's methods while Chile's regime jailed, tortured, and killed its opponents. The page preserves that judgment inside the declassified record on the regime. It names the agency plainly and without softening.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Wo: Armando Fernandez Larios was a Chilean intelligence operative under the Pinochet dictatorship, and his case later reached United States immigration authorities. This National Security Archive briefing book covers the ICE proceedings against him, under the label "worst of the worst." The evidence supplied here is limited to the title and a citation of Peter Kornbluh's Pinochet File dossier. Readers should treat the page as a pointer to that case rather than a full account of it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
Between 1977 and 2001, American intelligence analysts repeatedly assessed which countries might build nuclear weapons next. This briefing book gathers those assessments under the title Proliferation Watch. Its sources are reports from the Energy Department's Z Division and its special projects staff.

Those reports covered proliferation risks in countries including Pakistan and South Africa. Both pursued real weapons programs in that period, so the assessments can be checked against outcomes. A set spanning twenty-four years lets readers see how official forecasts changed as programs succeeded, stalled, or were abandoned, and how often the watchers were right.

Communist Parades as an Intelligence Target in the Cold War: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
Briefing Book number 673, published in May 2019 and edited by Carlos Osorio, Silvia Tandeciarz, and Johanna Weech, collects American intelligence documents on Argentina's killing machine. The records cover the years 1976 to 1983, when the military junta waged a dirty war against its own people and thousands disappeared.

The quotes are damning. A Buenos Aires police chief told the CIA he wanted no prisoners for interrogation, only cadavers. Junta leader Rafael Videla worked to hide mass murder to protect Argentina's image abroad. Before the coup, CIA analysts had already predicted a hardline mentality would dominate the army, and a senior State Department official called Argentina's record the worst anywhere. Few collections show foreknowledge and cruelty documented this plainly.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_colombia_Colombia:
In November 1985, guerrillas seized Colombia's Palace of Justice in Bogota. The army retook it in a fire that killed around a hundred people, including most of the supreme court. In December 2024, the National Security Archive reported that President Gustavo Petro had asked the United States to speed up release of its records on the case.

The request, covered in a posting edited by Michael Evans, rests on a simple fact. American agencies reported on the siege and its aftermath. Their files may answer questions Colombia still argues about, including the fate of people who left the building alive. For readers, the piece shows declassification as live diplomacy between two governments, nearly forty years after the event.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Joint_D:
In November 2019, the National Security Archive joined a public declaration on Guatemala's Historical Archive of the National Police, the AHPN. The statement says plainly that the archive is in trouble: a collection praised across the hemisphere and the world now limps along in a much reduced state.

The AHPN's files document the police role in Guatemala's civil war and have supported prosecutions and family searches for the disappeared. A joint declaration is a defensive weapon; scholars and archivists lend their names to make neglect politically costly. Readers get the text and context of an international attempt to protect evidence of state crimes from slow administrative erasure, a threat less visible than fire or theft but nearly as final.
herb-of-grace:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's English novel The Herb of Grace, published by Lippincott in 1901, runs to forty-four chapters of country-house feeling. It opens with Malcolm Herrick, a lover of the picturesque, arriving in a landscape the novel treats as medicine for tired spirits. The Herrick household, with Anna and her mother, anchors his parish world. Dinah and Hugh Rossiter appear early in the chapter list, marking the friendships and attachments the story will test.

Inside, visits, letters, and parish duties carry a slow courtship of temperament rather than incident. Carey writes goodness as a practice: small mercies, borne disappointments, and duties done without audience. The herb of grace itself, rue, gives the book its emblem of sorrow sweetened by patience. Characters learn to want what they can honorably have. Readers get a long, gentle argument that character, not event, is what changes a life.
history-of-france: The History of France, by Charlotte Yonge. The French story. This book preserves that history. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
history-of-the-conflict-between-religion:
John William Draper, professor at the University of New York, published his History of the Conflict between Religion and Science in 1874, a founding blast of the warfare school of history. His preface observes a great and growing departure from public religious faith among intelligent classes in Europe and America, much of it private and unacknowledged.

Draper traces science from Greek and Arab learning, through lake-dwellings a hundred thousand years old and the philosophy of Averroes, to the church's resistance against geology and evolution. He ends by reconciling faith with a universe animated by intellect. Andrew Dickson White later expanded the same thesis. Draper's book, whatever historians now qualify, shaped how the Victorian world argued about science.
holiday-romance:
Charles Dickens wrote Holiday Romance in four parts as tales supposedly penned by children, beginning with William Tinkling, Esq, aged eight. Tinkling insists his beginning-part is real and must be believed most, and quarrels with cousin Bob Redforth over the editorship. The children marry in a dancing-school closet with a green ring.

The parts continue with a pirate romance, a fairy tale of a magic fish-bone told by a small princess, and other schoolroom inventions. Dickens imitates childish spelling, logic, and grandeur while smuggling in satire of adult romance and fairy-tale morals. Grandmarina and the fish-bone show him playing. Written for Our Young Folks in 1868, the pieces charm as experiments by a master relaxing.
horace:
Theodore Martin's Horace, from the Ancient Classics for English Readers series, introduces the Roman poet to English readers. Martin follows Horace from birth and education through his campaign with Brutus and Cassius, and his return to Rome after Philippi.

Later chapters treat his introduction to Maecenas, the journey to Brundusium, the first satires, the gift of the Sabine farm, and his life in Rome. Love poetry, poems to friends, praises of contentment, and relations with Augustus complete the portrait. Martin stresses Horace's hold on the modern mind, and readers new to Latin poetry will find this a friendly doorway.
hypatia-or-new-foes-with-an-old-face:
Hypatia, or New Foes with an Old Face, by Charles Kingsley, is a novel of fifth century Alexandria. Kingsley warns readers in his preface that the age was hideous as well as great. Virtues and vices, he says, showed themselves side by side with startling openness. He insists that no suspicion of immorality touches his heroine. The great Neo-Platonists, he adds, were people of rigid and ascetic virtue, whatever their followers did.

Hypatia herself was the city's famed woman philosopher, a teacher of mathematics and Neo-Platonism. Around her Kingsley gathers monks, bishops, prefects, and Goths. Cyril's Alexandria is tearing itself apart between church and synagogue, palace and mob. The old face of the subtitle is fanaticism. The new foes are Victorian ones, Kingsley hints, wearing fifth century dress. His novel argues with his own century through a murdered woman of the ancient world.
in-freedom-s-cause-a-story-of-wallace-an:
G. A. Henty's In Freedom's Cause tells Scotland's war of independence as a story for boys. His preface, addressed to his dear lads, defends Wallace and Bruce against legend. Careful inquiry, he argues, verifies nearly every deed reported of them. Wallace especially suffered from the writings of his bitter enemies.

Young Archie Forbes of Glen Cairn joins Wallace after leaving home. The capture of Lanark, the Barns of Ayr, and the battles of Stirling Bridge and Falkirk follow. Bruce takes up the cause, through Methven, Dunstaffnage, and a mission to Ireland. The heiress of the Kerrs and the siege of Aberfilly fill the later chapters. Bannockburn crowns the tale. Henty mixes documented history with a fictional hero's adventures, his most popular recipe for teaching the past.
ivanhoe-a-romance:
Walter Scott published Ivanhoe in 1820, and it remade the historical novel. The scene is England under Prince John, while King Richard the Lionheart is away on crusade and held prisoner. Wilfred of Ivanhoe, a Saxon knight cast out by his father Cedric, comes home in disguise to fight in the great tournament at Ashby.

Around him Scott gathers Robin Hood under the name Locksley, the Templar knight Brian de Bois-Guilbert, the proud Rowena, and Rebecca, the Jewish healer whose courage carries much of the book. Tournaments, a castle siege, a witchcraft trial, and Richard's masked return drive the plot. Ivanhoe made the Middle Ages vivid for generations of readers and fixed the Robin Hood tale in its modern shape.
jack-sheppard-a-romance: Jack Sheppard, a romance, by William Harrison Ainsworth. Another edition. This book preserves that novel. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. The archive guards it with care.
jimgrim-and-allah-s-peace:
Jimgrim and Allah's Peace is an adventure novel by Talbot Mundy, built around a man called Grim. Mundy dedicates it to Jimgrim himself, promising never to print his real name, rank, or honors. The contents list twenty chapters with teasing, quoted titles. The story is told by a journalist sent out from Chicago.

Ordered to Jerusalem in 1920, the narrator lands in a city he knew before the World War. He recalls the bedbugs, the citadel moat, camel prices, and his shaky Arabic. His orders begin with the words, 'Look for a man named Grim.' Chapter titles promise escorts, outlaws, and enemies who prove useful. Mundy mixes spy work, desert politics, and dry humor in his hero's world.
justice:
Justice is John Galsworthy's play of 1910, printed here among his collected plays in the second series. The sample lists the full Galsworthy canon, series by series, from The Silver Box to Windows. Justice stands as number three of the second series, after The Eldest Son and Little Dream. Its subject, announced by the title, is the law itself and what the law does to men.

A young clerk, William Falder, commits a forgery and is ground through trial and prison. Galsworthy follows him from his employers' office to the assizes and into a cell. The play's prison scenes pressed the case against solitary confinement with unusual force. This edition places it among the plays that made Galsworthy's stage reputation.
king-midas-a-romance:
King Midas: A Romance is Upton Sinclair's early novel of 1901, written before his fame. A note explains the book's musical thread. Sinclair built the idea partly on a theme he linked to Beethoven's Appassionata sonata and Fifth Symphony. He admits the claim may be a fancy, but kept it, thinking it too good a story to lose.

Extracts from MacDowell's Woodland Sketches appear at pages 214 and 291. A motto verse speaks of a hero alone, wrestling heaven's fiery gold touch. Part One opens in the merry month of May, as its first words say. The Midas name promises the theme: wealth that turns to a curse in the hands that grab it. This romance shows the young Sinclair before The Jungle made him a muckraker.
lavender-and-old-lace:
Myrtle Reed published her novel Lavender and Old Lace in 1902. Seventeen chapters carry its quiet romance. The first chapter is called The Light in the Window.

A rickety carriage climbs a hill in the opening scene. Its single passenger studies the country with interest and admiration. An attic, a Miss Ainslie, and rumors of the valley follow. Old letters and a garden deepen the mystery and the love story. Reed's gentle tale links a past romance with a new one. Reed's fiction favors kindness over cynicism at every turn. A light in a window becomes the sign of patient love.
letters-from-france:
C. E. W. Bean wrote Letters from France as Australia's war correspondent. Cassell published the book in 1917, with a map and eight plates. A plate shows Australians watching the bombardment of Pozières.

Their mates lay beneath that bombardment at the time, the caption says. Bean reported the Western Front for the Commonwealth of Australia. His letters mix battle detail with soldiers' daily character. He later became Australia's official war historian. These early letters show the reporting that built that reputation. Bean's concern for common soldiers marks every dispatch. Anzac troops trusted him as their own witness.
lost-face:
Lost Face is a book of Jack London's northern tales, first published in 1916. The title story opens in Russian America, where Subienkow's long trail of horror ends. Around it stand six more stories, including 'To Build a Fire' and 'Trust.' All are set in the hard world of the far North.

London writes of cold, hunger, gold, and men pushed past their limits. 'Flush of Gold' and 'The Passing of Marcus O'Brien' add greed and rough justice. 'The Wit of Porportuk' turns on a clever and bitter bargain. The tales are short, stark, and pitiless in London's famous style. They show why his northern stories became classics of adventure writing.
louis-agassiz-his-life-and-correspondenc:
Louis Agassiz: His Life and Correspondence was edited by his widow, Elizabeth Cary Agassiz. She built it from his letters, journals, and family papers. She feared those scattered papers would be lost if not gathered. Her preface says his European years were little known in America, his adopted country.

The book traces a rare life of science with one steady aim. Agassiz rose in Europe as a student of fish and glaciers. He then crossed the Atlantic and became a famed Harvard teacher. Letters in his own words carry much of the story. It remains a warm, full portrait of a great naturalist.
malbone-an-oldport-romance:
Malbone is an Oldport romance by Thomas Wentworth Higginson. A motto from Thoreau's diary asks what Nature is without human life. The contents open with a prelude, an arrival, and place aux dames. Aunt Jane defines her position early and to the rescue late.

Oldport is Higginson's Newport in disguise, of yachts and summer society. Malbone is a charming man with what one chapter calls a multivalve heart. New engagements, dangerous ways, and remonstrances fill the season. Hope's vigil and a storm darken the tale's second half. It ends with a requiem for Malbone himself. Higginson writes with the polish of the genteel tradition.
marie-gourdon-a-romance-of-the-lower-st-:
Marie Gourdon is a romance of the Lower St. Lawrence by Maud Ogilvy. John Lovell and Son published it at Montreal in 1890. Ogilvy dedicated it to Lady Helen Munro-Ferguson, remembering happy days on the river. A French Canadian folk song sounds before the tale.

It opens on a bright August afternoon in the village of Rimouski. The sun shines with a brilliancy Ogilvy calls purely Canadian. Old French Canadian women nod sleepily at their doorsteps. Into this drowsy, beautiful world steps Marie Gourdon. Love and village custom shape her story on the great river. The book preserves a vanished French Canadian summer world.
marietta-a-maid-of-venice:
Marietta, a Maid of Venice, is a novel by F. Marion Crawford. Collier issued it at New York in 1901, in his authorized edition. The scene is Murano, famed for its glass furnaces. Old Angelo Beroviero keeps a Dalmatian waif, called Zorzi, in his service.

The servants distrust Zorzi and call him a likely heretic. Worse, they suspect he loves the master's only daughter, Marietta. Any hundred Murano glass-workers would seem safer matches for her. Yet Angelo keeps the stranger, who knows secrets of the glass. Crawford weaves love, craft pride, and Venetian color together. Marietta stands among his best-loved Italian tales.
mark-rutherford-s-deliverance:
Mark Rutherford's Deliverance continues William Hale White's quiet masterpiece. White wrote as 'Mark Rutherford,' and this text follows a 1913 edition. The narrator settles in new lodgings in Camden Town. He has ten pounds in his pocket and, once again, no outlook.

Chapters take him through newspaper work and new acquaintances. M'Kay and Miss Leroy enter his narrow, thoughtful life. 'Drury Lane Theology' names his wry study of popular religion. Rutherford is a failed minister remaking himself in London. His deliverance comes slowly, through work, love, and honesty. The book is a classic of Victorian religious doubt. Few novels search the conscience so gently and deeply.
martin-conisby-s-vengeance:
Jeffery Farnol published Martin Conisby's Vengeance in 1921. He gave the book to two aunts in a warm note at the front. Chapter heads promise pirates, sea fights, and a long held grudge.

The tale starts when Martin's lone life ends and his troubles begin. A song he knows stirs the past, and hard work fails to save him. He aids a Spanish gent, Don Federigo, then sails into danger aboard the Happy Despatch. A fight in the dark with Pompey stands among the chapter heads. Farnol writes in an old style, with thee and thou in the heads.
marvels-of-modern-science:
Paul Severing wrote Marvels of Modern Science, edited by Theodore Waters. The book came out in 1910, when flight and film were still new. Its chapters tour the fresh feats of the age one by one.

Readers meet flying machines, from Langley to the Wright brothers and Count Zeppelin. Then come wireless, radium, and the work of the Curies. Later chapters tour moving pictures, tall New York buildings, ocean liners, and Luther Burbank's plant work. Each chapter names its key men, dates, and trials in plain heads. Young readers of 1910 could see their own age taking new shape.
masters-of-space:
Walter Kellogg Towers wrote Masters of Space in 1917. Samuel Morse, shown at the front, leads the cast of makers. The book pairs each man with the tool that made him famed.

Morse stands for the telegraph, and Thompson for the cable. Bell stands for the telephone, and Marconi for wireless sending. Carty closes the set with the wireless telephone. Early chapters trace signals from old times through Wheatstone and other forerunners of the wire. First facts on wires and waves come in plain, short heads. Boys of that day could trace each new tool to one man's work.
mercy-philbrick-s-choice:
Helen Hunt Jackson published this novel in 1876. Two long poems about truth and guidance stand before the first chapter. The story then opens on a gray November afternoon in New England. A young man, Stephen White, leans on a gate as the light fails.

The title names Mercy Philbrick and the choice she must make. Jackson builds the tale around conscience, faith, and the claims of love. The opening poems announce the book's moral seriousness in advance. Readers of her later work on injustice will recognize the same earnest voice here. The story keeps its sorrows close to home and heart.
minnie-s-sacrifice:
Frances E. W. Harper wrote this novel of slavery and its aftermath. Harper was born free in Baltimore in 1825 and raised by an activist uncle. She became a lecturer, suffragist, poet, and novelist over a sixty-year career. This rediscovered text was edited by Frances Smith Foster.

The first chapter shows Miriam mourning her daughter Agnes in a lowly cabin. Agnes, enslaved and defenseless, fell victim to her master's power and died young. Harper calls it the old story of slavery's cruelty to women. The novel turns such private grief into an argument against the whole system.
misalliance:
George Bernard Shaw set this comedy in a glass pavilion at a Surrey country house. The house belongs to John Tarleton, who made a fortune from Tarleton's Underwear. His son Johnny is taking his weekly Friday-to-Tuesday visit, novel in hand. The stage directions describe garden games, a portable Turkish bath, and Viennese pottery in flamboyant colors.

Into this comfortable weekend come guests whose marriage plans cross and tangle. Shaw uses the country-house comedy to argue about parents, children, money, and wedlock. The text keeps his spelling without apostrophes, as the editor's note explains. Talk, in this play, is the real action, and nobody escapes undebated.
miss-caprice:
St. George Rathborne published this adventure with his Dr. Jack books behind him in 1893. The first chapter is titled simply Coward. A party of tourists stands on a hill behind Valletta, on the island of Malta. Below them lie two harbors, steep limestone streets, and massive fortifications.

Rathborne pauses to describe Malta as England's second Gibraltar. The Maltese, he says, are a swarthy, robust, fearless people. Against this Mediterranean scene, the tourists' romance and danger unfold. Rathborne wrote dozens of such tales, mixing travel scenery with quick-moving plots for popular readers. The opening cry of Coward sets the tone of honor and danger.
monism-as-connecting-religion-and-scienc:
Ernst Haeckel delivered this address connecting religion and science through monism. J. Gilchrist translated it from the German. Haeckel spoke for a society's seventy-fifth anniversary, answering Professor Schlesinger on scientific articles of faith. He argues that general problems, not narrow specialties, suit such an occasion.

Monism, he says, means one spirit living in all things. The whole knowable world develops under one common law. Organic nature evolved from inorganic nature late, with no sharp line between them. Animal and vegetable, lower animals and man, likewise shade into each other. Haeckel presents this unity as a creed a man of science can profess.
monsieur-maurice:
Amelia B. Edwards published this tale in 1873, told by an old woman remembering her childhood. The narrator was scarce ten years old when the events happened, more than fifty years before. Her father, Johann Ludwig Bernhard of Coblentz, had fought his way up from the ranks in Prussian service. He was wounded seven times and made colonel in 1814.

In 1819 the retired colonel became King's steward of the Château of Augustenburg at Brühl. He fetched his daughter from her strict Lutheran aunt at Nuremberg to live with him. There the child met Monsieur Maurice, the Frenchman of the title. Edwards shapes a child's memories of occupied, postwar Germany into a story of loyalty and pity.
mornings-in-florence:
John Ruskin leads readers through Florence's art in these morning lessons. The first morning is spent at Santa Croce. Giotto, Ruskin insists, is the artist to examine first in Florence. The city, Giotto's birthplace, holds his work of every date and kind, from age twelve to sixty.

Ruskin urges seeing Giotto first in his strong and earnest work. He explains the Franciscan world Giotto painted for, under Dante's advice. A footnote quotes the decree appointing Giotto to build the cathedral campanile, as without superior in the world. Ruskin teaches looking itself: slow, reverent, and exact, picture by picture.
mr-fortescue-an-andean-romance:
William Westall opens this Andean romance far from the Andes, on an Essex village green. Matching Green hosts the Essex Hunt's first meet of the season. The whole village turns out, from the oldest gaffer to the last baby. Huntsmen in scarlet and white breeches crowd the road with four-in-hands and donkey carts.

Tom Cuffe, the huntsman, leads hounds fit to go, while old hands refight historic runs. Westall lingers over the camaraderie of the hunting field. From this most English of scenes, his hero Fortescue's story will travel to South America. The title promises mountains; the opening gives the home the adventurer leaves behind.
my-garden-acquaintance:
James Russell Lowell writes of his garden in this famed nature essay. He starts with White's Natural History of Selborne, a book he loved. White takes readers out of doors on every page, Lowell says. The old parson watched birds and insects with endless calm.

Lowell compares White to Walton in taste and Cowper in kindness. He has walked White's haunts yet still sees them through White's eyes. His own garden at Elmwood gives him the same pleasures. Robins, squirrels, and seasons pass in witty, learned talk. V1 called it a gentle classic of American nature writing from the Atlantic's great age.
my-lady-caprice:
Jeffery Farnol sets this romance among outlaws, oaks, and moon magic. The contents name the Sheriff of Nottingham and desperadoes. A blasted oak and a land of heart's delight follow. The narrator opens while fishing, though he hates the sport.

He fishes because Lisbeth's aunt, Lady Warburton, demands a talk. The aunt fears Lisbeth mistakes friendship for love. Lisbeth is an orphan with one married sister. Farnol writes in a gay, old-fashioned voice of wooing. V1 praised its wit and swordplay in a Regency key. The tale blends Robin Hood airs with a courtship of a willful, charming lady.
my-mark-twain-from-literary-friends-and-:
William Dean Howells recalls his friend Mark Twain in this memoir. They first met in Boston, in James T. Fields's small office. Fields edited The Atlantic Monthly, and Howells was his assistant. In 1869 Howells had reviewed Innocents Abroad with praise and some doubts.

Clemens came in person to thank him for that notice. Their friendship then ran for forty-four full years. Howells praises Twain's broad, free way of speaking. He calls it Southwestern, Lincolnian, and Elizabethan at once. The piece is a warm record of the great friendship of American letters, told by the friend who knew him longest.
nasa-tm-19650013686-instruments-of-space:
G A Vacca, chief of instrumentation in NASA's Office of Advanced Research and Technology, gave this talk in Boston on November 2, 1964. He spoke to the Instrument Society of America. His theme was the instruments of space, the devices that gather data beyond Earth. Such systems serve engineering, science, and medical work alike.

Vacca argues that measuring is what turns curiosity into real research. Only when numbers can be tied to events, he says, can they be understood well. NASA's mission under the 1958 Space Act was to expand human knowledge. Instruments, in his account, are the tools that make that mission possible.
nasa-tm-19650018359-manned-space-flight-:
Goddard Space Flight Center issued this performance analysis on May 14, 1965, for the GT-2 mission. GT-2 was an uncrewed Gemini test flight, launched on January 19, 1965, from Cape Kennedy. The subject is the Manned Space Flight Network, the worldwide chain of tracking and communication stations that followed the flight.

Analysts reviewed how that network performed during the mission. A crewed flight program depends on near-constant contact with its spacecraft. Gaps or errors in tracking affect safety and data return. Reports like this one turned one flight into lessons for the next, as Gemini prepared to carry astronauts.
nasa-tm-19660025135-amtran-hardware-an-e:
Juris Reinfelds, R. N. Seitz, L. H. Wood, and C. A. Ely describe a piece of computing hardware in this May 1966 Marshall Space Flight Center memorandum. The hardware serves AMTRAN, a system meant to make talking to a computer simpler and faster. In 1966, that kind of direct communication was still new.

The device is an electronic interface between people and the machine. It works as an on-line remote terminal for an IBM 1620 computer. The memorandum presents the hardware so engineers could build and use the terminal. Its aim was to speed up the back-and-forth between a user and the computer.
nasa-tm-19670005594-proposed-manned-dyna:
Larry Kiefling, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, wrote this proposal on December 5, 1966. Large structures built in orbit bend and shake in ways that are hard to predict on the ground. Kiefling proposes that astronauts do the shaking tests themselves, in space.

He lists the kinds of motion problems such structures are likely to face. His plan calls for tests at each step as a space station is built and grows. He also wants failure study built into space rescue work, plus a test laboratory in orbit. A final section spells out one vibration test in full, meant to judge test gear and methods up there.
nasa-tm-19670020820-a-vacuum-ultraviolet:
Uri Feldman, Marvin Swartz, and Leonard Cohen, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, describe a light source in this June 1967 paper. The source produces vacuum ultraviolet light, which air absorbs and ordinary lamps emit poorly. Growing interest in solar and plasma spectroscopy had created demand for laboratory sources of highly ionized atoms.

Their device is a low inductance three-electrode spark source fed by a high-voltage capacitor. Its main feature is the ability to generate spectra of very high degrees of ionization. A modest spark already produced spectra of highly stripped carbon and iron ions. A stronger spark yielded still higher ionization stages, including iron and argon ions. The introduction contrasts this compact approach with the large hot-plasma machines built at major laboratories. Those new sources, it notes, share complexity and high cost.
nasa-tm-19670029351-on-dynamics-of-two-c:
Frank C. Liu, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on a futuristic configuration. Two space stations are joined by a long elastic cable. The pair rotates about an axis square to its orbital plane, so the spin supplies artificial gravity inside the stations. Liu analyzes the dynamic problems of that arrangement.

He derives the equations for vibration of the elastic cable and for the angular movements of the two stations. Those motions couple together through the cable's end conditions, a mathematical difficulty he resolves by introducing concentrated fictitious masses. The cable equation is then solved by Galerkin's approach for both free and forced oscillations. A general frequency equation for the system's free vibration follows, and the stations' responses to applied time-varying moments are presented in analytical form. The slack-cable, non-spinning case is explicitly left aside.
nasa-tm-19680016281-hydrogen-standard-wo:
H. E. Peters, T. E. McGunigal, and E. H. Johnson review two years of hydrogen standard work at Goddard Space Flight Center in this 1968 paper. The work, covering January 1966 to April 1968, aimed at field-ready time and frequency standards. Those standards rest on the atomic hydrogen maser, a very precise clock device.

Progress included better thermal control and a large storage bulb maser with an all-metal cavity. State selection grew more efficient, and the radio frequency dissociator design improved. A new digital tuning system needs only a good quartz crystal as reference. Earlier systems needed a second maser for that role. Prototype standards using these features were under construction.
nasa-tm-19680017688-information-processi:
Daniel L. Baty of Ames Research Center asks how task difficulty changes human information processing rate in this study. He used discrete tracking tasks with random inputs. Difficulty was given a firm number value for each task, so tasks could be compared fairly.

Fourteen tasks were tested in all. Nine tasks offered four target choices, and five offered sixteen choices. One-dimensional and two-dimensional tasks were compared at equal difficulty values. The study shows how processing rate depends on the degree of response difficulty. Results like these help designers set realistic demands on pilots and operators. They show how fast people can absorb and act on information.
nasa-tm-19690025535-internal-thrust-and-:
Ali H. Mansour and Richard R. Burley of Lewis Research Center wrote this June 1969 preliminary memorandum, TM X-52621. They measured the internal thrust and pumping performance of an auxiliary inlet ejector nozzle fitted with a clamshell thrust reverser. Ejector nozzles blend extra air into the exhaust to shape thrust across a jet's whole speed range.

Three hardware configurations simulated takeoff, transonic acceleration, and supersonic cruise flight. The clamshell reverser sat fixed at positions matching its working settings in flight. Adding a third air stream improved performance at low pressure ratios, the authors report. Peak thrust efficiency reached about ninety-nine percent at takeoff. It reached slightly higher still in the supersonic cruise configuration.
nasa-tm-19700016141-nuclear-power-for-ma:
H. O. Slone and L. I. Shure of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 meeting on aerospace nuclear uses. It asks how nuclear power would change the design of manned orbiting space stations. Both reactor systems and isotope systems are covered.

The authors discuss what nuclear power would mean for a space station and a larger space base. They compare the main candidate systems against each other. Much of their material comes from NASA's Phase B space station studies then under way. The paper helped planners weigh nuclear power against other ways to run a station.
nasa-tm-19710005528-vertical-tail-loads-:
Jerald M. Jenkins, Ming H. Tang, and George P. E. Pearson of the Flight Research Center in California wrote this report in December 1968. It reports loads measured on the M2-F2 lifting body in its first subsonic flight tests. The M2-F2 was a wingless craft that landed like a glider.

The team measured the forces on the vertical tail during those flights. They also measured hinge moments, the twisting loads on the control surfaces. A lifting body trades wings for a shaped hull, so its tail works hard. Flight data of this kind checked the design math against the sky. It also warned pilots where the craft's controls grew heavy or light.
nasa-tm-19720011311-computer-program-of-:
Charles G Miller III of the Langley Research Center wrote this program report in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2512. High speed wind tunnels and expansion tubes use exotic gas mixtures. Their raw pressure readings mean little until reduced to flow values. Miller's procedures compute the free stream and post shock conditions. The gases covered are carbon dioxide, nitrogen, oxygen, and argon, alone or mixed.

The math includes the effects of molecules breaking apart and ionizing. It assumes the flow rests in chemical balance at each point. The work answered an immediate need at Langley's expansion tube. There, planetary entry studies ran gases like the air of Mars and Venus. A shared program kept every facility reducing data the same way.
naudsonce:
H. Beam Piper wrote Naudsonce as a science fiction story about first contact on a strange planet. It opens with a note on Bishop Berkeley's old question about a falling tree and sound. Piper then asks a new question about sound that science, he says, needs to consider.

Mark Howell lands on a warm planet with soft, mosslike ground and a sweet smell in the air. Major Luis Gofredo, a Marine officer, watches villagers cross the fields toward them. Six men carry a long tube on poles, and no one can tell if it is a cannon. The story turns on how strangers read each other's signs.
newton-forster-or-the-merchant-service:
Frederick Marryat opens Newton Forster with a chapter that jokes about writing itself, before any sea tale starts. He quotes Sterne on the cant of criticism as the most tormenting cant of all. An author, he says, finds the beginning, middle, and end of a novel each hard to please readers with.

The story then follows young Newton Forster into the merchant service, per its subtitle. The record's summary lists impressment into the navy and prison in France for him. A West Indies shipwreck and a post on an East India ship bound for Asia follow. Pirates, treachery, and romance crowd the voyage. Marryat wrote sea life he had lived.
nicolette-a-tale-of-old-provence:
Baroness Orczy published Nicolette in 1922, calling it a tale of old Provence. A list of her books in this copy names Castles in the Air and The First Sir Percy. The League of the Scarlet Pimpernel and Flower o' the Lily stand there too. Her name alone promised romance to her readers.

The sampled pages give the title and author's list, but no opening chapter. The subtitle sets the tale in Provence of an older age. That region of southern France, with its castles and old towns, suits Orczy's taste for bygone courts. Readers who know her Pimpernel books will find her here in a new setting, still in the past she loved.
noteworthy-families-modern-science:
Francis Galton and Edgar Schuster compiled Noteworthy Families, on modern science, as volume one of the Eugenics Record Office publications. John Murray published it in London for the University of London office. Schuster held a Galton fellowship in national eugenics. The subtitle calls the book an index to kinships in near degrees.

The kinships link persons whose achievements are honourable and publicly recorded, per the subtitle. Galton hunted family patterns among notable folk of his day. Such lists fed his wider work on heredity, which later readers judge with great care. The book stands as a record of that project in its own terms: names, degrees of kin, and recorded honours.
o-t-a-danish-romance:
Hans Christian Andersen called O. T. a Danish romance, naming himself as author of the Improvisatore and the Two Baronesses. A Latin motto heads chapter one: quod felix faustumque sit, may it be lucky and of good omen. The narrator then praises a happiness no poet has yet sung.

No lady reader, he says, has felt or ever will feel that happiness. It belongs alone to the male sex, and even then to the elect. The moment is that of becoming a student, of passing the first examination. Cadets, scholars, and apprentices know lesser forms of it, he adds. A young soul first feels its freedom there. The romance grows from that threshold.
off-on-a-comet-a-journey-through-planeta:
Jules Verne wrote the space adventure Off on a Comet. It is also known by the name Hector Servadac. The editor's introduction calls it one of his finest tales. In the story, a comet strikes the Earth twice. It carries off people, land, air, and water.

The travelers tour the solar system on the comet. They return home unhurt after the long voyage. The introduction admits the premise breaks strict science. Verne uses it to teach real facts about planets. Charles Horne edited this edition of Verne's collected works. Ships pass through the great flip unhurt, the notes add. Air and water ride along for the trip as well.
okewood-of-the-secret-service:
Valentine Williams wrote this spy novel about Major Okewood. The contents promise murders, spies, and secret papers. Early chapters name Captain Strangwise and Mr. Mackwayte. Later chapters move to a mill house and a cellar. A chapter is set in Hohenlinden Trench.

The story opens with a shy, quiet clerk at dinner. From there it grows into a wartime spy plot. Williams writes fast scenes in the Buchan manner. The book is vintage spy fiction from the war era. Short chapters and cliff turns keep the plot moving fast. Heads name Nur-el-Din, a white paper pack, and a bridge night. The kit at stake is worth a full hundred thousand pounds.
oliver-wendell-holmes-from-literary-frie:
William Dean Howells wrote this memoir of Oliver Wendell Holmes. It comes from his book Literary Friends and Acquaintance. Howells recalls Boston when literature carried high social rank. Poets there came from noted, settled families, he says. To be a poet meant being good society.

Howells names Prescott, Lowell, Emerson, and other Boston leaders. Holmes, he says, would come first to a reader's mind. Holmes named Boston's upper caste the Brahminical caste. Wit and warmth fill Howells's portrait of his friend. The essay preserves a vanished literary world. He also names Motley, Parkman, Norton, and Dana with pride. Longfellow, though not of Boston, became of it, he says.
operation-outer-space:
Murray Leinster opens his science fiction novel Operation: Outer Space in a future city of rooftop gardens and fourteen million people, where advertising man Jed Cochrane has just learned he is expendable. His firm is sending him on the moon-rocket to Lunar City, by an order delivered thirty minutes ago. His secretary, two technicians, and a writer travel with him.

Cochrane rides the helicab to the rocket port raging at the humiliation and telling himself it must be a mixup. Instructions will come from Dr. William Holden on the way out. Leinster builds the future from office politics as much as from rockets, and the comedy of a self-important man demoted by his own company launches the space adventure.
our-admirable-betty-a-romance: Our Admirable Betty: A Romance is a novel by Jeffery Farnol, dated 1918 in the catalog. Farnol also wrote The Broad Highway and The Amateur Gentleman. The hosted sample shows only the title page. It also shows the publisher's list of his other books. That list includes The Money Moon, Beltane the Smith, and The Definite Object. No chapter of the novel itself appears in the sample. This note records the book's identity and its place in Farnol's list. It claims nothing about Betty or her story.
out-to-win-the-story-of-america-in-franc:
Coningsby Dawson had written Carry On and The Glory of the Trenches. In 1918 he published Out To Win. He called it a frank appreciation of his American brothers-in-arms. Its chapters promise the American effort in France under plain headings: We've Got Four Years, War as a Job, The War of Compassion, and The Last War.

His preface, addressed to fools only, is not for the conscious fool but for the self-deceived brother who thinks himself wise. Dawson hopes some readers will recognize themselves: people who contributed little to the war except mean views and endless talk. The book is wartime persuasion aimed at skeptics at home, arguing that America's arrival in France was both a military fact and a moral one.
over-paradise-ridge-a-romance: Maria Thompson Daviess wrote Over Paradise Ridge as a romance in four books. The contents name them: Food, Shelter, Laughter, and Love. A frontispiece shows a man declaring he got a land call he had to answer. The hosted sample shows the title pages, contents, and illustrations list. It stops at the heading of chapter one. No page of the story appears.
parables-of-a-province:
Gilbert Parker's Parables of a Province collects nine tales of French Canada. The Golden Pipes opens the book. The Guardian of the Fire and The White Omen follow. The Forge in the Valley closes the set. Parker, a Canadian who wrote of the St. Lawrence country, works here in parable. Each tale carries a moral weight lightly.

The Golden Pipes hang bronzed on Margath Mountain's side. They are the pipes of an organ played when the world was young. Hepnon the cripple told the legend as a child. Grown, he swears golden music still sounds at sunrise and sunset. No one laughs at Hepnon. His dark eyes dilate with his fancies, and rough men believe him. He climbs anywhere with crutch and shrivelled leg. Travellers now bare their heads passing the pipes.
parkman-pioneers-france:
Pioneers of France in the New World, from 1865, opens Parkman's grand series. France and England in North America begins with the first French footholds. Cartier sails the St. Lawrence, and Champlain founds Quebec in these pages.

Huguenot ventures in warmer lands meet ruin at Spanish hands early on. The fur trade, faith, and hunger shape the frail first settlements. Parkman writes the founding epic as high adventure from page one. His style made colonial history read like a great novel for many. The book launched one of the finest history series in English ever written. Parkman's fame rests on the road he starts here.
partners-of-chance:
Henry Herbert Knibbs wrote western novels such as The Ridin' Kid from Powder River and Sundown Slim. Partners of Chance, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1921, opens with Little Jim watching his father, Big Jim, sell off their cattle, team, and farm tools. The family keeps only the saddle-horses and a pack-horse.

The chapter titles map a Southwest ranch world of water-holes, horse trades, pony tracks, and the Box-S outfit. A boy, a drifting cowboy, and trouble around the ranch drive the story. Knibbs writes plain, fast-moving western adventure, with the land and its work always close at hand.
peace:
Aristophanes staged his comedy Peace in Athens while the Peloponnesian War had already lasted ten years. The introduction in this edition explains that it followed The Acharnians by four years, with the same leading motive. Ordinary citizens longed for relief from the miseries of war.

Trygaeus, a rustic patriot, finds no help among men, so he fattens a gigantic dung-beetle and rides it to heaven. The gods have left War in charge, and the goddess Peace lies imprisoned in a pit. Trygaeus rallies the peoples of Greece to haul her out, and the play ends in feasting and marriage.
pharos-the-egyptian-a-romance: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Pharos, the Egyptian, the title pages, copyright page, and a bare contents of numbered chapters, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Guy Boothby, author of Doctor Nikola, and calls the book a romance. D. Appleton of New York published it in 1899, with copyright in 1898 and 1899, and the contents promise a preface before the chapters begin.
philip-steele-of-the-royal-northwest-mou:
James Oliver Curwood's Philip Steele of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, published at New York in 1911, opens inside a log cabin in a furious gale. Constable Steele writes a hyacinth letter he may never mail, to lessen the loneliness. Sleet volleys off the lake, surf roars among the rocks, and snow tomorrow will cover everything to Hudson's Bay.

What troubles him is the skull on the shelf above his fireplace, a new skull, lately a living man. Steele keeps starting to take it down and falling back, shivering. Curwood starts his northern mystery with that grim relic and a storm.
philothea-a-grecian-romance: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Philothea: A Grecian Romance, the title pages, dedications, and the first sentences of the preface, with no story text visible. The title page names L. Maria Child and a new and corrected edition, dedicated to her beloved brother of Harvard University. Her preface begins by calling the volume purely romance, and most readers, she expects, will think it romance of the wildest kind.
poems-of-experience:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox called this collection Poems of Experience, first published in 1910 and reprinted steadily until this London edition of 1917 from Gay and Hancock. A notice at the front warns that any English edition from another firm is pirated, a sign of how valuable her name had become. Experience is the keynote: these are poems by a woman who had lived, lost, worked, and watched the world, speaking to readers doing the same.

Contents range from the Empty Bowl and Keep Going to a Battle Hymn of the Women and a poem simply called Woman. A piece on the London bobby and one read at a benefit for the actress Clara Morris show her public, occasional side. Wilcox's gift was turning private feeling into lines strangers could memorize, and this volume, reprinted six times in seven years, proves the demand.
police:
Robert W. Chambers published Police!!! in New York and London with D. Appleton in 1915, illustrated by Henry Hutt and dedicated, in verses dated Christmas 1915, to Louise Jocelyn. Chambers, famous for the King in Yellow and for society romances, here gathers four long stories: the Third Eye, the Immortal, the Ladies of the Lake, and One Over. An illustration caption lingers on dainty noses to the wind and beautiful wide-alert eyes, a hint of the animal world inside.

The stories belong to Chambers's outdoor vein, where sportsmen, scientists, and strange creatures meet beyond the edge of the known map. His expeditions after legendary beasts mix natural history, tall tale, and shiver. The dedication poem, turning autumn into May, frames the book as a love gift. Yet the contents promise pursuit and wonder: Chambers entertaining the reader who liked his romances and wanted monsters too.
prince-otto-a-romance:
Robert Louis Stevenson called Prince Otto a romance, and the new Chatto and Windus edition of 1905 reprints his dedication letter to Nelly Van de Grift, by then Mrs. Adulfo Sanchez of Monterey. The letter is a memoir in miniature: it recalls the old wooden house that had come round the Horn piecemeal in a ship's belly. The Scot who was then sick unto death, dreaming of the masterpiece he would make of Prince Otto.

Otto himself is prince of the little German state of Grünewald, a well-meaning, pleasure-loving ruler whose wife and ministers govern without him. Until conspiracy and love teach him his trade too late and just in time. The dedication, added to the tale, makes the volume double: the story of a prince who would not rule. Framed by the story of the invalid who would not stop writing.
public-school-domestic-science:
Mrs. J. Hoodless, president of a school of domestic science at Hamilton, wrote a textbook printed at Toronto in 1898 for use in Canadian high and public schools. School boards could adopt it by a vote of their trustees.

A long quotation from Sir Henry Thompson argues that bad habits of eating cause more illness than drink does, and the book builds its lessons on that claim. Pupils learn how food, health, and housekeeping join together. Readers get an early statement of home economics as a school subject, backed by faith in taught knowledge over custom.
public-speaking-principles-and-practice:
Irvah Lester Winter built a full course on platform speech, joining rules of delivery to a large body of pieces for student practice. The preface says the book serves class courses, work beside debating, and the many speakers who must train without a teacher.

Part one states the main rules of good delivery. Part two drills the voice itself, from forming tone to shaping expression. Part three sends the student to the platform with speeches for the varied occasions of public life. Winter praises Charles William Eliot as a model speaker. Readers get method, drill, and models in one volume.
put-yourself-in-his-place:
Put Yourself in His Place is a novel by Charles Reade, framed, in his epigraph from Horace, as fiction built upon notorious fact. Its setting is Hillsborough, a great working town of brick kilns, wool and cotton mills, and steel forges that turn out everything from needles to a ship's armor.

Reade paints the town as hideous for all its lovely site: broken streets, pubs at every turn, and round chimneys belching black smoke that veils the sun. Clear streams enter it and creep out black with dye and poison. Eastward the hills rise to Cairnhope, a forked, heather-covered mountain where the story's key events are to come.
quiet-talks-on-service:
Quiet Talks on Service, by S. D. Gordon, is dated 1906. It gathers eight talks on Christian service. They treat personal contact with Jesus and the triple life. They treat yokefellows and a passion for winning men. Deep-sea fishing and money as a golden channel follow. Worry is named a hindrance. Gideon's band, sifted for service, closes the set.

The first talk rests on John chapter one. It opens about a quarter of four one afternoon. Three young men stand on an old road. The road runs down to a swift river. It runs along its bank through a village by the fords. One of them, plainly dressed and spare of face, is clearly the leader, and the meeting begins an endless friendship.
red-fleece:
