Will Levington Comfort published this war novel in 1915, dedicated to the hour when troops turn home. Chapter titles set its world at once: The Court of Execution, The House of Amputations, and In the Bomb-Proof Pit. Later chapters name a skylight prison, a field of helmets, and the green of cedars.

The tale opens with Peter Mowbray seeing a woman at the corner of Palace Square nearest the river. Their eyes meet at length, in a stirring silence, though work matters crowd his mind. She seems very poor, and he hopes for some flaw to break the pull he feels. War and love plainly stand ready to collide.
representative-plays-by-american-dramati:
Francesca da Rimini, a tragedy by George Henry Boker, stands in this set of representative American plays with an essay on its author. Boker lived from 1823 to 1890, and a line from Dante's Inferno heads his play. The essay paints him first through his friends: Bayard Taylor, Richard Henry Stoddard, and Charles Godfrey Leland.

The four men were called the inseparables, writing poetry to each other and meeting for golden talks on Sundays. Boker, a Philadelphian born October 6, 1823, was a banker's son and entered Princeton in 1840. His father's honour, questioned after death, drew the son's defence in The Book of the Dead.
rhymes-of-the-rookies-sunny-side-of-sold:
W. E. Christian, who calls his book the sunny side of soldier service, published these army rhymes in 1917. A toast To the Colors opens it, hailing the red of the firing line and the blue of the Yankee sign. Christian dedicates the book to Theodore Roosevelt, colonel of the Rough Riders, as the spirit of the American soldier.

My Bunkie, Our Officers, and Pay Day lead the contents, with The Army Grouch and Weaning Time for the comic side of camp. The Hike, An A-B-C of Army Life, and A Soldier's Primer teach while they rhyme. Hiking in the Philippines, songs for mountain battery and cavalry, The Conscript, and The Slacker round out the rookie's world.
romance:
Joseph Conrad and F. M. Hueffer wrote this novel together, under a copyright of 1903 by Doubleday, Page of New York. They dedicate it to Elsie and Jessie, under a French line and verses on memory and romance in workaday hours. Its contents divide the tale into five parts with pictured titles.

Part first is The Quarry and the Beach, and part second The Girl with the Lizard. Casa Riego names the third part, and Blade and Guitar the fourth, promising Spanish ground and fighting. The Lot of Man closes the five. The parts move from an English shore to a world of smuggling seas and hot countries, as their names suggest.
round-anvil-rock-a-romance:
Nancy Huston Banks, author of Oldfield, wrote Round Anvil Rock, a romance dated 1903 and given to her father. A front picture shows the Angelus pealing from the bell of a little log chapel. In her preface Banks says she wove the tale round a real rock and through real events. She claims only the freedom of fiction, and she names just three places where she bent fact to bring places and events closer together.

Those three changes concern the Wilderness Road, the Sisters of Charity, and Philip Alston. Banks draws the road nearer the Ohio River than it truly was, brings the Sisters in a bit early, and keeps Alston in the Cedar House region past the point tradition allows. She defends each step at length.
roundabout-to-boston-from-literary-frien:
William Dean Howells recalls, in Roundabout to Boston, four years of life in Venice when the wish to write was with him at all times and in all places. He sent many verses to magazines across the English-speaking world, and they came back to him almost without fail. Only three pieces were kept and printed. One went to the Atlantic Monthly, one to Harper's Magazine, and one to the New York Ledger. That last success came through Dr. Edward Everett Hale, who helped a ballad by a young man he had not yet met.

Hale's brother Charles, later Consul-General for Egypt, had copied the ballad in his own large, fair hand so it could be read, and sent it on. Charles knew Lowell's classes at Harvard, had met Longfellow in Cambridge, and knew Dr. Holmes.
rudimental-divine-science:
Mary Baker Eddy wrote Rudimental Divine Science, issued by the trustees under her will with dates of 1891 and 1908 on the title page. She gives the little book, tenderly and with respect, to all loyal students working and waiting for the founding of the Science of Mind-healing. The contents list short heads that frame the teaching as questions and answers. They include a definition of Christian Science, its principle, the personality of God, and healing sickness and sin.

Later heads turn to the being of God, material and spiritual science, the non-being of matter, the basis of mind-healing, and means and methods. Asked how she would define Christian Science, Eddy answers that it is the law of God, the law of good. In her words, it reads and shows forth the divine Principle and rule of concord in all things.
sabotage-in-space: Carey Rockwell wrote Sabotage in Space, a Tom Corbett Space Cadet adventure issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap under a copyright of 1955. Willy Ley is named as technical adviser, and Louis Glanzman drew the pictures. A series page lists the Tom Corbett books in order: Stand By for Mars, Danger in Deep Space, On the Trail of the Space Pirates. Later books are The Space Pioneers, The Revolt on Venus, and Treachery in Outer Space. Sabotage in Space follows them, with The Robot Rocket listed after it.
self-help-with-illustrations-of-conduct-:
Samuel Smiles issued this famous guide to conduct and steady effort in a revised popular edition with John Murray in London in 1897. Smiles had won fame with his Lives of the Engineers. A preface notes printings in America and versions in Dutch and French, with more on the way.

Smiles fills his chapters with short lives and anecdotes of men who rose by work, thrift, and grit. He quotes Hamlet's charge to be true to one's own self on the title page. The book taught Victorian readers that character, more than luck or birth, builds a life worth honoring.
servia-youngest-member-of-the-european-f:
Andrew Archibald Paton published this account of Serbia with Longman in London in 1845. Paton had lived in Belgrade and traveled the highlands and woodlands of the interior during 1843 and 1844. He had written before on the modern Syrians.

Paton calls Serbia the youngest member of the European family of nations. His preface names the histories he drew on, from Von Engel to Ranke, and notes that men on the spot checked his facts. British readers met a little-known land inside the Ottoman world through a resident's eyes, in narrative that mixes travel scenes with national history.
shock-and-awe-achieving-rapid-dominance:
Harlan K. Ullman and James P. Wade led a study group that produced this defense study for NDU Press in December 1996. Senior officers, among them L. A. Edney, Fred M. Franks, and Charles A. Horner, joined the work. The text came from the Defense Department's Command and Control Research Program.

Rapid Dominance, the core idea, seeks to stun a foe's will and senses so fully that fight ends fast. Chapters cover groundwork, means, and use at policy and field levels, plus the tools such speed demands. Closing pieces by three former commanders weigh how far the idea can carry in real war.
somewhere-in-france:
Richard Harding Davis wrote Somewhere in France, dated 1915 and given to Hope Davis. The contents join the title tale with Playing Dead, The Card-Sharp, Billy and the Big Stick, The Boy Scout, and The Frame-Up. The first tale names its spy at once: Marie Gessler, also known as Marie Chaumontel, Jeanne d'Avrechy, and the Countess d'Aurillac, was German.

Marie's father served through the Franco-Prussian War as a German spy, and her mother taught her French so well that she passed in Paris as a native. Left with debts alone, she was trained as a nurse, then played politics in Berlin wards till scandal drove her out at twenty-five. She went to Monte Carlo as a paid traveling mate, left the doctor there for Henri Ravignac, a captain in the French flying corps, and moved into his Paris rooms.
studies-of-lowell-from-literary-friends-:
William Dean Howells wrote Studies of Lowell for his Literary Friends and Acquaintances. It records what he knew of James Russell Lowell. They first met at Cambridge in 1860. Howells had come east on a literary pilgrimage from the West. The record runs until Lowell's death.

Howells warns that his portrait shows Lowell as he looked to one friend, and that the painter cannot keep himself out of the picture. He recalls coming home from his consular post at Venice in the summer of 1865 and carrying Lowell an Italian inkstand, a bronze lobster whose back opened on an inkpot and sandbox. Lowell set it mid-table, where it stayed for twenty-five years, its inkpot likely dry the whole time.
supplementary-copyright-statutes-us-copy:
Supplementary Copyright Statutes collects short publications of the United States Copyright Office for the use of authors, publishers, and librarians. Five items are included, each parted from the next by a line of asterisks, so the set can be read as a pocket reference on American copyright practice.

The items start with Circular 3 on copyright notice. Circular 15 treats renewal of copyright. Circular 15t treats extension of copyright terms. Circular 22 gives highlights of the copyright changes in the Uruguay Round Agreements Act. The WIPO Copyright Treaty closes the set. Circular 3 explains that notice stopped being required under United States law, though it stays useful, and gives the proper form and placement of the notice for older and newer works.
thankful-s-inheritance:
Joseph C. Lincoln wrote Thankful's Inheritance, a Cape Cod novel that opens on the poor road from Wellmouth Centre to East Wellmouth. Chapter one sets scene and folk with a slow, fond hand.

The sandy road twists past cranberry swamps and scrubby pines to a bluff over the ocean and the village of East Wellmouth. Lincoln warns not to mix it up with South, North, or West Wellmouth, or Wellmouth Port. On a wet March night in a gale, depot driver Winnie S. swears once more to quit his job rather than drive it. Readers get Lincoln's salt-air humor and a widow's fight to make a go of a willed house.
the-albany-depot-a-farce:
W. D. Howells wrote The Albany Depot as a farce, printed in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1892, with the action set, despite the title, in Boston. Scene one joins Mr. and Mrs. Edward Roberts with a chorewoman in a railway waiting room.

Mrs. Roberts comes into the ladies' room loaded with an afternoon's shopping and scans the settees with a searching gaze. Suburban shoppers and old ladies in rocking chairs fill the room, while the chorewoman mops in the lull between two great expresses. Mrs. Roberts begs her help: her husband was to meet her at ten past three and is nowhere to be seen. Readers get Howells' light, exact fun with manners, class, and a missed train meet.
the-baronet-s-bride-or-a-woman-s-vengean:
May Agnes Fleming wrote a novel printed in New York in 1910, subtitled as a woman's vengeance. Fleming is listed for other tales such as Lady Evelyn, Queen of the Isle, and The Heiress of Glendower. Verses by John G. Whittier about clouds, rain, and wrongs stand at the front.

A second set of verses, headed Shadow, says sorrow and joy are mixed in human life and that no light comes without shade. Those poems set a mood of trouble and hidden pain before the story begins. Readers are warned, in effect, that love, wrong, and revenge will move through bright and dark scenes alike.
the-blue-lagoon-a-romance: H. de Vere Stacpoole wrote The Blue Lagoon: A Romance, set out in two books. The first book's parts move from a slush lamp and talk under the stars to mist, dawn at sea, and the tale of a pig and a goat. Later parts reach an isle, a lake of blue, death hid by lichen, and fair sights in the blue. The last part names the art of learning, a rat hunt, a wreath of blooms, and a move away. Only the part list is shown.
the-bravo-of-venice-a-romance:
The Bravo of Venice: A Romance came out in London from Cassell and Company in 1886, in the National Library set. It is billed as translated from the German by M. G. Lewis. A first word casts doubt on that claim in a kind way. Lewis, it says, professed to have translated the tale much as Horace Walpole professed to take The Castle of Otranto from an old Italian book.

The bulk of the first word is a life of Lewis himself. He was born in 1775 to a rich house. His mother was a daughter of Sir Thomas Sewell, Master of the Rolls under George III. From Westminster he went to Christ Church, Oxford, and wrote a comedy at sixteen. At seventeen he went to Germany, settled at Weimar, and met Goethe in July 1792.
the-broken-soldier-and-the-maid-of-franc: Henry Van Dyke wrote The Broken Soldier and the Maid of France, put out in New York and London by Harper and Brothers in 1919, with art by Frank E. Schoonover. A list of Van Dyke's books stands in front, naming The Americanism of Washington, The Christ Child in Art, The Lost Boy, The Mansion, and The Story of the Other Wise Man. Only the front pages are shown, with no page of the tale itself.
the-case-of-jennie-brice:
The Case of Jennie Brice, by Mary Roberts Rinehart, was published in 1913 with illustrations by M. Leone Bracker. Its narrator, who gives her name as Pitman while granting it is not really Pitman, keeps boarders in lower Allegheny, where rents are cheap because the houses flood every spring.

She opens in the aftermath of one flood, with the mud shovelled from the cellar and the body of Peter, a spaniel left behind by a vanished Mr. Ladley, found buried in the fruit closet. That discovery recalls the worse flood of five years before, which brought mystery and sudden death to some and the worst case of shingles she ever saw to her. A landlady's plain voice frames the mystery before it starts.
the-chronicles-of-the-imp-a-romance: Jeffery Farnol, author of The Broad Highway, wrote this romance. It is shown here in a new and cheaper edition from Sampson Low, Marston and Company of London in 1915. Its original date, 1906, stands at the head. Only the front matter is present here. A frontispiece line tells of edging along a branch to reach a boat. An appreciation of the author by Clement K. Shorter also begins here. Shorter calls Farnol an Englishman whose best-known book is The Broad Highway. No chapter text follows.
the-claim-jumpers-a-romance:
Stewart Edward White wrote this western romance, dated 1901, opening far from the West itself. Chapter I places four youths in a fifth-story sitting room of a New York boarding house, deep in discussion. The contents promise gold hunting, a spirit mountain, a pioneer's picnic, and the claim jumpers of the title.

The big square room stands in wild disorder, though a lit motto gives it a comic system. Have a place for everything, it says, and one place will never need looking. Easels and artists' materials against the wall mark the group as art students. Names in the chapter list include Jim Leslie, who writes the opening letter, and Bennington, who hunts for gold and finds a kiss. An old figure called Old Mizzou resigns in a later chapter. White moves his young Easterners toward Western land, greed, and romance.
the-courage-of-the-commonplace:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews tells The Courage of the Commonplace around Tap Day at Yale. A girl and her chaperon sit in a prized second-story window in Durfee, looking down on the tree. Brant, a senior and a Bones man with a leading part in the day's drama, must get the pair off his hands and be about his business.

The author pauses to explain Tap Day for readers who know Yale only from outside. In New Haven, on the last Thursday of May, toward five in the afternoon, the sea of boys over the city thickens into a river. It flows toward the campus. There the junior class gathers into a solid mass around a large, low-hanging tree.
the-delicious-vice:
Young E. Allison subtitled The Delicious Vice pipe dreams and fond adventures of an habitual novel-reader among some great books and their people. The second edition, revised with new material, came from the Prairieland Publishing Company of Chicago in 1918. The pieces first ran in the Louisville Courier-Journal. The first edition came from Burrows Brothers of Cleveland in 1907.

The opening rhapsody on novel reading starts with Thomas Moore turning a sigh into marketable copy at about the age of forty. At forty, Allison argues, the world has shrunk, time is no longer than a kite string, and all that can happen to a man, death aside, has happened. Then comes the day when the habitual novel reader looks back in anguish and wishes he hadn't, asking what he might have done instead.
the-dolliver-romance:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Dolliver Romance survives as three chapters plus fragments, and its front note tells why. Hawthorne took up his old elixir-of-life scheme again in 1863 and let it run as a serial in the Atlantic Monthly for January 1864. Ill health, family sorrow, and the Civil War slowed him, and the tale stopped short.

An aged Dr. Dolliver guards a cordial that grants long life, while a small child shares his house. What stands is a tender, sad fragment. Readers see Hawthorne's last design: age, youth, and a drug that cheats death.
the-door-through-space:
Marion Zimmer Bradley's The Door Through Space, an Ace Books paperback copyrighted in 1961, opens with a note on the Terran Empire. Across half a galaxy, Terra rules by compact, not conquest, and its peace is fought for in the minds of a few men caught between worlds. One such world is Wolf; one such man is Race Cargill of the Terran Secret Service.

Cargill, bound to Terra by duty and to Wolf by love, goes back to a world that exiled him. Bradley's own note tells how pulp magazines lit her urge to write such tales.
the-duke-s-prize-a-story-of-art-and-hear:
The Duke's Prize, a story of art and heart in Florence signed Lieutenant Murray and dated 1854 in its front pages, opens with a frank preface. Its scenes lie in Italy, the author says. They aim to teach as they please. Patience and grit win out. A poor coat may hide a rich heart. Love lifts the lowly. Chapter one then tours the Mediterranean in fancy.

A young artist seeks a duke's prize against rich rivals. Maturin Murray Ballou sets romance among Florence's studios and courts. Merit, not birth, takes the prize in the end.
the-fairy-land-of-science:
Arabella B. Buckley gave these ten talks to young hearers as The Fairy-Land of Science, treating fact as a kind of true fairy tale. Sunbeams, air, water, ice, sound, a primrose, coal, and bees fill the course.

In the first talk she grants that science looks like dry facts, then vows it holds real poetry and wonder-working fairies. She retells Sleeping Beauty to show the charm of old tales, then claims the same charm for the true world. A drop of water on its travels and the life of a primrose turn plain things into marvels a child can watch.
the-field-of-ice:
Jules Verne wrote The Field of Ice as part two of his tale of Captain Hatteras, first printed in French in 1866. This London printing of 1875, with one hundred and twenty-six pictures by Riou, uses an early English rendering whose maker is not named.

The tale takes up the Arctic crew where the first part left them. First heads in the contents name the doctor's stock of goods and the first words of Altamont, a rival found in the ice. Cold, hunger, and pride drive men at the top of the world, where a ship frozen fast turns friend against friend.
the-fighting-chance:
Robert W. Chambers wrote The Fighting Chance as a novel of sport, wealth, and love among the rich. The contents move from a first meeting and a country house party to bargains, prices, and an enemy who listens.

The tale opens on a train slowing at a river trestle, with brake screech and bell notes. At the Shotover stop, crowds in summer dress fill the platform. A dreamy young man steps down with gun case and bag, bound for a house party. Chambers, author of Cardigan and The Firing Line, sets his tale among horse folk and hunters where pride and money test a man's chance.
the-firefly-of-france:
Marion Polk Angellotti wrote The Firefly of France as a war tale, giving the book to the memory of Guynemer, the French ace of aces. This copy was made from an edition of 1918.

The narrator looks back on a night at the Hotel St. Ives in New York, the eve of his sailing. A fine meal, rich guests, and princes filled the room, yet a strange drama began there. He had meant to join an ambulance unit in France. Chance, a chance room, and one odd night bend his path toward spies, wounds, and crutches, far from the quiet plan he had made.
the-gates-of-chance:
Van Tassel Sutphen wrote The Gates of Chance as a set of tales of a club man drawn into odd errands by a stranger's card. Twelve tales make up the book.

The first tale starts when a card is thrust into the narrator's hand on a hot March day in New York. Penciled on it: a call at 4020 Madison Avenue at a quarter before eight that night, signed with the name Mr. Esper Indiman. The narrator means to dine at his club, yet the odd card pulls at him. Each tale in the set opens a fresh gate: a red duchess, an opal button, a brass baggage check.
the-golden-fleece-a-romance:
Julian Hawthorne wrote The Golden Fleece. Its subtitle is A Romance. Chapter I opens on a shady veranda. The heat stands at eighty-seven degrees. A lean professor punches down the ashes in his pipe. He scorns talk of sunken continents and lost Atlantises. He tells Trednoke that they live at the bottom of an old sea.

Trednoke listens with calm. He is a man near sixty, tall and massive. He has gray wavy hair, black brows, and a kind face. His bearing marks him as a retired warrior. The text soon names him General Trednoke. Talk of deep time and lost lands fills the opening. With the book's title, it points to a romance of a quest. The prize is an ancient one, argued out first by these two older men.
the-golden-silence: C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote The Golden Silence. Doubleday, Page and Company printed it at Garden City, New York, in 1911. Pictures are by George Brehm. Only front matter is present here. It gives a list of the Williamsons' other books, naming The Lightning Conductor and The Car of Destiny. A picture caption quotes a line of the tale. Allah sends thee a man, it says. He is a strong man, whose brain, heart, and arm are at thy service. No chapter text is present.
the-haunted-hotel-a-mystery-of-modern-ve: Wilkie Collins wrote The Haunted Hotel, subtitled a mystery of modern Venice, in an edition from Chatto & Windus, London, 1879. Collins is dated 1824-1889 on the title page. The contents divide the tale into four parts with twenty-eight chapters and a postscript, the chapters numbered in Roman numerals from I to XXVIII. The pages present go no further than the front matter.
the-hidden-masterpiece:
Honore de Balzac wrote The Hidden Masterpiece, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. Chapter one opens on a cold December morning toward the close of the year 1612, in the Rue des Grands-Augustins in Paris. A poor young man paces before a house, hesitating like a lover, then asks if Maitre Francois Porbus is within.

Told yes, the young man climbs the stair with pauses and doubts, feeling the keen thrill of a young artist nearing a man of genius. Balzac compares that first passion for art to love itself, full of boldness and timidity, sure hope and sure discouragement. The painter Porbus, once favored by Henry IV, works in the atelier above.
the-house-of-the-wolf-a-romance:
Stanley Weyman framed this romance as a translated memoir. A French writer apparently composed it around 1620. He was Anne, Vicomte de Caylus. Anne had been a figure at the court of Henry IV. The introduction sets the adventures in August 1572. Anne and his younger brothers were then little more than boys. Marie and Croisette shared the danger with him. A descendant brought the manuscript to England. That happened after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes.

The chapter headings promise flight, traps, and religious violence. The road leads to Paris. Headings name a priest and a woman. Others promise the Parisian matins and cries against the Huguenots. A night of sorrow gives way to joy in the morning. Weyman admits the memoir adds no fresh light to history. Its value is human interest. An old soldier remembers a boy's crisis. The crisis is the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre.
the-idler-in-france:
Marguerite Gardiner, Countess of Blessington, published this travel volume in 1841. Its first chapter lands in Nismes. She declines to redescribe the route. She notes improvement everywhere instead. People look cleaner than before. An air of business has replaced stagnation. Marseilles and Toulon were always busy cities. Nismes surpasses her raised expectations. Its amphitheatre and the Maison Carrée impress her most. Italy, she judges, has nothing to equal them.

Her reasoning is a traveler's. The Coliseum may be larger than the amphitheatre. Preservation makes the smaller one more interesting. The Maison Carrée stands without a competitor. French monuments also lack the foul surroundings of Italian ones. She then turns to the Hôtel du Midi. Dinner there is excellent. Silk sellers crowd in after it. They carry handkerchiefs, ribands, and stockings made in Nismes. Antiquities and shopping share her pages equally.
the-illustrious-prince:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens this novel aboard the Lusitania. Five hundred and eighty-seven saloon passengers fill the ship. A murmur of regret runs through them. Some use stronger language. The ship has missed the tide. No landing will happen that night. Chapter I is headed Mr. Hamilton Fynes, Urgent. The contents promise affairs of state. A fatal despatch and an inspector named Jacks follow. A figure called Prince Maiyo appears.

Thirty-four chapter headings map the plot. Penelope Morse intervenes and explains. Mr. Coulson is interviewed, outmatched, and indiscreet. A theatre party suffers an interruption. The action swings between East and West. Goodbyes and a cry of banzai close it. Oppenheim builds the book from short, titled episodes. That pattern defined the Edwardian thriller. He helped create the form.
the-inside-story-of-the-peace-conference: Dr. E. J. Dillon published this account with Harper and Brothers in 1920. He dedicated it to C. W. Barron. Conversations on historic occasions linked them, he writes. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The contents move through the conference city first. Signs of the times and the delegates follow. Censorship and secrecy get a chapter. Aims and methods come next. The lesser states and Poland's outlook close the book. The delegates chapter runs nearly sixty pages.
the-keepers-of-the-king-s-peace:
Edgar Wallace published these African tales in 1917. The first opens with Bones, Sanders and Another. At Isongo, a woman of the Isisi loses her husband. A tree falls on him beside the tributary. Wallace's narrator calls the death providential, dryly. The man was an evil beer-drinker. He made magic in the forest and beat his wives. He once set fire to his own house from sheer wickedness. His widows' death dance carries a hint of hilarity.

The story turns on the widow M'lama. Her gifts appear after a great storm. A choking child heals at her hand's touch. A baby in a fit sleeps at her touch. A woodcutter's severed foot is made whole. Ahmet, chief of the government spies, rides three days to test her. He leaves with his dislocated finger straightened. He carries a report to Sanders. Empire, magic, and paperwork collide in Wallace's river world.
the-key-to-peace:
A. Marie Miles wrote this devotional letter-book for her grandson, signed in May 1978. Its text is that great peace have they which love thy law. She begins with his question. What makes a thing right or wrong, he wants to know. Her answer is that the Bible holds the answer. He objects that the Bible is a big book. Where is a certain thing said, he asks. She sets out to guide him to the places.

Her reasoning runs on personal duty. There is no respect of persons with God. God renders to every man according to his deeds. Each soul must know how to be cleared before the great Judge. She shares verses from her own Bible. The psalmist's prayer to be taught the statutes is among them. A grandmother's catechism grows one scripture at a time.
the-knight-of-the-golden-melice-a-histor: John Turvill Adams published this historical romance with Derby and Jackson of New York in 1857. He had written The Lost Hunter before it. The title comes from Winthrop's History of New England. A German motto from Schiller fronts it, on fantasy never growing old. Only the title page and dedication are present here. The romance itself does not appear. Adams dedicates the book to his daughter. He calls it the fruit of their mutual studies and a parent's record of watching her young mind unfold.
the-life-everlasting-a-reality-of-romanc:
Marie Corelli frames her romance with an author prologue on voices in the wilderness. Contents list twenty chapters moving from a heroine opening story through a fairy ship, an angel of a dream, a house of Aselzion, a magic book, and a passage into the light. The prologue cites the Gospels voice crying in the wilderness.

Corelli notes that thousands of such voices have warned or pleaded in vain through history. She asks why she adds one more undesired note to that rejected chorus. Her tale answers through visions, past lives, and a love that claims to outlast death.
the-life-of-marie-antoinette-queen-of-fr:
Charles Duke Yonge published his life of Marie Antoinette in 1876 and built it chiefly on published letters. His preface names two great sources. Arneth collections hold letters among the queen, her mother Maria Teresa, and her brothers Joseph and Leopold, plus reports from the imperial ambassador Mercy d Argenteau at Paris.

A second source, edited by Feuillet de Conches, drew attacks as clever forgery. Yonge concedes a few early letters may be false yet defends most of the set, above all the later letters. Court life at Versailles emerges through family writing rather than gossip alone.
the-little-lady-of-lagunitas-a-franco-ca:
Richard Henry Savage wrote The Little Lady of Lagunitas, subtitled A Franco-Californian Romance. Its long introduction surveys California from the gold rush of 1848 and 1849 onward. Savage describes a state overrun first by free-lance adventurers, then by giant schemers who dominated the legislature, the courts, and public office while robbing Mexican landowners and Native people.

The introduction promises to show how Southern designs on the Golden West failed. Secession leaders hoped to seize California's treasure fields, yet Unionist activity and mistaken policy at Richmond lost them the chance. Against that backdrop of conspiracy and the later silver bonanza era, Savage sets his romance, giving readers history and intrigue woven together from the start.
the-little-lame-prince: Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, writing as Miss Mulock, published The Little Lame Prince in 1874. What is present stops at the title page and contents; the tales themselves do not appear. The contents give the title story ten chapters, then list five more tales: The Invisible Prince, Prince Cherry, The Prince with the Nose, The Frog-Prince, and Clever Alice. That makes the volume a small story collection for children rather than a single tale, though none of the stories can be read in what is present.
the-long-chance:
Peter B. Kyne's The Long Chance, illustrated by Frank Tenny Johnson and dated 1914, opens at sunrise on the Colorado desert. A coyote leaves his den in the tumbled malpais and salutes the dawn. Then he watches seven dark shapes crawl out of the waste. They are three desert rats with a train of four burros: possible breakfast and possible trouble. An illustration caption explains the desert call for help, three fires in a row by night and three columns of smoke by day. Kyne describes the party in close detail.

One man is a Cahuilla Indian in a peaked Mexican straw hat and shoes much too large for him, urging the burros along with a peeled catclaw stick. The novel begins as a slow procession across a waterless kingdom ruled by monotony.
the-lost-prince: Frances Hodgson Burnett's The Lost Prince was published in 1915 with four illustrations by Maurice L. Bower. A title page and contents are all that is present; the novel itself is absent. The thirty-one chapter titles introduce Marco, a boy at No. 7 Philibert Place, his friend the Rat, drills and a secret party, and a kingdom called Samavia. Later titles build toward a discovery: "It is the Lost Prince! It is Ivor!" and a closing chapter naming Marco as the son of Stefan Loristan.
the-man-between-an-international-romance:
Amelia E. Barr subtitled The Man Between an international romance, and its first part carries the motto, O Love Will Venture In! The narrator, Ethel Rawdon, introduces herself by admitting that the thing she knows least about is her own beginning. Life's shaping events, she reflects, seldom arrive with pomp; they steal in unannounced. She had no idea, returning from a stupid entertainment one Saturday night in January 1900, that a new chapter of her life was opening. Ethel is nineteen, at the age when the brook and the river meet.

At her open window she looks over miles of white lights. She whispers that the city is not New York at all but some magical city that will vanish by six in the morning. Barr gives her heroine a dreamy, waking imagination before romance arrives.
the-market-place:
Harold Frederic's The Market-Place opens after a financial battle. Its victor sits alone in a board room with the hurly-burly of his thoughts, master of everything within sight. His triumph is so sweeping that he alone can say whether there will be any mercy at all. Until he speaks, the rout of the vanquished goes on with multiplying ruin. He feels no wish yet to consider when to stop. In the firelight he pictures the faces of his ruined rivals as one composite mask of what he fought and overthrew.

Frederic presents the victor's vision in the harsh terms of his hatred, then grounds the scene. Brandy and glasses were left by dummy directors. A cigar is lit with deliberation, and a wondering laugh breaks the stillness. The novel opens inside the mind of a financier who has just destroyed his enemies.
the-master-of-silence-a-romance:
Irving Bacheller's romance The Master of Silence appeared in New York in 1892, in a series edited by Arthur Stedman. The narrator looks back to his fourteenth year, when his father died suddenly. A stepmother and a guardian held his property and sent him from London to Liverpool. There he was apprenticed to Valentine, King & Co., cotton importers, as an errand boy known by the firm as a pair of legs.

Lonely in modest lodgings near the Mersey, the boy spends his evenings over story books. One stormy night a loud rap sounds at his door, with no voice answering. He opens it to find a bent old man standing silent in the hallway, dripping wet. The stranger enters and faces him without speaking a word. Bacheller opens his tale with a mystery delivered, literally, in silence.
the-merchant-of-venice: Only an editor's note is present for this record, and it does not concern The Merchant of Venice at all. The note, signed by Michael S. Hart, discusses old printers' spelling substitutions, such as u for v, and quotes the opening lines of Hamlet as its example. It explains that the file it introduces is actually Shakespeare's First Part of Henry the Sixth, not the play this record names. No scene, speech, or character list from The Merchant of Venice appears here.
the-money-moon-a-romance:
Jeffery Farnol's romance The Money Moon, published in 1911 with a frontispiece by A. I. Keller, is present here only in title page, dedication, and the start of its contents. No chapter text appears. Farnol is billed as author of The Broad Highway, and the dedication, dated February 10, 1910, goes to Jennifer, whose faith and generosity he praises.

Contents visible here run through Chapter VI. George Bellew, the hero named in the headings, seeks counsel of his valet in Chapter II. A haycart and a fighting waggoner follow, and Small Porges, looking for a fortune for another, finds an uncle for himself instead. Bellew reaches Arcadia in Chapter V.
the-monk-a-romance:
M. G. Lewis's romance The Monk opens with a Latin epigraph from Horace, Englished on the page as dreams, magic terrors, spells, witches, and ghosts who rove at midnight. A contents list names a preface and twelve chapters, numbered without titles. Lewis is styled Esquire and Member of Parliament on the title page.

The preface is a verse imitation of Horace addressed to the book itself. Lewis pictures his vain, ill-judging volume casting wishful looks toward Paternoster Row, where reputations are won and lost. The book scorns lock and key and longs to sit bound and gilt in the windows of Stockdale, Hookham, or Debrett. It is warned that the road to publication is one no book returns from.
the-moon-and-sixpence:
W. Somerset Maugham's novel The Moon and Sixpence is present here only as a title page and a bare table of contents, so no narrative appears. Maugham is billed as the author of Of Human Bondage. The contents list forty chapters, numbered in Roman numerals from I to XL, with no chapter titles given.

Those forty numbered headings are the whole of what these pages show. Nothing in them names characters, places, or events, and no opening line of the novel is included. Readers meet only the book's frame: its title, its author's name and earlier success, and the promise of a long, evenly divided story told across forty short chapters.
the-mother-s-recompense-volume-1-a-seque:
Grace Aguilar's The Mother's Recompense, a sequel to Home Influence, appears in volume 1 of a two-volume Leipzig printing by Bernhard Tauchnitz, dated 1859. A preface, written by the author's mother, explains the book's history. Both Home Influence and its sequel were drafted early in 1836, when Aguilar was little above nineteen, and the plan saw little later alteration.

Her mother describes a daughter who learned to write almost as soon as she could read, and who left many works in manuscript, in prose and verse. A long, fatal illness kept Aguilar from revising this sequel for the press, and she never heard the praise Home Influence received. The preface asks readers to remember that disadvantage as they judge the volume.
the-mother-s-recompense-volume-2-a-seque:
Volume 2 of Grace Aguilar's The Mother's Recompense, the sequel to Home Influence, continues the two-volume Leipzig printing by Bernhard Tauchnitz dated 1859. Chapter I opens in a daughter's room one afternoon. Emmeline Hamilton sits drawing and embroidering with her friends, Lady Florence and Lady Emily Lyle, plus the usually quiet Ellen.

Mrs. Hamilton enters laughing and asks which of the merry party will sober down enough to help with a work of charity. A case of extreme distress has reached her, and clothing, more than money, is what the sufferers need. Every voice cries To me, and the girls crowd round her, eager for particulars. Even Ellen, who once pleaded no time for work, is drawn in by the appeal.
the-obstacle-race: Ethel M. Dell published the novel The Obstacle Race in 1921 and dedicated it to her dear half-sister Mary. A verse from First Corinthians, "So run, that ye may obtain," stands at the front with a short poem about running the race with a high heart. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. Part One lists chapters named Sacrifice, Magic, Brother Dick, The Great Man, and The Intruder.
the-pleasures-of-ignorance: Robert Lynd's The Pleasures of Ignorance was published by Grant Richards Ltd. at London in 1921 and dedicated to James Winder Good. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the essays themselves are absent. Fifteen essays are listed, opening with the title piece. They move through the herring fleet, the betting man, insects, and cats. Later entries cover May and June, New Year prophecies, horse-racing, and why we hate insects. Others treat virtue, feeling gay, life in the train, and the most curious animal.
the-portland-peerage-romance: Charles J. Archard's The Portland Peerage Romance was published by Greening and Co. at London in 1907. Here only the publisher's list and the title page appear, so the novel itself is absent. The list, headed Greening's New Novels, advertises other titles at six shillings. It names The Tangled Skein by the Baroness Orczy in its eighteenth thousand. The Mascotte of Park Lane by Lucas Cleeve is in a third edition, and The Dupe by Gerald Biss in a second. Nothing beyond the title page speaks for Archard's own story.
the-post-office:
Rabindranath Tagore's play The Post Office was translated from Bengali by Devabrata Mukherjee and published by the Macmillan Company at New York in 1914. The cast lists Madhav, his adopted child Amal, and Sudha, a little flower girl. It also lists a doctor, a dairyman, a watchman, a gaffer, a bullying village headman, the King's Herald, and the Royal Physician. The whole action turns on the sick child and the people who pass his window.

Act I opens in Madhav's house. Madhav tells the doctor that before Amal came, nothing mattered and he felt free. Now his heart is filled with the boy, and the home will be no home when he leaves. The physician answers in riddles from the medical scriptures, warning that bile or palsy, cold or gout spring all alike. The exchange sets the play's quiet dread beside Madhav's new-found love.
the-precipice:
Ivan Goncharov's novel The Precipice, whose Russian title is Obryv, reaches English readers here in a condensed translation by an unnamed translator. A preface places Goncharov, who lived from 1812 to 1891, in the circle around the journal Sovremmenik. Turgenev, Dostoevsky, and Tolstoy belonged to that circle. The preface grants that Goncharov lacked their marked genius. His strength lay in steady character drawing, calm amid the problems that distracted other minds.

The preface retells Tolstoy's teasing memory of Goncharov, who held that the lives of wealthy, dissatisfied people held endless matter for fiction. It recalls Oblomov, his great success, a lazy, gentle man of thirty-two. In the present novel the type returns as Raisky, a man who seems born tired. Raisky has intelligence, artistic gifts, charm, and kindliness, yet achieves nothing in work or love. Mark Volokov, a wolfish outlaw who quotes Proudhon, calls him only half a man.
the-price: Francis Lynde's novel The Price was published at New York by Grosset and Dunlap under a 1911 copyright held by Charles Scribner's Sons. Lynde is named as author of The Taming of Red Butte Western. A long dedication inscribes the book to Lathrop Brockway Bullene, sole friend of the author's boyhood. It recalls the youthful seed-time that led to the book's later conclusions. The pages shown end with the first contents entries: At Chaudière's, Spindrift, The Right of Might, and Io Triumphe! The novel itself is not shown.
the-rape-of-lucrece:
William Shakespeare dedicates his long poem to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton, in a letter professing devoted service. A prose argument then summarizes the Roman story before the verse begins, starting with Tarquin the Proud seizing the kingdom after murder.

At the siege of Ardea, officers praise their wives, and Collatinus wins the contest when his wife Lucretia alone is found spinning late at night among her maids. Sextus Tarquinius, inflamed by her beauty, returns secretly to her house at Collatium as a guest. The argument lays out the crime to come, so the poem can dwell on character, rhetoric, and grief.
the-rise-and-progress-of-palaeontology-e:
Thomas Henry Huxley traces fossil study as the second essay in a volume on science and Hebrew tradition. Palaeontology began, he argues, with the first person who found a shell or bone bedded in gravel or rock and wondered how it came there.

Xenophanes, five centuries before the Christian era, already reasoned from fossils in the quarries of Syracuse, and poets, historians, and geographers of antiquity kept noticing them. Only in the last two centuries, Huxley says, was their nature treated exhaustively. The essay gives general readers a brisk history of how fossils became evidence.
the-road-to-providence:
Maria Thompson Daviess opens in a Providence kitchen. Mother Mayberry teaches biscuit-making with a light hand there. Her son calls from the barn in alarm meanwhile. Spangles the hen is off the nest again. Contents promise two Doctors Mayberry at the head. A singer lady with a bread-bowl follows in the list. A peony girl, a raven, and a wedding day come next.

Mother answers from the kitchen door with doughy hands. She asks Tom to persuade the hen himself first. Village medicine and home cooking share one household voice. Daviess builds her small-town romance on such errands. Care shows itself through food and fussing there. A nest on Providence Nob waits in the later headings.
the-secrets-of-the-german-war-office:
Dr. Armgaard Karl Graves wrote The Secrets of the German War Office with Edward Lyell Fox collaborating. A publishers' foreword is dated August 7, 1914. Europe had just been precipitated into general war, the publishers note. Graves's completed manuscript had been in their hands since June 1. His qualifications need no further comment, they claim.

Chapter one is called How I Became a Secret Agent. It opens in the House of Commons on June 12, 1913. Mr. King, a Liberal member from Somerset, made a sensation there. He demanded the secrets of the strange case of Armgaard Karl Graves, German spy. Graves had supposedly been serving a sentence in a Scotch prison. He amazed the English press by announcing his presence in New York City. King asked when and why he had been released.
the-shadow-of-a-crime-a-cumbrian-romance: Hall Caine called The Shadow of a Crime a Cumbrian romance. His title page carries the date 1885, and a New York Hurst and Company imprint dated 1895. Caine also wrote The Manxman and The Deemster. He dedicated the novel to his fellow-journalist John Lovell. The pages shown give the dedication and the start of the contents only. Robbie's redemption appears in chapter eight. No narrative text follows.
the-shield-of-silence:
Harriet T. Comstock wrote The Shield of Silence, copyrighted by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1921. Grosset and Dunlap issued this New York edition. George Loughridge drew the frontispiece. Its caption shows Joan rising from a self-appointed task, throbbing with hate toward Thornton. Pity then replaces the hate, the caption says. Comstock dedicated the book to her son Philip S. Comstock.

The novel's opening begins with an invitation to agree at once. We are all on the Wheel, the narrator declares. The difference lies in our ability to cling, the sentence continues, and there the portion shown breaks off. Even that fragment sets the book's terms. Fate's wheel carries every character, and holding on is the measure of each, the opening implies.
the-sky-line-of-spruce:
Edison Marshall published The Sky Line of Spruce in 1922. Marshall also wrote The Voice of the Pack and The Snowshoe Trail. The contents divide the novel into three parts. They are The Wakening, The Wolf-Man, and The Taming. A frontispiece shows a man leaning forward, aware of nothing but a forthcoming crisis.

Part one opens with a convict road gang near Walla Walla. Their work had taken them miles from the town's outskirts, Marshall writes. Fields green with growing barley surround them. Western meadow larks sing exuberantly in the fresh spring air. The convicts are in a genial mood, easily moved to wide grins. An expert might recognize purely criminal types among them, Marshall says. To a layman they suggest merely unskilled laborers, he adds.
the-sleeping-car-a-farce:
William D. Howells's The Sleeping Car, a farce, was transcribed from the 1883 James R. Osgood and Company edition. Its single scene fills one side of a sleeping-car on the Boston and Albany Road. The porter is making up berths, the stage directions say. A young mother, Mrs. Agnes Roberts, sits facing her aunt Mary. A baby sleeps on the seat beside her.

Mrs. Roberts asks whether her aunt always takes down her back hair. Aunt Mary answers that she never does, at least not since a fright. She bought her hair from Madame Pierrot, she explains. One night she tucked the switch away in her pocket and slept sweetly. Near midnight she saw something long and black crawl off her bed. She shrieked that a snake was aboard, she recalls. The whole car erupted before she grabbed the switch back unseen.
the-squire-of-sandal-side-a-pastoral-rom: Amelia E. Barr, author of Jan Vedder's Wife and A Daughter of Fife, published this pastoral romance in New York in 1886. The pages present here hold the title page and a contents list. The eleven chapters run from Seat-Sandal and the sheep-shearing onward. They pass through wooing and wedding to the new squire. The opening heading of chapter one follows, with its Shakespeare motto. The romance itself does not appear.
the-story-of-creation-as-told-by-theolog:
T. S. Ackland sets theology and science side by side. He was once a fellow of Clare College, Cambridge. He served as vicar of Wold Newton in Yorkshire. His five chapters treat the difficulties raised by geology, astronomy, and physiology. His first chapter states the case. The Bible's history of creation is no small extra. It is the foundation of revelation. It sets out man's relation to God his Maker. It also sets out his relation to the world formed for his home.

Ackland grants the apparent conflict honestly. Geology shows rock layers many miles thick. Plants and animals fill them in fixed order. They could hardly have lived and died within six ordinary days. Astronomy points the same way. Changes in the heavens take ages. His later chapters argue that science can help interpretation rather than destroy it.
the-story-of-the-9th-king-s-in-france:
Enos Herbert Glynne Roberts wrote this history of the 9th King's in France. The Northern Publishing Company published it at Liverpool in 1922. Its chapters cover the battalion's service under three divisions. They are the 1st, the 55th, and the 57th. An appendix lists decorations. Chapter one reaches back before the war, to the volunteer movement that followed 1859.

Liverpool men of the newspaper and printing trades, Roberts explains, wanted a regiment of their own, and a Town Hall meeting carried the scheme forward. Sanction was obtained. On February 21, 1861, the new unit swore its oath at St. George's Hall. It took the name 80th Lancashire Rifle Volunteers. Renumbering followed in time. It became the 6th Volunteer Battalion of the King's Liverpool Regiment.
the-tale-of-terror-a-study-of-the-gothic: Edith Birkhead, a lecturer in English literature at the University of Bristol, published The Tale of Terror with Constable in 1921 as a study of the Gothic romance. This record presents her title page and detailed contents alone, so her arguments appear only as chapter summaries. Those summaries trace fear in myths and ballads, then move through Walpole's Castle of Otranto, Clara Reeve, and Mrs. Radcliffe's novels of suspense. Readers can map the whole study from the contents, yet Birkhead's own prose remains beyond the pages given.
the-tapestry-room-a-child-s-romance: Mrs. Molesworth wrote The Tapestry Room, a child's romance illustrated by Walter Crane and issued by Macmillan in an 1899 printing, though her dedication letter is dated October 1879. This record gives the front matter and the first contents entries only. Those entries name Mademoiselle Jean, Prince Chéri, and a moonlight night as the opening chapters. The dedication honors the young Crown Prince of Italy as one of her kindest readers. Molesworth's tapestry-room adventures themselves begin beyond the pages shown here.
the-vanishing-man-a-detective-romance:
R. Austin Freeman subtitled The Vanishing Man a detective romance when it appeared in 1911, dedicating the volume to a friend named only by initials. Chapter one introduces John Thorndyke through his lectures at St. Margaret's Hospital. The school, the narrator says, was lucky in its teacher of medical jurisprudence, a subject often handed to men fit for nothing else.

Thorndyke is instead an enthusiast of profound learning and great reputation. Contents pages promise an eavesdropper, legal complications, a contested will, a museum idyll, the probate court, and circumstantial evidence. Later chapters weigh the clues, sail on a voyage of discovery, and end the case. Freeman's forensic method drives the romance from the lecture room outward.
the-voice:
Margaret Deland sets The Voice among her Old Chester characters, opening with two doctors talking in a carriage. William King asks Dr. Lavendar to call at the old Grays house on the Perryville pike, now taken by a man named Roberts. Dr. Lavendar already knows the household: Roberts is an Irvingite from Lower Ripple on the Ohio, with a daughter, Philippa.

King calls the father a donkey over his tongues and his voice, meaning gifts of inspired speech in the Irvingite faith. Dr. Lavendar sobers and defends the man. Philippa, meanwhile, is praised as sweet-tempered, sensible, and funny, an old-fashioned girl drawn to the Perryville parson. Deland builds the conflict from belief, family, and village opinion before Roberts himself appears.
the-wanderer-s-necklace:
H. Rider Haggard first published The Wanderer's Necklace in 1914, offering the tale to Sir Edgar Vincent in memory of shared wanderings oversea. An editor's note then explains the strange frame: the editor has recovered knowledge of a former life of his own. That life ended early in the ninth century, and the Byzantine Empress Irene plays a part in it.

In that life his name was Olaf, later Michael after baptism. Memories return as separate scenes rather than a continuous narrative, so the journey from Aar in Jutland to Constantinople is missing entirely. Only the most important events, the editor says, burned themselves into his subconscious memory. He signs himself simply the Editor, hiding his present identity.
the-way-of-peace:
James Allen, author of As a Man Thinketh, gathers seven spiritual essays in The Way of Peace. Their titles move from the power of meditation through the two masters, self and truth, to spiritual power, selfless love, and entering into the infinite. A closing essay promises the realisation of perfect peace.

The first essay calls meditation the pathway to divinity, a mystic ladder from earth to heaven and from pain to peace. Every saint has climbed it, Allen writes, and every weary pilgrim must plant his feet on its golden rounds. What a person dwells on in thought, he argues, becomes incorporated into the self: pure meditation makes purity, and selfish meditation makes debasement. Character follows attention.
the-way-to-peace:
Margaret Deland dedicates The Way to Peace to Lorin Deland, dating the dedication at Kennebunkport, Maine, on August 12, 1910. Chapter one climbs a steep road above a covered bridge a little after five in the morning. Athalia Hall stops for breath and looks back over dawn air full of wood and pasture scents, while night still hangs like gauze in the valley.

Athalia is thirty-four but looks girlish, with forget-me-not eyes and an eager, unhumorous intensity. Her older husband plods behind, scholarly and mild, yet showing singular tenacity of purpose. She hates rest and declares the view will repay the climb. He breaks her a birch walking stick as the sun strengthens on the road.
the-winds-of-chance:
Rex Beach, author of The Spoilers and The Iron Trail, opens The Winds of Chance on the main street of Dyea. Mr. Lucky Broad works a shell game from a folding table among the stumps, paying out a crisp ten-dollar bill with an ostentatious flourish. His stock is three worn walnut shells and a pellet the size of a pill, and his patter never stops.

Broad proclaims that the gentleman wins and the gambler loses, calling his shells three tiny tepees with a little black medicine-man inside. He made his money packing grub to Linderman, he says, and easy come means easy go. A bland, blue-eyed newcomer named Olaf joins the circle and gets the invitation to try Danish dice. The gold-rush street supplies the crowd and the mark.
the-works-of-horace:
C. Smart translated The Works of Horace literally into English prose in the Handy Literal Translations series. Theodore Alois Buckley revised this new edition. Smart had been a fellow of Pembroke College, Cambridge. The first book of the Odes opens the volume. Ode one is addressed to Maecenas, Horace's patron. Horace calls him both protection and beloved honor.

The ode surveys what different men desire. Some chase Olympic chariot glory or political office. Farmers prize their fields, while merchants fear the sea yet sail again. Horace sets these restless ambitions against the poet's quieter calling. Students get a close prose rendering meant to follow the Latin line by line.
the-world-of-ice:
Robert Michael Ballantyne's The World of Ice, dated 1893, follows the whaling cruise of the Dolphin. Its subtitle promises the crew's adventures in the polar regions. Ballantyne's preface is deliberately brief. He hopes simply that readers gain profit and amusement. Chapter one introduces the crew and the hero's early life at sea. A pirate fight and a lashed helm are promised.

Ballantyne also wrote The Coral Island and The Gorilla-Hunters. His sea stories taught geography through adventure. Arctic ice, whaling danger, and youthful courage fill this tale. Chapter summaries in the contents act as teasers. Boys of his era devoured such polar adventures eagerly.
the-yates-pride-a-romance:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman opens The Yates Pride in the village of Wellwood. Miss Eudora Yates's old colonial mansion faces a perky modern house. Mrs. Joseph Glynn lives there with her daughter Ethel and sister Julia. Three visiting ladies fill the Glynn sitting-room with talk one afternoon. Their voices, Freeman writes, shrill like a flock of sparrows. Flowering plants crowd every window of the room.

Mrs. Bates praises the plants yet wonders how anyone sees outside. Ivy climbs over pictures, and the mantel cascades with greenery. Freeman sets old-family pride against newer village society. Gossip in a plant-filled parlor launches the romance. Small-town observation carries her quiet, sharp storytelling.
through-the-eye-of-the-needle-a-romance:
William Dean Howells introduced his 1907 romance with an account of Aristides Homos, an emissary of the Altrurian Commonwealth. Homos visited the United States through summer 1893 and the following winter. He stayed at a mountain resort hotel, visited Chicago's Columbian Exhibition, and wrote letters home from New York.

Howells warns that Homos judges competitive civilizations through Altrurian social beliefs, living for each other rather than upon each other. He cannot fully credit American charity practised beside denial of Christian spirit. Readers get a utopian visitor's letters used to criticise American wealth, giving, and self-satisfaction.
tongues-of-conscience: Robert Hichens first published Tongues of Conscience in 1900, reprinted at Freeport, New York in 1971 in a short story index reprint series. A contents page lists Sea Change in two parts, The Rainbow and The Grave, beginning on pages one and fifty-one. A second piece, William Foster, starts at page one hundred nine. The title and contents pages are what is on these pages, giving the collection's shape and its reprint history.
towards-the-great-peace:
Ralph Adams Cram, Litt.D. and LL.D., published his lectures in 1922, opening with Bishop Hacket's prayer for a great peace. Cram glosses it as replacing private-minded selfishness with public souls and a kingdom of righteousness. Daily offices, not great engines of power, accomplish that kingdom, he says.

Cram admits he strove for a generous heart even while condemning errors that led to the Great War. Consciousness of sin and repentance must precede amendment, he argues, and he apologises in advance for failures of temper. Readers get postwar lectures seeking peace through moral renewal rather than machinery.
treachery-in-outer-space: Carey Rockwell's Treachery in Outer Space belongs to the Tom Corbett Space Cadet stories, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1954. Willy Ley served as technical adviser, and Louis Glanzman drew the illustrations. The front matter lists seven companion adventures, from Stand By for Mars to The Robot Rocket. Only the series page, title page, and copyright page are present here, so the story itself does not appear. A note records that research found no evidence of a required copyright renewal.
trevelyan-garibaldi-defence:
Trevelyan opened his Garibaldi trilogy with the Defence of the Roman Republic in 1907. Rome in 1849 stands besieged by French troops sent to crush it. Garibaldi leads the young republic's brave, doomed stand on its walls.

Trevelyan writes as an English lover of Italian liberty and its heroes. Mazzini's dream, Garibaldi's raids, and the city's fall fill his pages. He walked the ground and read the letters of men who fought. The romantic age of nation-making glows at its noblest in his tale. Few English books did more to make Garibaldi a household hero.
true-stories-of-crime-from-the-district-: Arthur Train, formerly district attorney of New York County, published True Stories of Crime in 1908. The contents list eleven cases, from The Woman in the Case to A Case of Circumstantial Evidence. Other titles promise five hundred million dollars, a lost Stradivarius, wire-tappers, and the Franklin Syndicate. The illustrations list shows forged orders, practice signatures, and a forged will page. Only the contents and illustration list are present here, so the case narratives themselves do not appear.
true-to-himself-or-roger-strong-s-strugg:
Edward Stratemeyer's True to Himself, dated at Newark on April 15, 1900, forms the third volume of his Ship and Shore Series. His preface introduces Roger Strong, a country lad, and Roger's sister Kate. The story first ran as a serial for boys and girls.

An unhappy chain of events throws the pair on their own resources, with their father in prison on a serious charge. Neighbors shun them, and jeers test Roger's temper. The preface promises he will stay true to himself, make his place in the world, and triumph over those who ruined his parents. Chapter one opens with trouble in an orchard and a shout at Duncan Woodward.
un-doc-declaration-of-principles-on-tole:
The Declaration of Principles on Tolerance was adopted by UNESCO's General Conference at Paris on 16 November 1995. That year was the United Nations Year for Tolerance. Hate crimes, racism, and attacks on minorities were rising in many lands. The date also marked fifty years since UNESCO's own founding.

Tolerance, the text says, is respect for the rich range of human cultures and ways. It is a duty in morals, politics, and law alike. It never means putting up with injustice. States must give fair laws and a fair share of jobs and schooling to all. Teaching is named the best guard against hate. The text sets 16 November as a yearly world day for tolerance.
united-states-declaration-of-independenc:
The Declaration of Independence states the case of the American colonies for breaking with Britain. When one people must cut the ties that bound it to another, respect for the views of mankind calls on them to give their reasons. The text then sets out its core claim. All men are created equal, with rights that cannot be taken away. Among them stand life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.

Governments, the text argues, draw their just powers from the consent of the governed. When a government turns against the ends it exists to serve, the people may change or end it. They may build a new one. The writers grant that prudence warns against change for light causes. People tend to endure wrongs while they can. Yet a long train of abuses proves a design to rule by force, and then change becomes a duty.
us-declaration-of-independence:
Adopted by the Continental Congress in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776, the Declaration announced that thirteen American colonies were breaking away from Britain for good. Thomas Jefferson was its main writer. The signers acted in the name of the united colonies and addressed their case to King George III and to the wider world.

Early lines state that all men are created equal and hold rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness that no government should take away. A long list of complaints against the king follows, offered as proof the break was justified. Short as it is, the text became the founding statement of the United States.
virgie-s-inheritance:
Mrs. Georgie Sheldon, author of Nora, Trixy, and Helen's Victory, wrote Virgie's Inheritance, copyrighted by Street and Smith in 1887, 1888, and 1891. Chapter one introduces the heroine and a benighted traveller, and opens in a small, cozy room where a dying man sits by a blazing fire. He tells his daughter Virgie that he must give up the race: his strength fails fast, and cough, trembling limbs, and hard breathing warn him to set his house in order.

Sheldon paints him with care. Though a little over fifty, he looks old: silver-white hair, a colorless, haggard face, sunken eyes, and a frame thinned by the disease that eats him. He shivers over the blaze as if chilled to the marrow. The room, with its bright cheap carpet and embroidered cloth, speaks of care kept up in poverty. A father's deathbed charge and a hidden inheritance drive the tale from here.
warlock-o-glenwarlock-a-homely-romance: George MacDonald, author of Annals of a Quiet Neighborhood, wrote Warlock o' Glenwarlock, a homely romance. Pages present here hold the title page and a contents list, so the story itself is not shown. The frontispiece shows Cosmo leading a lady to the stable. Contents name Castle Warlock, a kitchen, and a drawing room. Grannie's cottage and her ghost story, a storm-guest, and a watchmaker follow. College days, a lost-and-found, and a knight who spoke the truth come later.
waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since:
Sir Walter Scott's Waverley, or 'Tis Sixty Years Since, stands here with the introduction he wrote for the edition of 1829. The plan of that edition, he says, leads him to set down the incidents on which the novel rests. They had reached the public before. His friend William Erskine told them in a review of the Tales of My Landlord, in the Quarterly Review in 1817, drawn from the author's own information.

Scott names the tale's hinge in that introduction: the mutual protection that Waverley and Talbot afford each other across the lines of the 1745 rising. Each man, in turn, stands between the other and death. This record gives the introduction, notes, and a glossary with the novel. Other records of Waverley in this library carry publishers' notes or Andrew Lang's apparatus instead.
weir-of-hermiston-an-unfinished-romance:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Weir of Hermiston, an unfinished romance, appears here in the fine-paper edition of Chatto and Windus at London in 1913. Stevenson addressed the book to his wife in a poem of thanks. Who sharpened his sword, fanned the drowsy coal, and held his target higher, he asks. Who was chary of praise and prodigal of counsel, if not she?

An introductory chapter opens at the wild far end of a moorland parish, out of sight of any house. A cairn stands there among the heather. A little east of it, down the brae, a monument bears verses half defaced. There Claverhouse shot the Praying Weaver of Balweary. The chisel of Old Mortality has worked on that stone. From Covenanting graves the tale moves to the Weirs, a hanging judge and his son, in the book Stevenson left broken off at his death.
westminster-sermons-with-a-preface:
Charles Kingsley gave the sermons in Westminster Sermons at Westminster Abbey and at chapels royal. Macmillan printed the book in London in 1881. Kingsley adds a paper he read at Sion College in 1871. That paper sets out the thought behind the whole set.

Kingsley argues that facts from nature and from the human heart do not clash with church teaching. He draws a line between natural religion and natural theology, which he defines as what can be learned about God himself. He praises Bishop Butler and his famed book on the same theme. Readers get Victorian sermons that try to hold faith and science in one frame.
who-cares-a-story-of-adolescence: Cosmo Hamilton's Who Cares? opens with a playful exchange in place of a preface, and the pages here end before the tale starts. A voice asks if the new novel is about a boy and a girl, and if they marry. The answers stay coy: it is a love story, and love stories are happy if the love is true. Hamilton gave the book to his young brother Arthur. The contents begin with part one, named Spring in the World.
with-our-soldiers-in-france: The front pages here give the title page, dedication, and contents for Sherwood Eddy's With Our Soldiers in France, printed in 1917, with no chapters shown. Eddy gives the book to the real heroes of the war: mothers who gave sons and wives who gave husbands. The contents open at the front and with General Pershing's force. A day in the bull ring and life in a base camp follow. Religion at the front gets its own chapter. A frontispiece shows the American Y.M.C.A. headquarters in Paris.
without-prejudice: I. Zangwill gathered these essays from his magazine work of the prior four or five years. His note says most pieces ran monthly in the Pall Mall Magazine under this same title. Pages present here hold that note and a contents list, but no essay text. The list groups pieces as Gossips and Fantasies. Titles cover art in England, Verlaine, general elections, gambling, and critics. The essays themselves do not appear in these pages.
witness-for-the-defence: A. E. W. Mason published this novel in 1914. Pages present here give a contents list covering twenty chapters, but no chapter text. The titles introduce Henry Thresk, scenes at Bignor Hill and in Bombay, and a character named Jane Repton. Later titles promise a photograph, a rifle, testimony in court, and trouble for a Mr. Hazlewood. The courtroom and India both seem central, judging by the titles alone. The story itself does not begin in these pages.
woman-and-the-new-race: Margaret Sanger published this book in New York in 1920, with a preface by Havelock Ellis. Pages present here hold the title page, her dedication to her mother of eleven children, and a chapter list. No chapter text appears. The titles argue that large families can be a harm, ask when a woman should avoid having children, and weigh continence against contraceptives and abortion. The list alone shows a direct birth control argument.
woman-s-endurance:
A chaplain signing himself A. D. L. kept this diary in the Bethulie concentration camp in 1901. It was printed in Cape Town in 1904. His preface praises South African women as heroines of the late war. Sale proceeds went to support the orphanage at Bethulie. The diary form promises a day-by-day witness record.

His introduction tells how the work began. Fresh from theology study at Stellenbosch and a trip to Europe, he got a telegram inviting him to serve as camp chaplain. He accepted a post in the Orange River Colony. Readers get faith, grief, and camp life from inside.
women-of-modern-france: Hugo P. Thieme, of the University of Michigan, wrote this volume on French women for a series covering women in all ages and countries. It was copyrighted in 1907 and 1908. Pages present here hold the title page and a chapter list, but no chapter text. The chapters move from women in politics and family life to the age of Louis XIV. Named women include Madame de Sevigne, Madame de La Fayette, and salon leaders such as Madame Geoffrin.
work-a-story-of-experience: Louisa May Alcott wrote this novel about a woman earning her living, shown here in a 1901 Boston edition. Pages present here hold the title page, her dedication to her mother, and a chapter list. No chapter text appears. The chapter titles follow Christie through work as servant, actress, governess, companion, and seamstress. Later titles promise despair, a new start, and a chapter called At Forty. The list alone maps a full working life.
world-s-best-histories-volume-7-france:
M. Guizot and Madame Guizot de Witt wrote this history of France, shown here in volume seven of eight. The contents cover the Consulate, Napoleon's glory, and the Russian campaign. Chapter seven opens after ten hard years. France had toppled a monarchy, tried a republic, and lived through the Terror. The Directory proved weak and muddled, the chapter says.

France still sought a free and steady government, the account continues. Napoleon fills this volume, from consul to emperor to divorce and disaster in Russia. Readers get a clear narrative of empire building and overreach. National pride and hard lessons sit side by side.
